A short textbook with computed figures

Fundamental Ideas from First Principles

Eighteen ideas worth thinking about for years, each one an equation that several fields discovered on their own

Preface

Claude wrote this book at Jai Sharma's direction in October 2026. Separate Claude agents audited its mathematics and checked its citations, and every figure computes its idea in the page.

This book is about one kind of idea: a single equation that physics, statistics, machine learning, control, economics, or pure mathematics found independently and named differently. Each name comes with tools the other fields lacked, so an idea with many names repays years of study. Diffusion is the model case. It generates images, it samples actions for reinforcement learning, and it simulates physical systems, and the same equation sits under all three.

Chapter 1 treats diffusion itself. Chapters 2 to 18 take one idea each, in an order where every chapter uses the ones before it, and the early chapters reach furthest into research on generative models and reinforcement learning. Every chapter has the same parts, in the order a seminal paper uses: the motivation (a concrete scene and the problem that forced the idea), the intuition (the smallest example worked with numbers, then the idea in one sentence and one computed picture), the statement, a derivation, figures, four ways to see the idea joined by short derivations, where it breaks and what is open, exercises, derivations to redo from a blank page, and notes for further reading. A line under each chapter's opening names the earlier chapters and the prerequisites it uses, and Appendix A states those prerequisites.

Every figure computes its idea in the page on a small problem, and the numbers in its caption come from that computation at the settings the caption names. The figure under "Where it breaks" computes the failure itself. The exercises come from a practice deck: each states a problem with numbers, and its answer, checked by a short computation, is folded under it. The derivations after the exercises each ask for a result of the chapter from a blank page, with a solution folded under it.

Introduction: ideas with many names

Diffusion passes three tests. It fits on a napkin: add noise with \(dx = g\,dW\), then run it backward with the score. Several fields found it on their own. Physicists call it Brownian motion and the heat equation, statisticians know its denoising step as Tweedie's formula, finance knows it as Black-Scholes, and machine learning calls it a diffusion model. Each name brings a tool the others lacked: the heat equation brings Fourier analysis, Tweedie brings empirical Bayes, and Langevin brings sampling.

The test can be applied to any idea: count the fields that have their own name for it. An idea with one name is a technique. An idea with five names is a place to stay for years, because every field that named it has already built tools to borrow. The table counts names for the eighteen ideas of this book.

Fields and ideas

Optimization and measure theory are fields, and each takes years. The kind of idea this book is about is one equation inside a field. Optimization's is convex duality: a convex function is described as well by its tangent lines as by its points. Chapter 2 applies it to \(\log \mathbb E[e^{f}]\) and KL. Measure theory's is the change of measure: an expectation under one distribution rewritten under another with a density, which on paths is Girsanov's theorem (Chapter 3). Most of measure theory exists to make statements like these two precise, so the statements come first here and the formalism is picked up when a proof needs it.

Chapter 1

Diffusion

Physics, statistics, and generative modeling

Add noise to data until nothing is left, and the density spreads by the heat equation. The score \(\nabla \log p_t\), the direction in which the noisy density rises, is all it takes to run the process backward, and it equals a denoiser, so it can be learned from data.

Uses Appendix A.1 and A.4.

1.1Motivation

Suppose you have the 60,000 handwritten digits of MNIST, each a 28 by 28 grid of gray levels, and you want a new digit that none of the writers drew. Each image is a list of 784 numbers, so the dataset is a cloud of 60,000 points in 784-dimensional space, and a new digit is one more draw from whatever distribution produced the cloud. But how do you draw from a distribution you know only through its examples?

The direct route is to write the density down and sample from it, and that is hopeless in high dimension, because the normalizing constant is an integral over every possible image. Earlier approaches paid to avoid it: adversarial networks trained a sampler against a discriminator and were unstable, and normalizing flows restricted their architectures to keep the density tractable.

Diffusion takes a detour through noise. Put a drop of ink in a glass of still water and wait: the ink spreads until the glass is an even pale blue, and nothing in the final glass says where the drop went in. Adding noise to an image does the same to its pixels. Loosely, the plan has three steps. First, add noise to every training image until each one looks like static, which is easy. Second, train a network to undo one small step of that noise. Third, start from fresh static and undo the steps one at a time until a digit appears. But how can a network learn to take noise out? The network needs the score \(\nabla \log p\), the direction in which the density of noisy images rises fastest. The score does not depend on the normalizing constant, it can be learned by regression on noisy copies of the data, and it is enough to run noise backward into data.

PAPERA document that moved capital

The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities

Price an option by the hedge that replicates it, and the price stops depending on anyone's appetite for risk.

Fischer Black and Myron Scholes, 1973 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Traders adopted the formula almost at once, the Chicago Board Options Exchange opened the same year, and the formula became the basis of the listed-options and derivatives markets.

The link to this chapter: a change to log-price and rescaled time turns the paper's pricing equation into what it calls "the heat-transfer equation of physics" (p. 644, its equation 10), which is (1.1) here, whose solution is the heat kernel. The stock's expected return drops out of the price, which Chapter 3 reads as a change of measure.

1.2Intuition

Start with the smallest dataset that has a shape: two numbers, \(-1\) and \(+1\), each drawn half the time. Blur it by replacing each draw \(x_0\) with \(x_0 + \sigma Z\), where \(Z\) is a standard normal draw and \(\sigma\) sets the amount of blur. The blurred draws have the density of two bells of width \(\sigma\), one on each data point:

\[ p_\sigma(x) = \tfrac12\, \mathcal N(x; -1, \sigma^2) + \tfrac12\, \mathcal N(x; 1, \sigma^2). \]

At \(\sigma = 0.5\) the bells barely overlap. The density is 0.3991 at each data point and 0.1080 at \(x = 0\), the valley between them. At \(\sigma = 1\) it is 0.2265 at the data points and 0.2420 at the valley, so the two bells have merged into one hump. The peaks fell and the valley rose, the way the hot spots of a metal bar cool and its cold spot warms.

How fast does the valley fill? Measure the blur by its variance \(\tau = \sigma^2\). At \(\sigma = 0.5\), the density at \(x = 0\) rises at 0.6479 per unit of \(\tau\), and half its curvature there, \(\tfrac12\, \partial^2 p_\sigma / \partial x^2\), is also 0.6479. At the peak \(x = 1\), both numbers are \(-0.7939\). A point that sits below its neighbors gains density, a point above them loses it, and the rate is half the curvature. This rule is the heat equation, \(\partial p / \partial \tau = \tfrac12\, \partial^2 p / \partial x^2\).

Now take one blurred draw, \(x = 0.5\), and ask which data point it came from. At \(\sigma = 0.5\), the bell on \(+1\) is \(e^{4} = 54.6\) times taller at 0.5 than the bell on \(-1\), so by Bayes' rule the draw came from \(+1\) with probability \(54.6/55.6 = 0.9820\). The best guess of the clean point is the posterior mean, \(0.9820 - 0.0180 = 0.9640\). The score, the slope of \(\log p_\sigma\) at 0.5, is 1.8561. Multiplied by \(\sigma^2 = 0.25\) it gives 0.4640, the step \(0.9640 - 0.5\) from the noisy point to its best guess.

At \(\sigma = 2\) the bells overlap so much that the probability falls to 0.5622, the best guess is 0.1244, and the score is \(-0.0939\). Times \(\sigma^2 = 4\) it is \(-0.3756\), again the step \(0.1244 - 0.5\). Under heavy blur the arrow points toward the middle of the one hump, and as the blur shrinks it turns toward the nearer data point. Following the arrows while the blur shrinks carries a noisy draw back onto the data.

Noise blurs data the way heat spreads, and at every level of blur the score, times the variance of the blur, is the arrow from a noisy point to its best guess of the clean one.

Figure 1.1The noised density as a surface

The noised density p_t(x) is a surface over position and time, and paths of the probability-flow ODE dx/dt = −½·∂x log p_t(x), run backward from draws of p_3, follow it from the wide noise at t = 3 into the data's three modes at t = 0.

Drag the surface, or slide turn, to see it from the side: the three peaks of p_0 at the back merge into one hump by t = 3 at the front. Of 2000 ODE paths started from draws of p_3, fractions 0.295, 0.497, and 0.207 end in the three modes, against weights of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.2, and the reverse SDE gives 0.303, 0.494, and 0.203. Switch to SDE paths: they jitter and cross on the way and land in the same proportions. Press resample: over five seeds every share stays within 0.027 of its weight. The flow carries each quantile of p_3 onto the same quantile of p_0, within 4.2e−8 on 200 quantiles, and both edges of the surface hold mass 1.0000.

1.3Statement

The two-point toy raised two questions: how the density of noisy draws changes as the noise grows, and how to walk a noisy draw back to the data. Theorem 1.1 answers both for any starting distribution, in any dimension, with noise whose rate may change over time. Theorem 1.2 says that the toy's arrow, the score times the noise variance, is always the step from a noisy point to the best guess of the clean one.

Theorem 1.1 (forward and backward)

Let \(dX_t = g(t)\,dW_t\) with \(X_0 \sim p_0\). In words, over each short time \(h\) the point \(X_t\) takes an independent Gaussian kick of variance \(g(t)^2 h\) in every coordinate, where \(W_t\) is Brownian motion and \(g(t) \ge 0\) is the rate of noise. Let \(p_t\) be the law of \(X_t\). Then \(p_t\) solves the heat equation, and the same marginals are produced backward in time by a stochastic and by a deterministic process:

\[ \partial_t p_t = \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \Delta p_t, \tag{1.1} \]
\[ dX_t = -g(t)^2\, \nabla \log p_t(X_t)\, dt + g(t)\, d\bar W_t \quad \text{(reverse SDE, time running down)}, \tag{1.2} \]
\[ \frac{dX_t}{dt} = -\tfrac12\, g(t)^2\, \nabla \log p_t(X_t) \quad \text{(probability-flow ODE)}. \tag{1.3} \]

Here \(\Delta\) is the Laplacian, the sum of the second derivatives along each coordinate, which in one dimension is the toy's curvature. \(\bar W_t\) is a Brownian motion run with time decreasing, so each \(dt\) in (1.2) is negative. For \(t\) with \(\int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds \gt 0\), \(p_t\) is \(p_0\) blurred by a Gaussian of that variance, so it is smooth and positive and its score exists, even when \(p_0\) is two points with no score of its own, as in the toy. The backward processes reproduce the marginals \(p_t\) only when they start from \(X_T \sim p_T\). Samplers start from a Gaussian instead and inherit the gap between the two.

Theorem 1.2 (Tweedie's formula)

If \(X_\sigma = X_0 + \sigma Z\) with \(Z\) standard normal and independent of \(X_0\), and \(p_\sigma\) is the density of \(X_\sigma\), then

\[ \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] = x + \sigma^2\, \nabla \log p_\sigma(x). \tag{1.4} \]

Independence is what makes \(\mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2)\) the likelihood of \(x\) given \(x_0\). Without it the formula fails: if \(Z = X_0\) for a standard normal \(X_0\), then \(X_\sigma = (1 + \sigma) X_0\), the left side of (1.4) is \(x/(1 + \sigma)\), and the right side is \(x(1 + 2\sigma)/(1 + \sigma)^2\).

1.4Derivation

Heat equation. Start in one dimension with the simplest noise, a walk that every \(h\) units of time steps left or right by \(\delta\), with probability \(\tfrac12\) each. Let \(p(x, t)\) be the probability of being at \(x\) at time \(t\). To be at \(x\) at time \(t + h\), the walker was at \(x - \delta\) and stepped right, or at \(x + \delta\) and stepped left:

\[ p(x, t + h) = \tfrac12\, p(x - \delta, t) + \tfrac12\, p(x + \delta, t). \]

Expand both sides in Taylor series about \((x, t)\). On the left, keep the first order in \(h\):

\[ p(x, t + h) = p + h\, \partial_t p + O(h^2). \]

On the right, keep the second order in \(\delta\):

\[ p(x \pm \delta, t) = p \pm \delta\, \partial_x p + \tfrac12 \delta^2\, \partial_x^2 p \pm \tfrac16 \delta^3\, \partial_x^3 p + O(\delta^4). \]

Averaging the two signs cancels every odd term, the first derivative included:

\[ \tfrac12\, p(x - \delta, t) + \tfrac12\, p(x + \delta, t) = p + \tfrac12 \delta^2\, \partial_x^2 p + O(\delta^4). \]

Set the two sides equal, subtract \(p\), and divide by \(h\):

\[ \partial_t p = \frac{\delta^2}{2h}\, \partial_x^2 p + O(h) + O\big(\delta^4 / h\big). \]

Now shrink the step and the time together, holding \(\delta^2 / h = g^2\) fixed, so that \(\delta = g\sqrt h\). The error terms vanish and \(\partial_t p = \tfrac12 g^2\, \partial_x^2 p\). The constant \(D = \tfrac12 g^2\) is called the diffusion coefficient, and with \(g = 1\) this is the toy's rule that density rises at half its curvature. The step has to shrink like \(\sqrt h\): a step proportional to \(h\) sends \(\delta^2/h\) to 0 and nothing spreads, and a step much larger than \(\sqrt h\) sends it to infinity. In \(d\) dimensions each coordinate walks on its own, and the second derivatives add up to the Laplacian.

The Gaussian kick \(g\sqrt h\, Z\) has the same mean 0 and variance \(g^2 h\) as the \(\pm\delta\) step, and the argument used nothing else. For a general density the same steps run through a smooth test function \(\varphi\) that vanishes far away. Over a short step \(h\), \(X_{t+h} = X_t + g\sqrt{h}\,Z\), and a second-order Taylor expansion about \(X_t\) gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \varphi(X_{t+h}) = \varphi(X_t) &+ g\sqrt h\, Z \cdot \nabla\varphi(X_t) \\ &+ \tfrac12 g^2 h\, Z^\top \nabla^2 \varphi(X_t)\, Z + o(h). \end{aligned} \]

Take expectations. \(Z\) is independent of \(X_t\), with \(\mathbb E Z = 0\) and \(\mathbb E\, Z Z^\top = I\), so the middle term vanishes and the last becomes the trace of \(\nabla^2\varphi\), which is \(\Delta\varphi\):

\[ \mathbb E\,\varphi(X_{t+h}) = \mathbb E\,\varphi(X_t) + \tfrac12 g^2 h\, \mathbb E\, \Delta\varphi(X_t) + o(h) \]

Write both sides as integrals against the densities, subtract, and divide by \(h\):

\[ \int \varphi\, \frac{p_{t+h} - p_t}{h}\, dx = \tfrac12 g^2 \int \Delta\varphi\; p_t\, dx + o(1). \]

Integrate by parts twice on the right. The boundary terms vanish because \(\varphi\) vanishes far away:

\[ \int \Delta\varphi\; p_t\, dx = -\int \nabla\varphi \cdot \nabla p_t\, dx = \int \varphi\, \Delta p_t\, dx. \]

Let \(h \to 0\). Then for every test function \(\varphi\),

\[ \int \varphi\, \partial_t p_t\, dx = \int \varphi\, \tfrac12 g^2\, \Delta p_t\, dx, \]

and two functions with the same integral against every test function are equal, which is (1.1).

Probability-flow ODE. Since \(p\, \nabla \log p = \nabla p\), and the divergence of a gradient is the Laplacian, \(\tfrac12 g^2 \Delta p = \nabla \cdot \big(\tfrac12 g^2\, p\, \nabla \log p\big)\). So equation (1.1) is the continuity equation \(\partial_t p = -\nabla\cdot(p\, v)\) for the velocity \(v = -\tfrac12 g^2 \nabla \log p\). By Appendix A.4, particles that move with \(v\) therefore have marginals \(p_t\), in either direction of time, which is (1.3). In the toy at \(\sigma = 0.5\), a particle at 0.5 moves with \(v = -\tfrac12 \times 1.8561 = -0.928\) per unit of \(\tau\): away from \(+1\) as the blur grows, and toward it when the film runs backward.

Reverse SDE. In reversed time \(s = T - t\), the density \(q_s = p_{T-s}\) satisfies \(\partial_s q = -\partial_t p = -\tfrac12 g^2 \Delta q\), by the chain rule and (1.1). A process with drift \(b\) and noise \(g\) has \(\partial_s q = -\nabla\cdot(q\, b) + \tfrac12 g^2 \Delta q\): the noise gives the heat term, as in the walk above, and the drift gives the continuity equation (Appendix A.4) for particles carried with velocity \(b\). Matching the two requires \(\nabla\cdot(q\,b) = g^2 \Delta q = \nabla\cdot(g^2 q \nabla\log q)\), and the gradient solution \(b = g^2 \nabla \log q\) is (1.2), Anderson's reverse drift. Half of this drift is the ODE's velocity, and the other half cancels the spreading that the added noise \(g\, d\bar W_t\) causes.

Tweedie. Write \(p_\sigma(x) = \int p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2)\, dx_0\) and differentiate under the integral. The gradient of \(\mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2)\) in \(x\) is the same Gaussian times \((x_0 - x)/\sigma^2\), so

\[ \nabla p_\sigma(x) = \int p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2)\, \frac{x_0 - x}{\sigma^2}\, dx_0. \]

Dividing by \(p_\sigma(x)\) gives \(\nabla \log p_\sigma(x)\) on the left. On the right it turns the integral into a posterior expectation, because by Bayes' rule \(p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2)/p_\sigma(x)\) is the density of \(X_0\) given \(X_\sigma = x\). Multiplying by \(\sigma^2\), \(\sigma^2 \nabla \log p_\sigma(x) = \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] - x\). In the toy this is \(0.25 \times 1.8561 = 0.4640\), the step from 0.5 to 0.9640. ∎

Consequence. The posterior mean minimizes \(\mathbb E\,\|D(X_\sigma) - X_0\|^2\) over denoisers \(D\), so a network trained to denoise at every noise level is, by (1.4), a network that knows the score. This is denoising score matching, and it is why diffusion models train by regression.

1.5Figures

Figure 1.2One noised mixture, four pictures

The same p_σ is a cloud of Brownian paths, a solution of the heat equation in τ = σ², a score field, and a denoiser, and Tweedie's formula E[x₀ | x] = x + σ²·∂x log p_σ(x) reads the denoiser off the score.

Slide σ from 0.05 to 3: p_σ keeps three modes until σ = 0.62 and two until 0.92, the score flattens, and the denoiser bends from the identity toward the data mean. At every σ the Bayes posterior mean and Tweedie's formula agree to within 1.6e−14, and p_σ solves ∂p/∂τ = ½∂²p/∂x² with a relative finite-difference residual of at most 1.4e−6. Press run: 200 particles start on the quantiles of p_3, follow dx/dσ = −σ·∂x log p_σ, and land 0.300, 0.500, and 0.200 in the three modes, each within 2.6e−9 of its quantile of p_0.05.

Figure 1.3Running the noise backward, two ways

The score alone runs the noise backward, as the reverse SDE dx = −∂x log p_σ d(σ²) + dW̄ or as the probability-flow ODE dx/d(σ²) = −½·∂x log p_σ, and both carry a Gaussian at σ = 3 onto the three-mode data.

Slide N from 10 to 400. At N = 10 both sets land too wide, the SDE more (variance 3.133 and 2.965 against the data's 2.732), and the SDE puts 0.443 of its particles in the middle mode against a weight of 0.5. As N grows both W1 distances to the data fall to the level of 2000 exact draws (median 0.039): the SDE's from 0.152 to 0.042, and the ODE's from 0.098 to 0.014, below that level because this seed's starting points happen to be lucky. Both sets of mode shares come within 0.011 of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.2. At large N the gap between the two is within seed-to-seed noise. Its paths are smooth and keep their order, and the SDE's jitter and cross.

1.6Four ways to see it

The same process is a cloud of particles, a spreading density, a vector field, and a denoiser (Figure 1.2). Each picture follows from the one before it.

  1. 1Particlesphysics

    Each particle takes independent Gaussian kicks, \(dX_t = g(t)\, dW_t\). Einstein used this picture of Brownian motion to count molecules, and a sampler simulates it.

  2. 1 → 2Average a test function over the particles. A second-order Taylor step gives \(\tfrac{d}{dt}\mathbb E\,\varphi(X_t) = \tfrac12 g^2\, \mathbb E\, \Delta\varphi(X_t)\) (Appendix A.1), and integrating by parts against \(p_t\) moves the Laplacian onto the density, which is (1.1).

  3. 2A densityanalysis

    The density solves the heat equation, so it is the data convolved with a Gaussian of variance \(\int_0^t g^2\). Fourier analysis applies: each frequency decays on its own (Chapter 7), and the surface \(p(x, t)\) flattens as \(t\) grows (Figure 1.1).

  4. 2 → 3Write the Laplacian as a divergence, \(\tfrac12 g^2 \Delta p = \nabla\cdot\big(\tfrac12 g^2\, p\, \nabla\log p\big)\). The heat equation becomes the continuity equation (Appendix A.4) with velocity \(v = -\tfrac12 g^2 \nabla \log p_t\), so the whole density moves along one vector field built from the score.

  5. 3A vector fielddynamical systems

    The score \(\nabla\log p_t\) points where the noised density rises. Following \(-\tfrac12 g^2 \nabla\log p_t\) forward in time spreads the data, and following it backward from noise gathers the data again (1.3).

  6. 3 → 4Differentiate the Gaussian convolution under the integral (Theorem 1.2): \(\sigma^2 \nabla \log p_\sigma(x) = \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] - x\). The score is the step from a noisy point to its best guess of the clean one, divided by the noise variance.

  7. 4A denoiserstatistics

    The posterior mean minimizes squared error, so a network trained to denoise at every noise level has learned the score. Statisticians know the identity as Tweedie's formula and use it for empirical Bayes, and machine learning uses it to train diffusion models by regression.

1.7Where it breaks and what is open

Theorem 1.1 holds for every starting distribution, including the empirical distribution of a training set. The noised density is then a mixture of Gaussians centered on the training points, its score has a closed form, and the reverse process run with that exact score returns the training points themselves, however many there are (Figure 1.4). A network that minimized the denoising loss perfectly would do the same. Trained networks make new samples because they fit the score imperfectly, in ways their architecture decides, and the largest of them still reproduce some training images (Carlini et al.). A second limit is cost: every sample takes tens of sequential network calls, and taking fewer steps adds discretization error (Figure 1.3).

Figure 1.4The exact score of a training set returns copies

With the exact score of a finite training set, the score of (1/n)·Σ N(x_i, t·I), the probability-flow ODE carries noise back onto copies of the training points, while the score of the density they came from spreads the same noise over the whole ring.

At the default n = 16 and σ = 0.01, 100.0% of the 1000 samples from the training-set score land within 0.05 of a training point, at a median distance of 0.012. From the same starting noise, the true-density score puts 2.8% there, at a median distance of 0.243. Slide n to 64: the copy rate stays at 100.0%, and only the true-density rate rises, to 11.2%, because 64 points cover more of the ring. Slide the stopping level up to σ = 0.1: the copies blur into small clouds and the rate falls to 14.4%.

  1. Why trained denoisers generalize. Two accounts compete. Networks are biased toward bases adapted to the geometry of images (Kadkhodaie et al.), and denoisers that are local and shift-equivariant create new images as mosaics of training patches (Kamb and Ganguli, and Chapter 7). Which mechanism dominates in large models, and how the balance shifts with the size of the training set, is open.
  2. Few steps without distillation. Sampling is sequential in the number of steps. Speculative decoding suggests guessing the trajectory and checking it in parallel. Chapter 4 gives the theory and its limits.
  3. Unmasking several tokens at once. Masked diffusion language models unmask several tokens per step and sample each from its own marginal. Given the tokens already revealed, the error of one such step is the total correlation of the tokens unmasked together, \(\mathrm{KL}\big(p(x_S \mid x_{\text{seen}}) \,\|\, \prod_{i \in S} p(x_i \mid x_{\text{seen}})\big)\). Mutual-information samplers measure the pairwise part of this quantity, and a bound on generation quality in terms of it is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 1.1Tweedie's formula

    With \(X_\sigma = X_0 + \sigma Z\), derive \(\mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] = x + \sigma^2 \nabla\log p_\sigma(x)\). Then show that the posterior mean minimizes \(\mathbb E\,\|D(X_\sigma) - X_0\|^2\) over denoisers \(D\).

    Solution

    \(p_\sigma(x) = \int p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I)\, dx_0\), and \(\nabla_x \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I) = \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I)\, (x_0 - x)/\sigma^2\). Differentiating under the integral and dividing by \(p_\sigma(x)\),

    \[ \nabla\log p_\sigma(x) = \int \frac{p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I)}{p_\sigma(x)}\, \frac{x_0 - x}{\sigma^2}\, dx_0 = \frac{\mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] - x}{\sigma^2}, \]

    because the fraction is the posterior density of \(X_0\) given \(X_\sigma = x\). For the second part, condition on \(X_\sigma\) and let \(m\) be the posterior mean:

    \[ \mathbb E\big[\|D - X_0\|^2 \mid X_\sigma\big] = \|D - m\|^2 + \mathbb E\big[\|X_0 - m\|^2 \mid X_\sigma\big], \]

    which is smallest at \(D = m\).

  2. Derivation 1.2The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process

    For \(dX_t = -X_t\, dt + \sqrt 2\, dW_t\) on the line, derive the Fokker-Planck equation, show that \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) is stationary, and find the law of \(X_t\) given \(X_0 = x_0\).

    Solution

    Itô's lemma gives the generator \(\mathcal L\varphi = -x\varphi' + \varphi''\) (Appendix A.1). Integrating by parts in \(\tfrac{d}{dt}\mathbb E\varphi(X_t) = \mathbb E\,\mathcal L\varphi(X_t)\) gives \(\partial_t p = \partial_x(x p) + \partial_x^2 p = \partial_x\big(x p + \partial_x p\big)\).

    For \(p \propto e^{-x^2/2}\), \(\partial_x p = -x p\), so the flux \(xp + \partial_x p\) vanishes and \(p\) is stationary. Solving the linear equation, \(X_t = x_0 e^{-t} + \sqrt 2 \int_0^t e^{-(t - s)}\, dW_s\), a Gaussian with mean \(x_0 e^{-t}\) and variance \(2\int_0^t e^{-2(t-s)} ds = 1 - e^{-2t}\).

Chapter 2

The tilt

Convex duality, from optimization

Multiply a distribution by \(e^{f}\) and renormalize. The result is the best trade between expected \(f\) and KL from the starting distribution, and the log of the normalizer is the value of that trade.

Uses Appendix A.2 and A.5.

2.1Motivation

Suppose you have a language model that writes well and a reward model that scores its answers, and you want the model to earn more reward while still writing like itself. Push on the reward alone and the model finds the one answer the reward model likes best and gives it to every prompt. Leave the model alone and it earns no more than before. But how far should it move, which answers should gain probability, and by how much?

The same trade appears whenever a distribution must score well without straying far from a reference: a language model fine-tuned on human preferences that still writes like the pretrained model, a posterior that respects both a prior and the data, a physical system held at a temperature. Optimizing the score alone collapses onto its maximum and forgets the reference, and staying at the reference ignores the score. The trade has a closed-form answer: multiply the reference by the exponential of the score and renormalize. That reweighting is the tilt, and the log of its normalizer, \(\log Z\), is the value of the trade.

PAPERA document that moved capital

DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning on checkable answers can teach a language model to reason, at a fraction of frontier cost.

DeepSeek-AI, 2025 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Its release in January 2025 set off a one-day sell-off in AI stocks of roughly a trillion dollars, led by NVIDIA, because it suggested that reasoning could be bought cheaply.

The link to this chapter: its GRPO objective (equation 1) maximizes a clipped advantage term minus \(\beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}})\) with \(\beta = 0.001\), so the policy it aims at is the tilt \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\, e^{r/\beta}/Z\) of Theorem 2.1. The clipping only approximates that objective, and the reference is reset from time to time, so training runs a sequence of tilts.

2.2Intuition

Take the smallest case with a real choice. A model answers a prompt with one of three replies, and the pretrained model picks them with probabilities \(p = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1)\). A reward model scores the replies \(f = (0, 1, 2)\), so the rarest reply is the best. You want a new distribution \(q\) over the replies with a high expected reward \(\mathbb E_q[f]\), the average of \(f\) under \(q\), and you charge it for moving away from \(p\) by the KL divergence

\[ \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \sum_i q_i \log \frac{q_i}{p_i}, \]

which is 0 when \(q = p\) and grows as \(q\) moves mass onto replies that \(p\) rarely picks. The net score of a choice is \(J(q) = \mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)\).

Try the two extremes first. Staying at \(p\) earns \(0.3 \times 1 + 0.1 \times 2 = 0.5\) and pays nothing, so \(J(p) = 0.5\). Putting all the mass on the best reply earns 2 and pays \(\log(1/0.1) = 2.3026\), so \(J = -0.3026\), worse than not moving at all.

The best \(q\) lies in between. To find it, move a sliver \(\varepsilon\) of mass from reply \(i\) to reply \(j\). The reward changes by \(\varepsilon (f_j - f_i)\), and to first order the KL changes by \(\varepsilon \big(\log(q_j/p_j) - \log(q_i/p_i)\big)\). At the best \(q\) no such move helps, so every reply has the same reward minus log ratio:

\[ f_i - \log \frac{q_i}{p_i} = c \quad \text{for every } i. \]

Solving for \(q_i\) gives \(q_i = p_i\, e^{f_i}\, e^{-c}\). No reply is left empty, because near \(q_i = 0\) the log ratio is very negative, and a sliver moved onto reply \(i\) gains more than it costs. Each reference probability is multiplied by \(e\) raised to its reward, and \(e^{-c}\) renormalizes. The products \(p_i e^{f_i}\) are 0.6, 0.8155, and 0.7389, their sum is \(Z = 2.1544\), and dividing by it gives \(q^* = (0.2785, 0.3785, 0.3430)\). The best reply rises from 0.1 to 0.3430, and the worst falls from 0.6 to 0.2785. This \(q^*\) earns \(\mathbb E_{q^*}[f] = 1.0645\) and pays \(\mathrm{KL}(q^* \,\|\, p) = 0.2970\), so \(J(q^*) = 0.7675\), which is \(\log Z = \log 2.1544\). The shared constant \(c\) is the same 0.7675.

Every other \(q\) falls short, by an amount you can compute. The choice \(q = (0.2, 0.4, 0.4)\) earns 1.2 and pays 0.4499, so \(J(q) = 0.7501\). That is short of \(\log Z\) by 0.0174, and \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, q^*)\) is also 0.0174.

Multiply the reference by \(e^{f}\) and renormalize, and you get the best compromise between chasing \(f\) and staying close to where you started, and the compromise is worth \(\log Z\).

Figure 2.1The tilt attains log Z

Among all densities q, the objective E_q[βf] − KL(q‖p) peaks at q* ∝ p·e^{βf}, where it equals log E_p[e^{βf}], and any other q falls short by exactly KL(q‖q*).

At the default β = 4 and δ = 0.3, q falls short of log Z = 1.5410 by 0.162245, and KL(q‖q*) is the same 0.162245. Slide δ to 0: J(q) reaches log Z and the gap closes. Slide β to 12: q* puts 0.980 of its mass on the taller bump and E_q*[f] climbs to 0.945, while at β = 0 the tilt does nothing and q* = p.

2.3Statement

The three replies asked for the distribution with the best trade between expected reward and KL from the reference, and the answer weighted each reply by \(e\) raised to its reward, with value \(\log Z\). Theorem 2.1 says the same holds for any reference and any reward, on three points or on a continuum, under two finiteness conditions explained after it.

Theorem 2.1 (Gibbs variational principle)

For a distribution \(p\) and a function \(f\) with \(Z = \mathbb E_p[e^{f}] \lt \infty\) and \(\mathbb E_p\big[|f|\, e^{f}\big] \lt \infty\), with the maximum over distributions \(q\) with \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \lt \infty\),

\[ \log \mathbb E_p\big[e^{f}\big] = \max_{q}\, \Big\{ \mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \Big\}. \tag{2.1} \]

The maximum is attained only at the tilt \(q^*(x) = p(x)\, e^{f(x)} / Z\), and every other \(q\) falls short by exactly \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, q^*)\).

Each condition rules out a case that breaks. If \(Z = \infty\), there is nothing to renormalize and no tilt: for \(p = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(f(x) = x^2/2\), the product \(p\, e^f\) is the constant \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\), whose integral is infinite (Section 2.7). The second condition makes \(\mathbb E_{q^*}[f]\) finite. Without it, (2.1) holds only as a supremum that no \(q\) attains. On the positive integers, take \(p_n = 2^{-n}\) and \(e^{f_n} = 2^n / n^2\). Then

\[ Z = \sum_{n \ge 1} 2^{-n}\, \frac{2^n}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}, \qquad q^*_n = \frac{6}{\pi^2 n^2}, \]

and \(\mathbb E_{q^*}[f]\) is infinite, since \(f_n\) grows like \(n \log 2\) while \(q^*_n\) falls only like \(1/n^2\). So \(\mathrm{KL}(q^* \,\|\, p) = \mathbb E_{q^*}[f] - \log Z\) is infinite too, and \(q^*\) is outside the set the maximum ranges over. The restriction to \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \lt \infty\) keeps the objective from reading \(\infty - \infty\).

2.4Derivation

Since \(\log (q^*/p) = f - \log Z\), replace \(f\) by \(\log(q^*/p) + \log Z\) inside the first expectation:

\[ \mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p) = \mathbb E_q\Big[\log \frac{q^*}{p} + \log Z\Big] - \mathbb E_q\Big[\log \frac{q}{p}\Big] = \log Z - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, q^*). \]

The last step combines the two logs, \(\log(q^*/p) - \log(q/p) = \log(q^*/q)\), whose expectation under \(q\) is \(-\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, q^*)\). In the toy, \(0.7675 - 0.0174 = 0.7501\).

KL is nonnegative and vanishes only when \(q = q^*\). The reason is Jensen's inequality for the concave logarithm:

\[ -\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, q^*) = \mathbb E_q\Big[\log \frac{q^*}{q}\Big] \le \log \mathbb E_q\Big[\frac{q^*}{q}\Big] \le \log 1 = 0, \]

since \(\mathbb E_q[q^*/q]\) is the mass of \(q^*\) where \(q \gt 0\), at most 1. Both inequalities are equalities only when \(q^*/q\) is constant and \(q^*\) has no mass where \(q = 0\), that is, when \(q = q^*\). ∎

Read as convex duality, (2.1) says that \(f \mapsto \log \mathbb E_p[e^f]\) is the Legendre transform of \(q \mapsto \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)\). Appendix A.2 defines the transform of a function \(F\) as

\[ F^*(y) = \sup_x \big\{ \langle x, y\rangle - F(x) \big\}. \]

Here the point \(x\) is a distribution \(q\), the slope \(y\) is a function \(f\), and the pairing \(\langle q, f\rangle\) is \(\mathbb E_q[f]\), so (2.1) is this definition with \(F = \mathrm{KL}(\cdot \,\|\, p)\). Both functions are convex and lower semicontinuous, which means each one's value at a limit is no larger than the limit of its values, so the graph never jumps up at a single point. For such functions the Fenchel-Moreau theorem says that applying the transform twice returns the function, so the transform also runs the other way, which is the Donsker-Varadhan formula below. Applied twice to a function that is not convex, the transform returns the largest convex, lower semicontinuous function below it. Each familiar result below is (2.1) with a particular \(f\).

  • Maximum entropy. With \(p\) uniform and \(f = \lambda\, T(x)\), the tilt is \(q^* \propto e^{\lambda T}\), one distribution for each \(\lambda\). A family of this shape is called an exponential family, and it is the Boltzmann distribution when \(T\) is minus an energy. The multiplier \(\lambda\) is the dual variable of the constraint \(\mathbb E[T] = t\): choose \(\lambda\) so that \(\mathbb E_{q^*}[T] = t\). Then (2.1) gives, for every \(q\) with \(\mathbb E_q[T] = t\),
    \[ \lambda t - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \le \log \mathbb E_p\big[e^{\lambda T}\big], \]
    with equality at \(q^*\). So \(q^*\) has the least KL from uniform, which is the most entropy, among all distributions with that mean.
  • KL-regularized RL. Maximizing \(\mathbb E_\pi[r] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}})\) is (2.1) with \(f = r/\beta\), so \(\pi^* \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}\, e^{r/\beta}\). Inverting, \(r = \beta \log (\pi^*/\pi_{\text{ref}}) + \beta \log Z\), which is DPO's implicit reward.
  • Bayes. With \(f(x) = \log p(y \mid x)\), the tilt of the prior is the posterior, the maximum is \(\log p(y)\), and the objective is the ELBO.
  • Temperature. Replacing \(f\) by \(f/\tau\) and multiplying by \(\tau\), the value tends to \(\operatorname{ess\,sup}_p f\), the largest value of \(f\) that \(p\) can produce, as \(\tau \to 0\). Log-sum-exp becomes max, the forward algorithm becomes Viterbi, and soft Bellman backups become hard ones.
  • Estimating KL. The dual statement \(\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q) = \sup_T \{\mathbb E_p[T] - \log \mathbb E_q[e^{T}]\}\) (Donsker-Varadhan) is attained at \(T = \log (dp/dq)\), and MINE, a neural estimator of mutual information, maximizes it.

2.5Figures

Figure 2.2The tilt is a tangent line

A(β) = log E_p[e^{βf}] is convex, every distribution q gives the line β·E_q[f] − KL(q‖p) under it by (2.1), and the tilt q_β₀ ∝ p·e^{β₀f} gives the line that touches it at β₀, with slope E_q_β₀[f] and intercept −KL(q_β₀‖p).

At the default β₀ = 1.2 the tangent's slope by finite difference is 0.571489, and the tilt's mean reward computed directly is the same 0.571489. The tangent meets the A axis at −0.044586, which is −KL(q_β₀‖p) computed directly. The 20 random lines stay under the curve, the closest by 0.0146. Slide β₀ to 4: the slope climbs to 0.715304, the intercept falls to −0.404999, and q_β₀ piles onto the high-reward answers. At β₀ = 0 the tangent passes through the origin with slope E_p[f] = 0.496656, because q_0 = p.

Figure 2.3One dial from shortest path to sum over paths

The soft-min recursion V(cell) = c(cell) − τ·log Σ_next e^{−V(next)/τ} computes −τ·log Σ_paths e^{−cost/τ}, the tilt over all 924 paths, so it is the shortest path (Dijkstra, Viterbi) as τ → 0 and the forward algorithm at τ = 1.

At τ = 1 the recursion and the sum over all 924 paths both give 37.1698, inside 31.17 ≤ V_τ ≤ 38, and the Gibbs law spreads over 6.5 effective paths. Slide τ down to 0.02: the shading collapses onto the hard path and V_τ = 38.0000, the shortest-path cost. Slide τ up to 5: 422.9 effective paths and V_τ = 18.8822. Soft Q-learning runs this recursion at a fixed τ, and attention weights its keys by the same Gibbs rule.

Figure 2.4The same duality, read backward

KL(p‖q) = sup over T of E_p[T] − log E_q[e^T], and a critic T falls short by exactly KL(p‖q·e^T/Z), so the bound touches the true KL when T = log dp/dq up to a constant.

At a = 0.8 and b = 0 the bound is 0.48000, short of KL(p‖q) = 0.6017 by 0.12167, the same number as KL(p‖q·e^T/Z) on a grid. Slide a to 1: the best linear critic still misses by 0.1017, because log dp/dq is quadratic. Set a = 2.04 and b = −0.52: the critic lies on log dp/dq and the bound reaches 0.60167, short by 4e−8. MINE trains a neural T on this bound.

2.6Four ways to see it

The tilt is a statement about convex functions, a statement about Bayes' rule, a statement about heat, and a statement about rare events. All four are (2.1).

  1. 1Convex dualityoptimization

    Let \(A(\beta) = \log \mathbb E_p[e^{\beta f}]\). Every distribution \(q\) gives a line \(\beta \mapsto \beta\, \mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)\) that stays below \(A\), by (2.1) applied to \(\beta f\). The tilt \(q_\beta\) gives the line that touches \(A\) at \(\beta\): its slope is \(\mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f]\) and its intercept is \(-\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p)\), so a convex curve is the upper envelope of its tangents (Figure 2.2).

  2. 1 → 2Put \(\beta = 1\) and \(f(x) = \log p(y \mid x)\) for an observation \(y\). Then \(Z = \int p(x)\, p(y \mid x)\, dx = p(y)\), the tilt \(p(x)\, p(y \mid x)/p(y)\) is the posterior, and (2.1) reads

    \[ \log p(y) = \max_q \Big\{ \mathbb E_q[\log p(y \mid x)] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p\big) \Big\}. \]

  3. 2Bayes and the ELBOstatistics and machine learning

    The bracket is the evidence lower bound. Maximizing it over a family of \(q\) is variational inference, the gap is \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, \text{posterior})\), and a VAE maximizes it over an encoder and a decoder at once.

  4. 1 → 3Put \(p\) uniform on \(N\) states and \(f = -E/T\) for an energy \(E\) and a temperature \(T\). Then \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \log N - H(q)\) and \(\mathbb E_p[e^f] = Z/N\) with \(Z = \sum_x e^{-E(x)/T}\). Multiplying (2.1) by \(-T\),

    \[ -T \log Z = \min_q \Big\{ \mathbb E_q[E] - T\, H(q) \Big\}. \]

  5. 3Free energyphysics

    The bracket is the Helmholtz free energy \(U - TS\), and the Boltzmann distribution \(e^{-E/T}/Z\) minimizes it. A system in contact with a heat bath trades energy against entropy at the rate the temperature sets, and \(-T\log Z\) is the value of that trade.

  6. 1 → 4Draw \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) from \(p\). By Sanov's theorem their empirical distribution lands near \(q\) with probability about \(e^{-n\, \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)}\). For a fair coin this is a count. The sequences with \(an\) heads number \(\binom{n}{an}\), each has probability \(2^{-n}\), and Stirling's formula gives

    \[ \binom{n}{an}\, 2^{-n} = e^{-n\,(\log 2 - H(a)) + O(\log n)}, \]
    \[ H(a) = -a \log a - (1 - a) \log (1 - a), \]

    where \(\log 2 - H(a)\) is the KL between coins that land heads with probabilities \(a\) and \(\tfrac12\). At \(a = 0.7\) it is 0.0823, and \(-\tfrac1n \log\) of the exact probability is 0.1067 at \(n = 100\) and 0.0828 at \(n = 10{,}000\). Given the rare event that the sample mean of \(f\) is near \(a \gt \mathbb E_p f\), it lands near the \(q\) with \(\mathbb E_q f = a\) that is closest to \(p\) in KL. A multiplier \(\lambda\) for the constraint gives \(q \propto p\, e^{\lambda f}\), and

    \[ -\frac1n \log P\Big(\tfrac1n \textstyle\sum_i f(X_i) \approx a\Big) \to \min_{\mathbb E_q f = a} \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \sup_\lambda \big\{ \lambda a - A(\lambda) \big\}. \]

  7. 4Gibbs conditioningprobability

    Condition many independent samples on a rare average, and each one looks like a draw from the tilt. The cost of the rare event is the Legendre transform of \(A\) (Cramér's theorem). The tilt appears for this reason in large deviations, in importance sampling for rare events, and in the proof of Hoeffding's inequality (Appendix A.6).

2.7Where it breaks and what is open

The tilt needs \(Z = \mathbb E_p[e^f] \lt \infty\). When \(f\) grows faster than the tails of \(p\) fall, there is no tilt: for \(p = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(f = \beta x^2/2\), \(Z = (1 - \beta)^{-1/2}\) for \(\beta \lt 1\) and \(Z = \infty\) for \(\beta \ge 1\). A Monte Carlo estimate of \(\log Z\) from samples of \(p\) always returns a finite number. The weights \(e^f\) have infinite variance from \(\beta = \tfrac12\), since \(\mathbb E_p[e^{2f}] = \infty\) there, so they pile onto a few samples in the tail and the estimate is wrong well before \(\beta = 1\) (Figure 2.5). A milder form of the same failure sits under reward overoptimization: a learned reward that is too large where the reference has little mass drags the tilt there, and the true reward falls as the KL from the reference grows (Gao, Schulman, and Hilton).

Figure 2.5An infinite normalizer, estimated as a finite one

When f grows faster than p's tails fall, E_p[e^f] is infinite and there is no tilt, and a Monte Carlo estimate of log Z from draws of p still reports a finite number.

At the default β = 0.8 the exact log Z is 0.8047 and the estimate from 1000 draws reads 0.7127, short by 0.0920, and the self-normalized weights have an effective sample size of 143.2 of 1000. The draws stop at |x| = 3.38, and the tilt N(0, 5) still has mass beyond. The gap opens before Z diverges because the weights have infinite variance from β = ½ on, where E_p[e^{2f}] = ∞. Slide β to 0.95: the gap grows to 0.4937 and the effective sample size falls to 56.7. Past β = 1 the true log Z is infinite and no tilt exists, and the estimate still reads 1.1215 at β = 1 and 2.0659 at β = 1.3.

  1. Choosing \(\beta\) when the reward is learned. The tilt's KL from the reference is a known function of \(\beta\) (Derivation 2.2), and along that curve the true reward rises and then falls. Predicting the turning point from the reward model's uncertainty, for example with earlier checkpoints as references, is open.
  2. Estimating large information from samples. Any lower bound on mutual information computed from \(n\) samples without assumptions on the distribution, Donsker-Varadhan's included, stays below about \(\log n\) (McAllester and Stratos). Pairwise information between tokens is small enough to stay under this ceiling. Estimating large information, such as that between a prompt and a long response, is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 2.1The tilt from a Lagrange multiplier

    Maximize \(\mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)\) over densities \(q\) with \(\int q = 1\) using a multiplier for the constraint (Appendix A.5), and recover the tilt and the value \(\log Z\).

    Solution

    The Lagrangian is \(\int q f - \int q \log(q/p) + \lambda(\int q - 1)\). Setting its derivative in \(q(x)\) to zero gives \(f(x) - \log(q(x)/p(x)) - 1 + \lambda = 0\), so \(q = p\, e^{f}\, e^{\lambda - 1}\), and normalizing gives \(e^{1 - \lambda} = Z\). The objective is concave in \(q\), so this is the maximum, and its value is \(\mathbb E_q[f] - \mathbb E_q[f - \log Z] = \log Z\).

  2. Derivation 2.2The tangent of \(\log Z\)

    Let \(A(\beta) = \log \mathbb E_p[e^{\beta f}]\) and \(q_\beta \propto p\, e^{\beta f}\). Show \(A'(\beta) = \mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f]\), \(A''(\beta) = \mathrm{Var}_{q_\beta}(f) \ge 0\), and \(\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p) = \beta A'(\beta) - A(\beta)\). Read the last identity off the tangent line of \(A\) at \(\beta\).

    Solution

    \(A'(\beta) = \mathbb E_p[f e^{\beta f}] / \mathbb E_p[e^{\beta f}] = \mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f]\), and differentiating again gives \(\mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f^2] - (\mathbb E_{q_\beta} f)^2\). Since \(\log(q_\beta/p) = \beta f - A(\beta)\), \(\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p) = \beta\, \mathbb E_{q_\beta} f - A(\beta) = \beta A'(\beta) - A(\beta)\).

    The tangent at \(\beta\) is \(b \mapsto A(\beta) + A'(\beta)(b - \beta)\). At \(b = 0\) it equals \(A(\beta) - \beta A'(\beta) = -\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p)\).

Chapter 3

Change of measure

The core of measure theory

An expectation under one distribution equals an expectation under another, weighted by the ratio of their densities. On paths that ratio is Girsanov's, its cost is the energy of the drift that turns one process into the other, and the best drift for a terminal reward is the gradient of \(\log h\), a log-probability when the reward is an indicator. Control becomes inference.

Uses Chapter 2 and Appendix A.1 and A.3.

3.1Motivation

Suppose you want the chance that a standard normal draw lands above 4, and all you have is a random number generator. The direct method draws many normals and counts the ones above 4. The true chance is about 3 in 100,000, so a run of 10,000 draws finds none at all nearly three times in four and reports a probability of zero. But how do you measure an event that your samples almost never see?

Many expectations are hard to compute under the distribution that defines them in the same way: the probability of a rare event, the price of an option whose real-world drift nobody knows, the value of a new policy estimated from data an old one collected. Sampling from the defining distribution wastes almost every sample, or cannot be done at all. A change of measure moves the expectation to a distribution that is easy to sample or easy to know, and pays with a weight, the density ratio. On paths that weight is a drift, which made pricing, conditioning, and control one computation.

3.2Intuition

Work the rare event through. Under \(p = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) the chance of landing above 4 is \(P(Z \gt 4) = 3.167 \times 10^{-5}\). Counting hits in 10,000 draws expects 0.317 of them and finds none with probability 0.729, and its standard error is 178% of the answer.

Now push every draw up by 4. Sample \(Y = Z + 4\), whose law \(q = \mathcal N(4, 1)\) is the same noise moved onto the event, and half of these draws land above 4. Draws near 4 are far more common under \(q\) than under \(p\), so weight each one by the ratio of the two densities:

\[ w(y) = \frac{p(y)}{q(y)} = \frac{e^{-y^2/2}}{e^{-(y - 4)^2/2}} = e^{8 - 4y}. \]

The weight is \(e^{-8} = 3.35 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(y = 4\) and smaller beyond it. The weighted count is exact on average, because the weight cancels the density the draw came from:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E_q\big[\mathbf 1\{Y \gt 4\}\, w(Y)\big] &= \int_4^\infty \frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\, q(y)\, dy \\ &= \int_4^\infty p(y)\, dy = P(Z \gt 4). \end{aligned} \]

With 10,000 draws its standard error is 2.1% of the answer. Plain counting would need about 7,000 times as many draws to do as well.

When does the weight break? Suppose you sample only above 5 instead, say from \(q(y) = e^{-(y - 5)}\) for \(y \gt 5\). The weights are still \(p/q\) wherever a draw can land, but no draw ever lands in \((4, 5)\), which holds 99.1% of the event's probability. The weighted average then converges to \(P(Z \gt 5) = 2.87 \times 10^{-7}\), less than 1% of the answer, and more draws do not help. Reweighting needs \(q\) to be positive wherever \(p\) is.

Read the weight the other way. Weighting draws of \(Z\) by \(1/w(z) = e^{4z - 8}\) turns averages over \(Z\) into averages over \(Z + 4\). Completing the square gives \(\varphi(z)\, e^{4z - 8} = \varphi(z - 4)\) for the standard normal density \(\varphi\), so for every \(g\)

\[ \mathbb E\big[g(Z)\, e^{4Z - 8}\big] = \int g(z)\, \varphi(z - 4)\, dz = \mathbb E\big[g(Z + 4)\big]. \]

For a Gaussian draw, a weight that is the exponential of a linear function of the draw, normalized to mean 1, is a shift of the draw. A Brownian path is a sum of many small Gaussian steps, and weighting each step this way shifts each step, which adds a drift to the whole path.

Weighting each draw by the ratio of two densities turns averages under one law into averages under the other, and for paths of noise that weight is the same as pushing them with a drift, with the same noise.

Figure 3.1Conditioning is a drift

Conditioning Brownian motion on landing in a window A adds the drift ∂x log h, with h(t, x) = P(B₁ ∈ A | B_t = x), and the energy E[½∫u² dt] that drift spends is the KL of the conditioned paths from the free ones, −log P(A).

At the default window [1, 1.5], P(A) = 0.0918: 14 of 200 free paths land in it, and 99.9% of 800 steered paths do. The energy the controller spends equals the surprise of the event: the steered paths spend ½∫u² dt = 2.43 ± 0.08 on average, against −log P(A) = 2.388. Slide c to 2.5 and w to 0.1: the surprise rises to 6.344 and the energy to 6.41 ± 0.13, and 98.8% of steered paths still land.

3.3Statement

The toy measured a rare event under one law by sampling another and weighting each draw by the ratio of their densities, and the method failed exactly where the sampler put no mass. Theorem 3.1 states that rule together with the condition that rules out the failure. Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 carry the toy's last step to whole paths, where the weight becomes a drift.

Theorem 3.1 (change of measure)

Call \(p\) absolutely continuous with respect to \(q\) when every event that \(q\) gives probability zero also has \(p\)-probability zero (Appendix A.3). For densities this means \(q\) is positive wherever \(p\) is, apart from a set of zero length, which the sampler above 5 violated on \((4, 5)\). If \(p\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(q\), the density ratio \(dp/dq\) exists, it equals \(p(x)/q(x)\) for densities, and for every \(g\) with \(\mathbb E_p|g| \lt \infty\)

\[ \mathbb E_p[g] = \mathbb E_q\Big[g \cdot \frac{dp}{dq}\Big]. \tag{3.1} \]

Theorem 3.2 (Girsanov, in KL form)

Let \(P\) be the law of \(dX_t = b_t\, dt + \sigma\, dW_t\) and \(Q\) the law of \(dX_t = \sigma\, dW_t\) on \([0, T]\), from the same start, where the drift \(b_t = b(t, X_{[0, t]})\) depends only on the path so far and \(\mathbb E_P \int_0^T |b_t|^2\, dt \lt \infty\). Then

\[ \log \frac{dP}{dQ} = \int_0^T \frac{b_t}{\sigma^2}\, dX_t - \frac12 \int_0^T \frac{|b_t|^2}{\sigma^2}\, dt, \qquad \mathrm{KL}(P \,\|\, Q) = \frac12\, \mathbb E_P \int_0^T \frac{|b_t|^2}{\sigma^2}\, dt. \tag{3.2} \]

Here the law of a process is the distribution of its whole path, and \(X_{[0, t]}\) is the path up to time \(t\). Each hypothesis has a case that fails without it. The drift may use only the path so far, because \(\int b_t\, dX_t\) is an Itô integral, which multiplies each increment by a drift fixed before the increment is drawn. A drift that peeks ahead breaks (3.2): with \(T = \sigma = 1\), \(c \gt 0\), and the constant drift \(b = c\, X_1/(1 + c)\), which reads the endpoint, the process is \(X_t = W_t + c\, t\, W_1\), and the weight that (3.2) assigns has mean \(1 + c\) under \(Q\), where a density ratio has mean 1. The energy must be finite: the Brownian bridge of Derivation 3.2 has drift \((y - X_t)/(T - t)\) and infinite energy, and it pins \(X_T\) to the single point \(y\), an event of \(Q\)-probability zero, so no density \(dP/dQ\) exists. The noise level \(\sigma\) must be the same under both laws, because the quadratic variation of a path reveals \(\sigma\) (Appendix A.3).

Theorem 3.3 (Doob's h-transform and Cole-Hopf)

Under \(dX_t = dW_t\), let \(h(t, x) = \mathbb E\big[e^{r(X_T)} \mid X_t = x\big]\), which must be finite, as Chapter 2's \(Z\) must be. For \(r(x) = x^2\) and \(T = 1\) it is infinite at \(t = 0\), since \(X_1\) given \(X_0\) has variance 1 and \(e^{x^2}\) outgrows the Gaussian tail. Tilting the path measure by \(e^{r(X_T)}\) gives the process \(dX_t = \nabla \log h(t, X_t)\, dt + dW_t\), and its drift solves the control problem

\[ \min_u\; \mathbb E\Big[\tfrac12 \int_0^T |u_t|^2\, dt - r(X_T)\Big] \quad \text{for } dX_t = u_t\, dt + dW_t, \quad \text{with value } -\log h(0, x_0). \tag{3.3} \]

3.4Derivation

(3.1). \(\int g\, p = \int g\, \frac{p}{q}\, q\). The division is safe because, by absolute continuity, \(p = 0\) wherever \(q = 0\), so the set where \(q\) vanishes adds nothing to either side. The toy's sampler above 5 is the case where it fails: there \(q = 0\) on \((4, 5)\) while \(p \gt 0\), and the right side loses the part of \(\mathbb E_p[g]\) that lies in \((4, 5)\).

(3.2). Discretize time with step \(h\). Given the path so far, the drift \(b\) is a fixed number, so under \(P\) the next increment \(\Delta X\) is \(\mathcal N(b\,h, \sigma^2 h)\), and under \(Q\) it is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 h)\). This is the toy's shift, scaled down to one step. The log ratio of the two Gaussian densities at \(\Delta X\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} -\frac{(\Delta X - b h)^2}{2 \sigma^2 h} + \frac{(\Delta X)^2}{2 \sigma^2 h} &= \frac{2 b h\, \Delta X - b^2 h^2}{2 \sigma^2 h} \\ &= \frac{b\, \Delta X - \tfrac12 b^2 h}{\sigma^2}, \end{aligned} \]

so one step contributes \((b\,\Delta X - \tfrac12 b^2 h)/\sigma^2\) to the log ratio. The density of a path is the product of its step densities, so the log ratios add, and summing gives the integrals as \(h \to 0\). For the KL, take the expectation under \(P\), where \(\Delta X = b\,h + \sigma\,\Delta W\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E_P\Big[\frac{b\,(b h + \sigma\, \Delta W) - \tfrac12 b^2 h}{\sigma^2}\Big] &= \mathbb E_P\Big[\frac{\tfrac12 b^2 h}{\sigma^2}\Big] \\ &\quad + \mathbb E_P\Big[\frac{b\, \Delta W}{\sigma}\Big]. \end{aligned} \]

The \(\Delta W\) term has mean zero, because \(b\) is fixed before \(\Delta W\) is drawn and \(\Delta W\) has mean zero. This is where the drift must depend only on the path so far. Summing, the expected log ratio is \(\sum \tfrac12 b^2 h / \sigma^2\), which tends to the KL in (3.2).

(3.3). The function \(h\) solves the backward Kolmogorov equation \(\partial_t h + \tfrac12 \Delta h = 0\) with \(h(T, x) = e^{r(x)}\), because \(h(t, X_t)\) is a martingale, so the \(dt\) term that Itô's lemma gives it must vanish (Appendix A.1). Substitute \(h = e^{-V}\), that is, \(V = -\log h\). The chain rule gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_t h &= -e^{-V}\, \partial_t V, \\ \nabla h &= -e^{-V}\, \nabla V, \\ \Delta h &= e^{-V}\big(|\nabla V|^2 - \Delta V\big). \end{aligned} \]

Put these into \(\partial_t h + \tfrac12 \Delta h = 0\) and divide by \(-e^{-V}\):

\[ \partial_t V + \tfrac12 \Delta V - \tfrac12 |\nabla V|^2 = 0, \qquad V(T, x) = -r(x). \]

Now write the equation that the value of the control problem satisfies. Let \(V(t, x)\) be the least expected cost to go from \(x\) at time \(t\). Over a short time \(dt\), a control \(u\) costs \(\tfrac12 |u|^2\, dt\) and moves the state to \(x + u\, dt + dW\), where by Itô's lemma the expected value of \(V\) is \(V + (\partial_t V + u \cdot \nabla V + \tfrac12 \Delta V)\, dt\). Choosing the best \(u\) at every step gives the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation (Theorem 17.1 states it in general):

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_t V + \tfrac12 \Delta V + \min_u \Big\{ u \cdot \nabla V + \tfrac12 |u|^2 \Big\} &= 0, \\ V(T, x) &= -r(x). \end{aligned} \]

Completing the square,

\[ u \cdot \nabla V + \tfrac12 |u|^2 = \tfrac12 |u + \nabla V|^2 - \tfrac12 |\nabla V|^2, \]

so the minimum over \(u\) is \(-\tfrac12 |\nabla V|^2\), reached at \(u = -\nabla V\), and the HJB equation of (3.3), with terminal cost \(-r\), is the equation for \(-\log h\) above. The optimal control is \(u = -\nabla V = \nabla \log h\), and the optimal cost is \(V(0, x_0) = -\log h(0, x_0)\). ∎

Two readings. By (3.2) the controller's energy \(\tfrac12 \mathbb E \int |u|^2\) is the KL of the controlled path measure from the free one, so (3.3) is Theorem 2.1 on path space: the free process tilted by \(e^{r(X_T)}\). Conditioning on an event \(A\) is the case \(r = \log \mathbf 1_A\), where the energy spent equals the surprise, \(-\log P(A)\).

3.5Figures

Figure 3.2A reward on the endpoint is a drift on the path

Tilting Brownian motion by a terminal reward, dQ/dP = exp(r(X₁))/Z, is the drift ∂x log h with h(t, x) = E[exp(r(X₁)) | X_t = x], and its KL from the free process is both E_Q[½∫u² dt] and E_Q[r(X₁)] − log Z.

At the defaults (the right bump at 2 with weight 0.6), log Z = −2.372. The steered paths spend ½∫u² dt = 1.161 ± 0.027, their endpoints give E_Q[r] − log Z = 1.175, and the exact KL is 1.162. Of the 1,000 endpoints, 40.9% land right of 0.25, against 40.8% under the exact tilt. Slide the bump to 3 and its weight to 0.95: the KL grows to 2.16. Tilting the endpoint distribution is a drift change, which is what reward fine-tuning of a diffusion model learns (adjoint matching).

3.6Four ways to see it

A change of measure reweights samples, adds a drift to a process, conditions on an event, and prices an asset. On paths these are one operation.

  1. 1Reweightingstatistics

    Sample from \(q\), weight each sample by \(dp/dq\), and averages estimate expectations under \(p\) (3.1). Statisticians call it importance sampling, and off-policy RL and PPO's ratio apply it to actions.

  2. 1 → 2On paths the weight is Girsanov's (3.2). Weighting the paths of the driftless process \(Q\) by \(\exp\big(\int b/\sigma^2\, dX - \tfrac12 \int |b|^2/\sigma^2\, dt\big)\) gives the same expectations as sampling the process with drift \(b\). Under the reweighted measure, \(W_t - \int_0^t b_s/\sigma\, ds\) is a Brownian motion, so the same paths read as noise plus the drift \(b\).

  3. 2A driftstochastic calculus

    Reweighting paths and adding a drift are the same act. The weight's log is linear in the path, and its expected value under the drifted process is the drift's energy, so the KL between the two processes is the energy a controller spends.

  4. 2 → 3Conditioning on \(X_T \in A\) reweights paths by \(\mathbf 1_A(X_T)/P(A)\). Its expectation given the path up to \(t\) is \(h(t, X_t)/h(0, x_0)\) with \(h(t, x) = P(X_T \in A \mid X_t = x)\). With \(\sigma = 1\), Itô's lemma and the backward equation \(\partial_t h + \tfrac12\Delta h = 0\) (Appendix A.1) give

    \[ d \log h(t, X_t) = \nabla \log h \cdot dX_t - \tfrac12\, |\nabla \log h|^2\, dt, \]

    the Girsanov exponent (3.2) with \(b = \nabla\log h\). Conditioning is the drift \(\nabla \log h\).

  5. 3Conditioningprobability

    Doob's h-transform turns a process conditioned on its future into a process with an extra drift (Figure 3.1). A terminal reward \(e^{r(X_T)}\) in place of an indicator gives Theorem 3.3, and guidance in diffusion models is the same drift with \(h(t, x) = p(y \mid X_t = x)\).

  6. 1 → 4Under the real-world measure a stock follows \(dS = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW\). Reweight by \(Z_T = e^{-\theta W_T - \theta^2 T/2}\) with \(\theta = (\mu - r)/\sigma\). By Girsanov, \(\tilde W_t = W_t + \theta t\) is a Brownian motion under the new measure \(Q\), and

    \[ dS = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, (d\tilde W - \theta\, dt) = r S\, dt + \sigma S\, d\tilde W. \]

  7. 4Pricingfinance

    Under \(Q\) every asset grows at the risk-free rate on average, and the price of a payoff \(H\) at time \(T\) is \(e^{-rT}\mathbb E_Q[H] = \mathbb E_P[e^{-rT} Z_T H]\). The state-price density \(e^{-rT} Z_T\) is the Radon-Nikodym weight, and Black-Scholes is this expectation for a call.

3.7Where it breaks and what is open

Equation (3.1) is exact whenever \(p\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(q\), and the estimator built on it is not. Importance sampling needs at least about \(e^{\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)}\) samples before its averages settle, and that many suffice only when the log weights concentrate (Chatterjee and Diaconis). In \(d\) dimensions small mismatches add up: shifting each coordinate of a standard Gaussian by \(a\) costs \(\mathrm{KL} = d a^2/2\), and the effective sample size falls like \(n e^{-d a^2}\). Past the point where it should drop below one sample, the measured effective sample size stays high while the weighted averages are wrong, so the diagnostic hides its own failure (Figure 3.3). On paths, (3.2) makes that KL the energy of the missing drift, so reweighting paths from a poor controller costs samples exponential in the energy it failed to supply. Sampling methods learn the control for this reason instead of reweighting.

Figure 3.3Importance weights collapse with dimension

When p and q differ by a shift of a in each of d coordinates, KL(p‖q) = d a²/2 grows with d, the sample size importance sampling needs grows like e^KL, and the weights of a fixed sample pile onto a few draws.

Slide d up at a = 0.2. At the default d = 50, KL(p‖q) = 1: the measured effective sample size (ESS) is 322 of 2,000 against the large-n value of 271, the largest weight holds 1.6% of the total, and the mean weight is 0.960 where (3.1) promises 1. At d = 200 the large-n ESS is 0.671 draws, while the measured ESS still reads 49.1 and the mean weight falls to 0.486. The draws never reach the rare large weights that set E_q[w²], so the measured ESS overstates the sample. Push a to 0.5 as well: the largest weight holds 49.4% of the total, the mean weight is 2.05e−5, the estimate of a = 0.5 comes out 0.200, and e^KL = 7.20e10 draws are needed against the 2,000 drawn.

  1. Learning the control so the weights stay near 1. ASBS and adjoint matching learn a drift whose paths need almost no reweighting. A sampler that uses a learned \(-Q\) as its energy will chase that function's errors. How the variance of the weights grows from Pendulum to Hopper, and whether the bridge from the behavior policy keeps it small, is open.
  2. Twisted sampling for language. Twisted sequential Monte Carlo learns h-functions, called twists, for language models (Zhao et al.), which is Theorem 3.3 on token sequences. Using it to sample prompts conditioned on a target response, the task of Diffusion Investigator Agents, is open.
  3. Guidance without a trained classifier. Training-free guidance replaces \(h(t, x) = \mathbb E[p(y \mid X_0) \mid X_t = x]\) by \(p(y \mid \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_t = x])\), moving the expectation inside. How large the resulting error is, and when it matters for jailbreak search, is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 3.1Girsanov's KL for a constant drift

    For a constant drift \(b\) on \([0, T]\) with \(N\) steps of size \(h\), compute the KL between the laws of the increments under \(P\) and \(Q\), and take \(N \to \infty\). Compare with the KL between the endpoint laws \(\mathcal N(bT, \sigma^2 T)\) and \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 T)\), and explain why they agree.

    Solution

    The increments are independent, so the path KL is \(N\) times \(\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal N(bh, \sigma^2 h) \,\|\, \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 h)\big) = \frac{b^2 h^2}{2\sigma^2 h}\), which totals \(\frac{b^2 T}{2 \sigma^2}\) for every \(N\). The endpoint KL is \(\frac{(bT)^2}{2\sigma^2 T} = \frac{b^2 T}{2\sigma^2}\), the same.

    Under both laws the path given its endpoint is the same Brownian bridge, so the endpoint carries all the information that separates them. In general the data-processing inequality makes the path KL at least the endpoint KL, with equality exactly when the paths given their endpoint have the same law under both measures. The h-transform drifts of Theorem 3.3 have this property, and a drift that varies in time without depending on the endpoint does not.

  2. Derivation 3.2The Brownian bridge as an h-transform

    Condition Brownian motion started at 0 to be at \(y\) at time \(T\). Using \(h(t, x) = p_{T-t}(y - x)\), with \(p_s\) the \(\mathcal N(0, s)\) density, derive the drift of the conditioned process and check that it pulls the path to \(y\).

    Solution

    \(\log h(t, x) = -\frac{(y - x)^2}{2(T - t)} + \text{const}\), so \(\nabla\log h = \frac{y - x}{T - t}\) and \(dX_t = \frac{y - X_t}{T - t}\, dt + dW_t\).

    The pull grows without bound as \(t \to T\). Solving the linear equation gives mean \(\frac{t}{T} y\) and variance \(\frac{t(T - t)}{T}\), which vanishes at \(t = T\), so the path ends at \(y\).
