Chapter 4

Fixed points

Contraction, from analysis

A map on a complete space that shrinks every distance by a fixed factor \(\gamma \lt 1\) has exactly one fixed point, and iterating the map reaches it geometrically fast. A step-by-step computation is the fixed point of a map on its whole sequence, so it can be solved in parallel rounds.

Uses Chapter 1.

4.1Motivation

Suppose you type a number into a calculator set to radians and press the cos key again and again. From 1 the display reads 0.5403, 0.8576, 0.6543, 0.7935, swinging above and below a middle value and closing in on it. After 35 presses its first six decimals stop changing at 0.739085. Start from 100 instead, or from −3, and the display settles on the same 0.739085. That number is the one \(x\) with \(\cos x = x\). The equation cannot be solved with algebra, yet the calculator found its solution by pressing one key.

Many quantities are defined the same way, by an equation they must satisfy instead of a formula: the value of a policy, the stationary distribution of a chain, the importance of a web page, the trajectory of an ODE. Solving such an equation directly means inverting a large system or running a long sequential loop. But when does pressing the key again and again work? Why does every start land on the same answer, and how many presses does a given accuracy take? The answer is a property of the map: it brings any two inputs closer together by at least a fixed factor. A map with this property is a contraction, and it gives a third way to solve: apply the defining map again and again from any start, and the error shrinks by a fixed factor each time. The same view turns a sequential computation into a map on its whole trajectory, which can be iterated in parallel.

PAPERA document that moved capital

The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

Rank a page by the ranks of the pages that link to it, and let the link structure of the web do the judging.

Sergey Brin and Lawrence Page, 1998 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

PageRank was the core of Google's search, which outranked keyword matching and built the company.

The link to this chapter: the paper defines \(\mathrm{PR}(A) = (1 - d) + d \sum_i \mathrm{PR}(T_i)/C(T_i)\) with \(d = 0.85\) and computes it by "a simple iterative algorithm" (Section 2.1.1). When every page has an outgoing link, each iteration is a contraction with factor \(d\) in the \(\ell_1\) norm, so the error shrinks by a factor of at most 0.85 per sweep (Theorem 4.1, and the PageRank exercise). As printed, with \(1 - d\) where \((1 - d)/N\) would make the ranks sum to one, they sum to the number of pages.

4.2Intuition

Start with the smallest map that shows the idea, \(T(x) = x/2 + 1\). Its fixed point is 2, because \(2/2 + 1 = 2\). Start at 10 and apply \(T\) again and again: 6, 4, 3, 2.5, 2.25. The distance to 2 goes 8, 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, halving at every step, because

\[ T(x) - 2 = \tfrac12\, (x - 2). \]

Start at −6 instead, and the run is −2, 0, 1, 1.5, 1.75, with the same distances 8, 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25. The two runs start 16 apart and are 8, 4, 2, 1 apart after each step, since \(|Tx - Ty| = \tfrac12 |x - y|\) for every pair. Every run is squeezed onto every other, so they all end at one point. Could \(T\) have a second fixed point? Two fixed points stay where they are under \(T\), and their distance would also have to halve, so it is zero.

Now double instead of halving. The map \(T(x) = 2x - 2\) has the same fixed point 2, and from 3 it runs 4, 6, 10, 18, doubling the distance at each step. Iteration runs away from it because the factor is 2.

The calculator's cos key is the first kind. After one press the display lies between −1 and 1, and on that interval cos brings any two numbers closer by at least the factor \(\sin 1 = 0.841\). Near the fixed point the curve has slope \(-\sin(0.739085) = -0.674\), so each press multiplies the error by about −0.674. The error loses a third of its size and changes sign, which is why the display swings above and below 0.739085: from 1 the errors are 0.261, −0.199, 0.118, −0.085.

A map that shrinks every distance by a fixed factor, applied again and again, walks every starting point into its one fixed point, and each step cuts the error by at least that factor.

Figure 4.1A cobweb into the fixed point

Iterating a map whose slope at its fixed point is under 1 in size walks a cobweb into the fixed point, and near it the error shrinks by that slope at every step.

The map is T(x) = 2 + s·sin(x − 2). Its slope at x* = 2 is s, and its Lipschitz constant on the whole line is γ = |s|, so (4.1) applies whenever |s| < 1. At the default s = 0.6 the cobweb climbs a staircase into x*, the error ratio over the last four steps is 0.6000, equal to |T′(x*)|, and at k = 10 the error is 5.5e−3 under Banach's bound of 1.5e−2. Slide s to −0.6: the staircase becomes a spiral with the same ratio. At s = 0.9 the ratio is 0.8984, and the bound loosens to 2.44 against an actual error of 0.229. Past 1 in size the fixed point repels: at s = 1.3 the cobweb settles on another fixed point at 0.7785, and at s = −1.3 on a 2-cycle between 0.7785 and 3.2215.

4.3Statement

The halving map and the cos key raise three questions: which maps find their fixed point this way, on what spaces, and how many steps a given accuracy takes. Theorem 4.1 answers all three on any complete space with a distance, and for the halving map started at 10 its bound is \(8 \cdot 2^{-k}\), which is the exact error.

A metric space is a set with a distance \(d(x, y)\), such as the real line with \(|x - y|\), or the value tables of Theorem 4.2 with the largest gap over states. It is complete when every sequence whose later points all lie within any chosen distance of one another, a Cauchy sequence, has a limit inside the set.

Theorem 4.1 (Banach)

If \(T\) maps a complete metric space to itself and \(d(Tx, Ty) \le \gamma\, d(x, y)\) with \(\gamma \lt 1\), then \(T\) has exactly one fixed point \(x^*\), and the iterates \(x_{k+1} = T x_k\) satisfy

\[ d(x_k, x^*) \le \frac{\gamma^k}{1 - \gamma}\, d(x_1, x_0). \tag{4.1} \]

Each hypothesis is needed. Without completeness the limit can be missing: on the interval \(0 \lt x \le 1\) the map \(T(x) = x/2\) shrinks distances by \(\tfrac12\), and its iterates 1, 1/2, 1/4, ... head for 0, which is not in the space. The factor must be fixed below 1. On \(x \ge 1\) the map \(T(x) = x + 1/x\) brings every pair strictly closer, because its slope \(1 - 1/x^2\) lies in \([0, 1)\), yet \(T(x) \gt x\) everywhere, so it has no fixed point. At \(\gamma = 1\) the shift \(T(x) = x + 1\) keeps every distance and has no fixed point, while \(T(x) = x\) fixes every point. The map must also send the space into itself: on \([0, 1]\) the halving map \(x/2 + 1\) contracts, and its fixed point 2 lies outside.

The second statement values a plan. Suppose a job pays 1 every day forever, and a payment one day later is worth 0.9 of one today. Its value \(V\) must satisfy \(V = 1 + 0.9\, V\), so the value is 10, and the map \(V \mapsto 1 + 0.9\, V\) shrinks distances by 0.9. From \(V = 0\) it gives 1, 1.9, 2.71, 3.439, and the gap to 10 goes 10, 9, 8.1, 7.29, 6.561. The gap falls below 0.1 after 44 sweeps. With a discount of 0.99 the value is 100, and the gap needs 688 sweeps to fall below 0.1.

A real problem has many states \(s\), a choice of action \(a\) in each, a reward \(r(s, a)\) for taking \(a\) in \(s\), a probability \(P(s' \mid s, a)\) of landing in state \(s'\) next, and a discount \(\gamma \lt 1\) on each later step. A guess \(V\) gives a value to every state, and the gap between two guesses is measured at the state where it is largest, \(\|V - W\|_\infty = \max_s |V(s) - W(s)|\). The map that improves a guess is the Bellman backup \(\mathcal T\). With one state, one action, \(r = 1\), and \(\gamma = 0.9\), it is the map above.

Theorem 4.2 (the Bellman operator contracts)

\[ (\mathcal T V)(s) = \max_a \Big[ r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V(s') \Big] \quad\text{satisfies}\quad \|\mathcal T V - \mathcal T W\|_\infty \le \gamma\, \|V - W\|_\infty. \tag{4.2} \]

The third statement turns a loop into a fixed point. Euler's method for \(dx/dt = x\) with step 0.1 from \(x_0 = 1\) multiplies by 1.1 at each step, one entry after another, and ends at \(x_{10} = 1.1^{10}\), which is 2.59374. Write the whole run as one list. Each entry is the start plus the steps before it,

\[ x_i = 1 + 0.1\, (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_{i-1}), \]

so the true list is a fixed point of the map that recomputes every entry this way from the current list, and that map updates all ten unknown entries at once. From the guess \((1, 1, \dots, 1)\), the last entry reads 2, 2.45, 2.57, 2.591, and 2.59352 after five rounds, within 0.00022 of the sequential answer. After round \(k\) the first \(k\) steps are exact, and the rest are already close.

Proposition 4.3 (a sequence, solved in parallel)

The Euler trajectory \(x_{i+1} = x_i + h\, f(x_i)\), \(i \lt N\), is the fixed point of the map \(\Phi(x)_i = x_0 + h \sum_{j \lt i} f(x_j)\) on the whole sequence. Iterating \(\Phi\) from a guess \(x^{(0)}\) with the right \(x_0\), one round \(x^{(k+1)} = \Phi(x^{(k)})\) at a time, makes the first \(k\) steps exact after \(k\) rounds. Let \(e_{k, i} = |x^{(k)}_i - x_i|\) be the error of entry \(i\) after \(k\) rounds. If \(f\) has Lipschitz constant \(L\), so that \(|f(x) - f(y)| \le L\, |x - y|\), and \(T = Nh\) is the time the trajectory covers, the error after \(k\) rounds is at most

\[ \frac{(L T)^k}{k!}\, \max_i |e_{0, i}|. \tag{4.3} \]

For the toy, \(L = 1\) and \(T = 1\), and the guess starts 1.594 off at the last entry, so (4.3) promises an error of at most \(1.594/5! = 0.013\) after five rounds. The measured error, 0.00022, sits well inside it.

4.4Derivation

(4.1). Each step shrinks the gap between consecutive iterates by at least \(\gamma\), and applying this \(k\) times,

\[ d(x_{k+1}, x_k) = d(T x_k, T x_{k-1}) \le \gamma\, d(x_k, x_{k-1}) \le \dots \le \gamma^k\, d(x_1, x_0). \]

For \(m \gt k\), walk from \(x_k\) to \(x_m\) one step at a time. The triangle inequality bounds the distance by the sum of the steps, and the finite geometric sum is at most the infinite one:

\[ d(x_m, x_k) \le \sum_{j=k}^{m-1} d(x_{j+1}, x_j) \le \big(\gamma^k + \gamma^{k+1} + \dots + \gamma^{m-1}\big)\, d(x_1, x_0) \le \frac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma}\, d(x_1, x_0). \]

The right side shrinks to zero as \(k\) grows, so the sequence is Cauchy, and completeness gives it a limit \(x^*\) inside the space. The limit is fixed. \(T\) is continuous, because \(d(Tx_k, Tx^*) \le \gamma\, d(x_k, x^*)\), so \(T x_k\) tends to \(T x^*\). But \(T x_k = x_{k+1}\) also tends to \(x^*\), so \(T x^* = x^*\). Letting \(m \to \infty\) in the display, \(d(x_m, x_k)\) tends to \(d(x^*, x_k)\), which gives (4.1). Two fixed points would satisfy \(d(x^*, y^*) = d(Tx^*, Ty^*) \le \gamma\, d(x^*, y^*)\), and with \(\gamma \lt 1\) this forces \(d(x^*, y^*) = 0\), so they coincide.

(4.2). Fix a state \(s\), and write \(f(a)\) and \(g(a)\) for the bracket in (4.2) with \(V\) and with \(W\), so that \((\mathcal T V)(s)\) is the largest \(f(a)\) and \((\mathcal T W)(s)\) the largest \(g(a)\). For any two functions of the action, and because the weights \(P(s' \mid s, a)\) sum to one,

\[ \big|\max_a f(a) - \max_a g(a)\big| \le \max_a |f(a) - g(a)|, \qquad \Big|\gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\,(V - W)(s')\Big| \le \gamma\, \|V - W\|_\infty. \]

The first holds because if \(f\) peaks at \(a^*\), then \(\max f - \max g \le f(a^*) - g(a^*)\), and the same holds with \(f\) and \(g\) swapped. The second holds because an average of numbers no larger than \(\|V - W\|_\infty\) in size is no larger in size itself. In \(f - g\) the rewards cancel and only the sum is left, so chaining the two,

\[ \big|(\mathcal T V)(s) - (\mathcal T W)(s)\big| \le \max_a \Big|\gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\,(V - W)(s')\Big| \le \gamma\, \|V - W\|_\infty. \]

This holds at every state, and the largest left side over \(s\) is \(\|\mathcal T V - \mathcal T W\|_\infty\), so together the two facts give (4.2).

(4.3). Entry \(i\) of \(\Phi^k(x)\) depends only on entries before it, and entry 0 is given, so exactness spreads one entry per round. The true trajectory is a fixed point, \(x = \Phi(x)\), so the error \(e_{k, i} = |x^{(k)}_i - x_i|\) after \(k\) rounds compares two values of \(\Phi\). Subtracting term by term and applying the Lipschitz bound to each term, it obeys

\[ e_{k+1, i} = \big|\Phi(x^{(k)})_i - \Phi(x)_i\big| \le h \sum_{j \lt i} \big|f(x^{(k)}_j) - f(x_j)\big| \le hL \sum_{j \lt i} e_{k, j}. \]

Write \(E = \max_j e_{0, j}\), and suppose that \(e_{k, j} \le (hL)^k \binom{j}{k} E\) for every \(j\), which holds at \(k = 0\). Then

\[ e_{k+1, i} \le hL \sum_{j \lt i} (hL)^k \binom{j}{k} E = (hL)^{k+1} \binom{i}{k+1} E, \]

by the identity \(\sum_{j \lt i} \binom{j}{k} = \binom{i}{k+1}\), which counts the subsets of \(\{0, \dots, i-1\}\) with \(k + 1\) elements by their largest element \(j\). That completes the induction. Writing out the binomial coefficient and bounding each factor of its numerator by \(i\),

\[ e_{k, i} \le (hL)^k\, \frac{i(i-1)\cdots(i-k+1)}{k!}\, E \le \frac{(L\, ih)^k}{k!}\, E, \]

and \(ih \le T\). ∎

Linear recurrences. When each step is affine, \(x_{i+1} = a_i x_i + b_i\), composing two steps gives another affine step, \((a_1, b_1)\) then \((a_2, b_2)\) is \((a_1 a_2,\; a_2 b_1 + b_2)\), and this composition is associative. A prefix scan therefore computes every \(x_i\) in \(\log_2 N\) parallel rounds with no iteration at all, and Newton's method reduces a nonlinear recurrence to a few such scans.

4.5Figures

Figure 4.2Value iteration contracts by γ

The Bellman backup is a γ-contraction in the max norm, so value iteration from any start reaches the one fixed point V* with ‖V_k − V*‖∞ ≤ γ^k ‖V_0 − V*‖∞.

Every move costs 0.04, slips sideways with probability 0.2, and the goal pays +1 and ends the episode. Press play: value spreads out from the goal one cell per sweep. At γ = 0.9 the largest measured ratio is 0.880 and the error reaches 1e−6 in 37 sweeps, where γ^k alone guarantees it by sweep 131. Slide γ to 0.99: the ratio rises to 0.981, still below γ, and 44 sweeps suffice against a guarantee of 1,369. For the first 13 sweeps, while value spreads, the error shrinks by 0.85 to 0.88 per sweep at γ = 0.9. Once value reaches every cell, it shrinks by about 0.55.

Figure 4.3A sampler's steps, solved in parallel rounds

N Euler steps of an ODE are the fixed point of a map on the whole trajectory, x_i = x_0 + h·Σ f(x_j, t_j) over j < i, so Picard rounds that update all N states at once reach the sequential answer in far fewer than N rounds when the drift is smooth.

Press play: after round k the first k steps are exact, yet the whole trajectory settles long before k reaches N. At N = 100 the largest change drops below 1e−4 in 13 rounds (7.7 steps per round), and the error is 2.7 at the default k = 3, 0.26 at k = 6, and 3.4e−6 at k = 13. Slide N from 10 to 400: the rounds go from 9 to 13 while the sequential steps grow 40-fold, so each round does the work of 30.8 steps at N = 400. This is the mechanism behind parallel sampling of diffusion models (ParaDiGMS).

Figure 4.4A linear recurrence in log₂ T rounds

Each step h ↦ a(t)·h + b(t) is an affine map, and composing affine maps is associative, so a prefix scan computes every h(t) of h(t) = a(t)·h(t−1) + b(t) in log₂ T parallel rounds.

Slide r from 0 to 4 at T = 16: the positions that match the loop double each round, 1, 2, 4, 8, then all 16, and the final scan differs from the loop by 4.4e−16. Switch T to 32: one more round, five in all, against 32 sequential steps. Mamba trains its selective recurrence with this scan, and linear attention is the case a = 1.

4.6Four ways to see it

A fixed point is where a cobweb ends, where gradient descent stops, where a parallel solver agrees with a sequential one, and where no player wants to move. The first three use contraction, and the fourth shows what is left without it.

  1. 1A contractionanalysis

    Iterate a map whose slope is below 1 in size and the iterates walk a cobweb into the fixed point, shrinking the error by the slope each step (Theorem 4.1, Figure 4.1). Value iteration is this picture with the max norm (Theorem 4.2).

  2. 1 → 2Gradient descent is the map \(T(x) = x - \eta \nabla f(x)\), whose fixed points are the stationary points of \(f\). Its Jacobian is \(I - \eta \nabla^2 f\), so if \(\mu I \preceq \nabla^2 f \preceq L I\),

    \[ \|T x - T y\| \le \max\big(|1 - \eta\mu|,\, |1 - \eta L|\big)\, \|x - y\|, \]

    a contraction for \(0 \lt \eta \lt 2/L\), with the smallest factor \((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)\), \(\kappa = L/\mu\), at \(\eta = 2/(\mu + L)\).

  3. 2Gradient descentoptimization

    Convergence rates of first-order methods are contraction factors, and the condition number \(\kappa\) sets them. Chapter 9 keeps the same argument when \(f\) is not convex, with \(f\) itself as the quantity that shrinks.

  4. 1 → 3The whole-trajectory map of Proposition 4.3 is no contraction in the max norm, and it becomes one in a weighted norm. With \(\|e\|_\lambda = \max_i e^{-\lambda i h} |e_i|\),

    \[ e^{-\lambda i h}\, |\Phi(x)_i - \Phi(y)_i| \le e^{-\lambda i h}\, hL \sum_{j \lt i} e^{\lambda j h}\, \|x - y\|_\lambda \le \frac{hL}{e^{\lambda h} - 1}\, \|x - y\|_\lambda \le \frac{L}{\lambda}\, \|x - y\|_\lambda, \]

    so \(\lambda = 2L\) gives the factor \(\tfrac12\).

  5. 3A sequence solved in parallelnumerical analysis

    A sequential computation is the fixed point of a map on its whole trajectory, and every entry of an iterate can be computed at once (Figure 4.3). Jacobi decoding of language models, ParaDiGMS for diffusion, and DEER for recurrent networks iterate this map, and a prefix scan solves the affine case exactly (Figure 4.4).

  6. 1 → 4Drop contraction and keep only continuity on a compact convex set. Brouwer's theorem still gives a fixed point, with no uniqueness and no promise that iteration finds it. Nash applied it to the map that moves each player's mixed strategy \(\sigma_i\) toward the pure strategies \(k\) that beat it, with gains \(g_{ik} = \max\big(0,\, u_i(k, \sigma_{-i}) - u_i(\sigma)\big)\):

    \[ \sigma_{ik} \mapsto \frac{\sigma_{ik} + g_{ik}}{1 + \sum_{k'} g_{ik'}}. \]

    The map is continuous on a product of simplices, and its fixed points are exactly the equilibria.

  7. 4Equilibriumeconomics

    Every finite game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies (Nash, by Brouwer's theorem), and an exchange economy under mild conditions has prices that clear every market (Arrow and Debreu, through an existence theorem for generalized games that rests on a fixed-point theorem). Existence comes without an algorithm: iterating best responses can cycle (Chapter 8).

4.7Where it breaks and what is open

Proposition 4.3 bounds the error after \(k\) rounds by \((LT)^k/k!\), and the bound falls below a tolerance only once \(k\) passes about \(e \cdot LT\). A stiff drift has a large \(L\), and once \(LT\) is comparable to the number of steps \(N\), the rounds needed approach \(N\) and parallel rounds buy nothing over sequential steps (Figure 4.5). Chaotic dynamics fail the same way, because errors grow along the trajectory. Newton's method on the whole trajectory converges in far fewer rounds (DEER), at the price of a Jacobian per step and an instability that damping repairs (Gonzalez et al.).

Figure 4.5A stiff drift needs as many rounds as steps

Picard rounds on a whole trajectory shrink the error like (LT)^k/k!, which starts to fall only once k passes LT, so a stiff drift with a large L needs nearly as many rounds as there are sequential steps, and the parallel speedup disappears.

The drift has Lipschitz constant L = λ on [0, T] with T = 1, and the map is the one in Proposition 4.3. At the default λ = 4 the error first grows, to 3.87 at round 3, then falls below 1e−6 at round 17, a speedup of 3.76 over the 64 sequential steps, and (4.3) guarantees it by round 20. Slide λ to 60, still a stable Euler step with λh = 0.9375: the error peaks at 1.2e17 at round 30, the bound promises nothing before round 64, and the iterate matches the sequential trajectory only at round 64, when the exact prefix covers every step, a speedup of 1.00. At λ = 0.5, 6 rounds suffice.

  1. An acceptance rule for parallel sampling. A rule that stops where the parallel guesses disagree is closer to speculative decoding's acceptance test than to ParaDiGMS's fixed tolerance. Whether it keeps the samples' distribution exact, and how many model calls it saves on a flow-matching image model, is open. The project below measures it.
  2. Fixed points with no contraction. Equilibria of games, and the saddle points GAN training looks for, exist by Brouwer's theorem, and no known algorithm finds them fast in general: computing a Nash equilibrium of a two-player game is PPAD-complete. Which learning dynamics reach equilibrium in the games of machine learning, such as self-play and red-teaming, is open. Chapter 8 takes it up.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 4.1 Contraction

    • Three states in a ring, γ = 0.9. In state s, stay earns s and keeps you there, except that it slips to s + 1 (mod 3) with probability 0.1. Move earns 0 and goes to s + 1 (mod 3).
    • Run value iteration from V = 0. How many sweeps reach ‖V − V*‖∞ ≤ 1e-6, and how many does γ alone guarantee before running?
    Answer
    optimal_values()        # [13.834, 15.371, 17.079]
sweeps_to(1e-6)         # 158
a_priori_sweeps(1e-6)   # 160

  2. Exercise 4.2 Parallel sampling of an ODE

    • dx/dt = −2x + cos(3t), x(0) = 1, on [0, 2] with 100 Euler steps.
    • Each round may evaluate the right-hand side at all 100 steps at once. Starting from x_i = 1 everywhere, how many rounds until no state changes by more than 1e-8?
    Answer
    parallel_rounds()          # 21
parallel_solution()[-1]    # 0.09315

  3. Exercise 4.3 A linear recurrence in three rounds

    • h_t = a_t·h_{t−1} + b_t for t = 1..8, with h_0 = 0.
    • Compute all eight h_t in three rounds, where each round may combine any pairs of steps at once.
    Answer
    combine((0.5, 1), (1, 2))                                        # (0.5, 3)
scan([0.5, 1, 2, 0.5, 1, 2, 0.5, 1], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8])   # [1.0, 3.0, 9.0, 8.5, 13.5, 33.0, 23.5, 31.5]

  4. Exercise 4.4 A nonlinear RNN over the whole sequence

    • h_t = tanh(0.9·h_{t−1} + x_t) with x_t = sin(t), h_0 = 0, for t = 1..64.
    • Each iteration may run one linear recurrence over all 64 positions. Starting from h_t = 0, how many iterations reach a max error of 1e-10 against the 64 sequential steps?
    Answer
    iterations()    # 4
final_state()   # 0.4177

  5. Exercise 4.5 Decoding 16 tokens in parallel

    • A toy model picks each next token deterministically from the sequence so far. Greedy decoding of 16 tokens takes 16 calls in a row.
    • Each round may call the model at all 16 positions at once, on the current guess. Start from 16 zeros, and count rounds until the guess is the greedy output.
    Answer
    rounds(lambda seq: (seq[-1] + 1) % 10, prompt=[3])        # 16
rounds(lambda seq: seq[-1] // 4 + len(seq), prompt=[9])   # 3

  6. Exercise 4.6 PageRank

    • Four pages: A links to B and C, B to C, C to A, and D to C. Damping 0.85.
    • Iterate r ← 0.15/4 + 0.85·M r from the uniform vector. Report the ranks and the largest ratio between successive errors ‖r_k − r*‖₁.
    Answer
    pagerank()              # [0.3725, 0.1958, 0.3941, 0.0375]
largest_error_ratio()   # 0.85

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 4.1The Bellman contraction

    Prove (4.2). Then, with rewards in \([0, 1]\) and \(V_0 = 0\), find how many sweeps of value iteration guarantee \(\|V_k - V^*\|_\infty \le \varepsilon\).

    Solution

    For each state,

    \[ \big|\max_a F(a) - \max_a G(a)\big| \le \max_a |F(a) - G(a)|: \]

    if the left maximum is attained at \(a^*\) by \(F\), then \(\max F - \max G \le F(a^*) - G(a^*)\), and symmetrically. Apply it with \(F(a) = r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) V(s')\) and \(G\) the same with \(W\). The rewards cancel, and \(|\gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)(V - W)(s')| \le \gamma \|V - W\|_\infty\) because the weights sum to 1.

    \(\|V^* - V_0\|_\infty \le 1/(1 - \gamma)\), so \(\|V_k - V^*\|_\infty \le \gamma^k/(1 - \gamma)\), which is at most \(\varepsilon\) once \(k \ge \log\big(1/(\varepsilon(1 - \gamma))\big) / \log(1/\gamma)\). For \(\gamma\) near 1 that is about \(\frac{1}{1 - \gamma} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon(1 - \gamma)}\) sweeps.

  2. Derivation 4.2A scan, then Newton on the whole trajectory

    Show that composing affine steps \(x \mapsto a x + b\) is associative, and that a prefix scan computes every \(x_i\) of \(x_{i+1} = a_i x_i + b_i\) in \(\lceil \log_2 N \rceil\) rounds. Then write one Newton step for the nonlinear recurrence \(x_{i+1} = F(x_i)\) as an affine recurrence.

    Solution

    Composition is function composition, which is associative, and in coordinates \((a_1, b_1)\) then \((a_2, b_2)\) is \((a_2 a_1,\, a_2 b_1 + b_2)\). In round \(r\) every position \(i\) combines its partial result with the one \(2^r\) places earlier, so after round \(r\) position \(i\) holds the composition of the last \(\min(i, 2^{r+1})\) steps, and \(\lceil \log_2 N \rceil\) rounds cover every prefix.

    Linearize \(F\) at the current guess \(x^{(k)}\): \(x_{i+1} = F(x^{(k)}_i) + J_i\, (x_i - x^{(k)}_i)\) with \(J_i = F'(x^{(k)}_i)\). This is the affine recurrence with \(a_i = J_i\) and \(b_i = F(x^{(k)}_i) - J_i x^{(k)}_i\), solved by one scan per Newton step, as in DEER.

Chapter 5

Optimal transport

The geometry of distributions

Distributions form a space whose distance is the least cost of moving mass from one to the other. In that space the straight line between two distributions moves mass instead of fading it, diffusion is gradient descent on free energy, and adding entropy gives the Schrödinger bridge.

Uses Chapters 1, 2, and 4, and Appendix A.2, A.4, and A.5.

5.1Motivation

Suppose two piles of sand sit on a table a millimeter apart, and you want a number for how different they are. Slide one pile onto the other, and the number should shrink smoothly to zero. A generative model needs exactly this number when its samples sit just beside the data, because training follows its gradient.

Comparing two distributions by how much their densities overlap fails when they barely overlap: KL is infinite and total variation is maximal for two point masses a millimeter apart, and both stay the same at a meter, so a learning signal built on either gives no gradient. But how else could two piles be compared? Count the work it takes to shovel one into the shape of the other. Monge asked in 1781 for the cheapest way to move a pile of earth into a hole, and Kantorovich relaxed the question to plans that may split mass. The distance that results grows smoothly as one distribution slides away from another, and it turns the space of distributions into a geometric space with straight lines and gradients.

5.2Intuition

Start with one grain of sand at 0 that must end at 2. Charge each unit of mass the square of the distance it travels, so the move costs \(2^2 = 4\), and call the square root of the cheapest cost the distance between the two piles, here 2. A grain 0.001 from where it should be is 0.001 away. KL and total variation see only that the grain is in the wrong place, at 0.001 or at 1000 alike.

Now ask for the pile halfway between. Moving the grain gives one grain at 1, at distance 1 from each end, so the two halves add up to the whole 2. Averaging the two pictures gives half a grain at 0 and half at 2. Its distance from the start is \(\sqrt 2\), about 1.41, since half the mass must travel 2 and \(\tfrac12 \cdot 2^2 = 2\). Its distance from the end is \(\sqrt 2\) too, a total of 2.83. The average is a detour, because it fades one pile out and the other in. Slide the grain to \(2t\) and its distance from the start is \(2t\), growing at a steady rate. Mix instead, with weight \(t\) on the end, and the distance is \(2\sqrt t\), which shoots up at the start: at \(t = \tfrac14\) the mixture is already 1 away, and the sliding grain only 0.5.

Two grains bring in the choice of plan. Put half a unit of mass at 0 and half at 1, to be moved to 2 and 3. Sending 0 to 2 and 1 to 3 costs \(\tfrac12 \cdot 4 + \tfrac12 \cdot 4 = 4\). Crossing, with 0 to 3 and 1 to 2, costs \(\tfrac12 \cdot 9 + \tfrac12 \cdot 1 = 5\). Splitting each grain evenly over both holes costs 4.5. The cheapest plan pairs the grains in order, the distance is again 2, and halfway along it the grains sit at 1 and 2.

Move mass along straight lines instead of fading it out in one place and in at another, and distributions acquire distances, midpoints, and gradients.

Figure 5.1Moving mass against fading it

The straight line between two distributions in W2 moves every quantile of p₀ along the monotone map T = F₁⁻¹∘F₀, so the distance from p₀ grows exactly like t.

Slide t. The displacement curve carries p₀'s two bumps toward each other until they merge into p₁, and its W2 from p₀ is exactly t times W2(p₀, p₁) = 4.023. The mixture keeps both of p₀'s bumps and grows p₁ in place, and at t = 0.5 it sits 0.549 of the way. Each particle travels straight from its quantile in p₀ to the same quantile in p₁.

5.3Statement

The grains raise the general question: for any two distributions, what does the cheapest plan cost, and what does it look like? A plan, called a coupling, says how much mass goes from each \(x\) to each \(y\), so it is a joint distribution of a start \(X\) and an end \(Y\) whose two marginals are the starting and ending piles. For the two grains a coupling sends \(a\) from 0 to 2 and \(\tfrac12 - a\) from 0 to 3, and the grain at 1 sends the rest, so its cost is

\[ 4a + 9\big(\tfrac12 - a\big) + 1\big(\tfrac12 - a\big) + 4a = 5 - 2a, \qquad 0 \le a \le \tfrac12, \]

and the cheapest, at \(a = \tfrac12\), costs 4.

Definition 5.1 (the 2-Wasserstein distance, and its dual)

\[ W_2(p, q)^2 = \min_{\pi \in \Pi(p, q)} \mathbb E_{(X, Y) \sim \pi}\, |X - Y|^2, \tag{5.1} \]

where \(\Pi(p, q)\) is the set of couplings with marginals \(p\) and \(q\). By Kantorovich duality the same number is a maximum over prices,

\[ W_2(p, q)^2 = \max_{\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le |x - y|^2} \Big\{ \mathbb E_p[\varphi] + \mathbb E_q[\psi] \Big\}, \]

and an optimal plan moves mass only between pairs where the prices are tight, \(\varphi(x) + \psi(y) = |x - y|^2\).

The prices certify that a plan is cheapest. Think of a shipper who charges \(\varphi(x)\) to collect a unit of mass at \(x\) and \(\psi(y)\) to deliver it at \(y\). The constraint \(\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le |x - y|^2\) means no customer would rather move the mass directly, and then the shipper's income can never exceed the cost of any plan. For the two grains, the prices \(\varphi(0) = 4\), \(\varphi(1) = 0\), \(\psi(2) = 0\), and \(\psi(3) = 4\) meet all four constraints, are tight on the straight pairs (0, 2) and (1, 3), and earn

\[ \tfrac12 (4 + 0) + \tfrac12 (0 + 4) = 4, \]

the cost of the straight plan, so no plan is cheaper.

On a line the two grains were paired in order, and the next statement says the cheapest plan on a line always pairs mass in order, as a map when \(p\) has no atoms. Write \(F_p(x)\) for the fraction of \(p\)'s mass at or left of \(x\), and \(F_q^{-1}(u)\) for the first point with fraction \(u\) of \(q\)'s mass at or left of it. The monotone map \(T = F_q^{-1} \circ F_p\) sends each point to the point of \(q\) with the same rank, so the lowest tenth of \(p\) goes to the lowest tenth of \(q\). With equal grains it sends 0 to 2 and 1 to 3, because each grain lands on a grain of the same mass. An atom, a single point carrying positive mass, breaks this when the masses do not match: no map can send a full grain at 0 onto half a grain at −1 and half at 1, though a plan can split it. In the plane, sand spread along a segment has no density, and the same failure appears: to move a segment onto two parallel segments one unit to either side, the cheapest plan splits every grain in half, and no map reaches its cost.

The last part of the statement watches the sand move. Let \(\rho_t\) be the density of sand at time \(t\) between 0 and 1, and \(v_t\) the velocity that carries it. The continuity equation (Appendix A.4) says sand is neither made nor lost, and the integral of \(\rho_t |v_t|^2\) over space and time is the flow's kinetic energy, counted without the physicist's factor \(\tfrac12\). A single grain moving from 0 to 2 at the constant speed 2 for one unit of time has energy \(2^2 \times 1 = 4\), the squared distance. Moving at speed 4 for the first half and resting for the second covers the same ground and costs \(4^2 \times \tfrac12 = 8\).

Theorem 5.2 (optimal maps and straight lines)

Let \(p\) and \(q\) have finite second moments. If \(p\) has no atoms, the optimal map on the line is the monotone one, \(T = F_q^{-1} \circ F_p\). In \(\mathbb R^d\), if \(p\) has a density, the optimal map exists, is unique, and is the gradient of a convex function (Brenier). The cost is the least kinetic energy of any flow between the two (Benamou-Brenier):

\[ W_2(p, q)^2 = \min_{\rho, v} \int_0^1 \!\! \int \rho_t\, |v_t|^2\, dx\, dt \quad \text{subject to}\quad \partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot (\rho v) = 0,\; \rho_0 = p,\; \rho_1 = q. \tag{5.2} \]

Distances and straight lines give a meaning to downhill. The particles of Chapter 1 spread under noise, and if each one also pays an energy \(V(x)\) for sitting at \(x\), it drifts toward low \(V\) as it spreads. The free energy

\[ F(\rho) = \int V \rho + \int \rho \log \rho \]

adds the cloud's average energy to its negative entropy, which is low when the cloud is spread out. A gradient flow of \(F\) in \(W_2\) moves mass, at every instant, in the direction that lowers \(F\) fastest for its cost in transport. Take \(V(x) = x^2/2\) and start the cloud as \(\mathcal N(2, 1)\). Every particle then moves with the same velocity, minus the current mean, so the cloud slides toward 0 without changing shape and its mean is \(2e^{-t}\). Its free energy falls from 1.081 toward the floor of −0.919 at a rate equal to the squared mean, 4 at the start.

Theorem 5.3 (Jordan, Kinderlehrer, and Otto)

The Fokker-Planck equation \(\partial_t \rho = \nabla \cdot (\rho \nabla V) + \Delta \rho\) is the gradient flow in \(W_2\) of the free energy \(F(\rho) = \int V \rho + \int \rho \log \rho\), and

\[ \frac{d}{dt} F(\rho_t) = -\int \rho_t\, \big|\nabla (V + \log \rho_t)\big|^2. \tag{5.3} \]

With many grains the cheapest plan is a large linear program, and its answer jumps from one pairing to another as the points move. Rewarding plans that spread their mass fixes both: the best blurred plan has a closed form and changes smoothly. Write \(C_{ij}\) for the cost of moving a unit from point \(i\) to point \(j\), and let \(\varepsilon \gt 0\) set how much spreading is worth. For the two grains the blurred plan sends 73% of each grain along the straight pairs at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 98% at \(\varepsilon = 0.25\), and all of it as \(\varepsilon\) goes to 0.

Proposition 5.4 (entropic transport)

With the entropy \(H(P) = -\sum_{ij} P_{ij} (\log P_{ij} - 1)\), the coupling that minimizes \(\langle C, P \rangle - \varepsilon H(P)\) with given marginals has the form

\[ P_\varepsilon = \mathrm{diag}(u)\; e^{-C/\varepsilon}\; \mathrm{diag}(v), \tag{5.4} \]

and Sinkhorn's algorithm finds \(u\) and \(v\) by fixing the row sums and the column sums in turn.

5.4Derivation

Duality. For any plan and any prices that satisfy the constraint, integrating \(\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le |x - y|^2\) against the plan gives \(\mathbb E_p\varphi + \mathbb E_q\psi \le \mathbb E_\pi |X - Y|^2\), so every price pair bounds every plan from below, with equality exactly when the plan sits on tight pairs. For finitely many points the two optima are equal by linear-programming duality (Derivation 5.2 does the bookkeeping).

Monotone maps. For \(a \lt b\) and \(c \lt d\), crossing costs more:

\[ (a - d)^2 + (b - c)^2 - (a - c)^2 - (b - d)^2 = 2(b - a)(d - c) \gt 0. \]

Uncrossing any crossing pair lowers the cost, so the optimal plan on a line is monotone.

(5.3). One step of size \(\tau\) minimizes \(F(\rho) + W_2(\rho, \rho_k)^2 / 2\tau\). To find its optimality condition, let the step carry each grain from \(x\) to \(x + \tau v(x)\), and price the move to first order in \(\tau\). The first variation \(\tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} = V + \log \rho + 1\) is the change in \(F\) per unit of mass added at a point, so carrying a unit of mass by \(\tau v\) changes \(F\) by \(\tau\, v \cdot \nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho}\). For small \(\tau\) and a velocity that is a gradient the move is optimal, so its squared transport cost is \(\tau^2 |v|^2\) per unit of mass, averaged over \(\rho_k\). Together,

\[ F(\rho) + \frac{W_2(\rho, \rho_k)^2}{2\tau} = F(\rho_k) + \tau \int \rho_k \Big( v \cdot \nabla \frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} + \tfrac12 |v|^2 \Big) + o(\tau). \]

Completing the square, \(v \cdot w + \tfrac12 |v|^2 = \tfrac12 |v + w|^2 - \tfrac12 |w|^2\) for any vector \(w\), so the minimum over \(v\) is at \(v = -\nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} = -\nabla (V + \log \rho)\), where the constant 1 has no gradient. As \(\tau \to 0\) the continuity equation with this \(v\) is

\[ \partial_t \rho = \nabla \cdot (\rho \nabla V) + \nabla \cdot (\rho \nabla \log \rho) = \nabla\cdot(\rho \nabla V) + \Delta \rho. \]

Along the flow, the first variation gives the rate of change of \(F\). Substitute the continuity equation \(\partial_t \rho = -\nabla \cdot (\rho v)\), and integrate by parts, with no boundary term for a density that vanishes far out:

\[ \frac{d}{dt}F = \int \frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho}\, \partial_t \rho = -\int \frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho}\, \nabla \cdot (\rho v) = \int \rho\, v \cdot \nabla \frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} = -\int \rho\, |v|^2. \]

The last step uses \(\nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} = -v\), and with \(v = -\nabla(V + \log \rho)\) it is (5.3).

(5.4). Attach a multiplier \(\alpha_i\) to each row constraint, that row \(i\) of \(P\) sums to \(p_i\), and \(\beta_j\) to each column constraint, that column \(j\) sums to \(q_j\). Writing \(-\varepsilon H(P)\) out in full, the Lagrangian is

\[ \sum_{ij} C_{ij} P_{ij} + \varepsilon \sum_{ij} P_{ij} (\log P_{ij} - 1) - \sum_i \alpha_i \Big( \sum_j P_{ij} - p_i \Big) - \sum_j \beta_j \Big( \sum_i P_{ij} - q_j \Big). \]

The derivative of \(P (\log P - 1)\) is \(\log P\), so stationarity in \(P_{ij}\) reads \(C_{ij} + \varepsilon \log P_{ij} - \alpha_i - \beta_j = 0\). Solving for \(P_{ij}\),

\[ P_{ij} = e^{\alpha_i/\varepsilon}\, e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}\, e^{\beta_j/\varepsilon}, \]

which is (5.4) with \(u_i = e^{\alpha_i/\varepsilon}\) and \(v_j = e^{\beta_j/\varepsilon}\). The objective is strictly convex in \(P\) and the constraints are linear, so this stationary point is the minimum. Write \(K = e^{-C/\varepsilon}\), entry by entry. Row \(i\) of the plan sums to \(u_i (K v)_i\) and column \(j\) to \(v_j (K^\top u)_j\), so Sinkhorn alternates

\[ u_i \leftarrow \frac{p_i}{(K v)_i}, \qquad v_j \leftarrow \frac{q_j}{(K^\top u)_j}, \]

each update making one set of sums exact. ∎

Links. The free energy is \(F(\rho) = \mathrm{KL}(\rho \,\|\, \pi) - \log Z\) with \(\pi \propto e^{-V}\), so diffusion comes to rest at a tilt (Chapter 2). The entropic plan (5.4) also minimizes \(\langle C, P\rangle + \varepsilon\, \mathrm{KL}(P \,\|\, p \otimes q)\) over couplings. It is the independent coupling tilted by \(e^{(f_i + g_j - C_{ij})/\varepsilon}\), where the potentials \(f\) and \(g\) restore the marginals, and Sinkhorn is a fixed-point iteration that finds them (Chapter 4). The same construction on path measures is the Schrödinger bridge.

5.5Figures

Figure 5.2Prices that certify a plan

The cheapest transport plan and the best prices φ, ψ with φ(x) + ψ(y) ≤ (x − y)² reach the same total, and the plan only uses pairs where the prices are tight.

Slide the shift or draw new points. The primal cost and the dual value agree at every setting: at the default shift of +0.30 both are 0.1535, and the largest φᵢ + ψⱼ − Cᵢⱼ is 0 up to rounding. The plan's 7 pairs are tight, and 6 more pairs are tight but unused (dashed), 13 of the 49. The faint curves extend the prices to every point as φ(x) = minⱼ (x − yⱼ)² − ψⱼ and its mirror for ψ, and they pass through every stem. Tap a source: its slacks Cᵢⱼ − φᵢ − ψⱼ are 0 at its partner and never negative, so at these prices no other target is cheaper.

Figure 5.3The geodesic as a surface

Along the W2 geodesic every quantile of p₀ rides a straight line in (x, t), so the density surface slides its bumps across, while the straight line in density space fades one bump out and the other in.

Slide t and switch the path. On the geodesic W2(p₀, ρₜ) equals t·W2(p₀, p₁) at every t, 2.011 at t = 0.5, and every quantile path projects to a straight line on the (x, t) floor. On the mixture the same readout is 2.209 at t = 0.5, off the constant-speed line, and the variance swells to 5.269 because the mixture holds mass at both ends at once. The geodesic's variance falls from p₀'s 2.214 to p₁'s 0.563 and reads 1.223 at t = 0.5. Drag to turn the surface.

Figure 5.4Diffusion as gradient descent on free energy

In the W2 geometry the Fokker-Planck equation is steepest descent on F(ρ) = ∫Vρ + T∫ρ log ρ, so F falls at exactly the rate ∫ρ|∂x(V + T log ρ)|² and comes to rest at the Boltzmann density.

Press Play or slide t. At T = 0.4 and t = 0.5 the measured dF/dt is −0.1410 and the dissipation is −0.1412, a ratio of 0.999, and F − F_min = T·KL = 0.1874. Slide T down to 0.15: the mass fills the right well quickly and then waits at the barrier, so at t = 10 the gap is still 0.088, near T·log 2 = 0.104, the gap of a density that fills one well of two.

Figure 5.5Entropic transport by Sinkhorn

Adding ε times the plan's negative entropy to the transport cost makes the optimal plan diag(u)·exp(−C/ε)·diag(v), and Sinkhorn finds u and v by fixing the row sums and the column sums in turn.

Slide ε. At the default ε = 0.05 the error shrinks by a factor of 0.733 per iteration and the plan costs 0.3744 against the exact 0.3539. Slide ε down to 0.005 and the iterations up to 400: the plan approaches the exact matching, at cost 0.3548 after 400 iterations, and the decay slows to 0.997 per iteration, leaving an error of 2.1e−3. The plan is the independent coupling tilted by exp((f ⊕ g − C)/ε), where the potentials f and g restore the marginals (the tilt), and Sinkhorn is a fixed-point iteration (the fixed point).

5.6Four ways to see it

Optimal transport has four standard pictures. Each comes with tools of its own, and each follows from the one before it in a few lines.

  1. 1A linear programoperations research

    A plan is a nonnegative matrix with row sums \(p_i\) and column sums \(q_j\), and its cost is linear in the plan. With equal weights on \(n\) points each, an optimal plan can be chosen to be a permutation (Birkhoff's theorem), and transport is the assignment problem.

    \[ \min_{\pi \ge 0}\; \sum_{ij} \pi_{ij} C_{ij} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \textstyle\sum_j \pi_{ij} = p_i,\; \sum_i \pi_{ij} = q_j. \]

  2. 1 → 2Attach a price \(\varphi_i\) to each row constraint and \(\psi_j\) to each column constraint. Linear-programming duality gives the same optimal value from the prices, and complementary slackness says the plan moves mass only between pairs where the prices are tight: \(\pi_{ij} \gt 0\) implies \(\varphi_i + \psi_j = C_{ij}\) (Figure 5.2).

  3. 2Priceseconomics

    A shipper charges \(\varphi(x)\) to collect at \(x\) and \(\psi(y)\) to deliver at \(y\), and no customer would rather move the mass directly as long as \(\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le c(x, y)\). The best such prices earn exactly the transport cost.

    \[ \min_{\pi \in \Pi(p, q)} \mathbb E_\pi\, c(X, Y) = \max_{\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le c(x, y)} \Big\{ \mathbb E_p[\varphi] + \mathbb E_q[\psi] \Big\}. \]

  4. 2 → 3Take \(c = \tfrac12 |x - y|^2\) and write \(u(x) = \tfrac12|x|^2 - \varphi(x)\). At the best prices \(u\) is convex, and at a tight pair the function \(x \mapsto \varphi(x) + \psi(y) - c(x, y)\) reaches its maximum of zero, so its gradient vanishes: \(\nabla\varphi(x) = x - y\), that is, \(y = \nabla u(x)\), Brenier's map. Moving each particle at constant speed along \(x \mapsto x + t(\nabla u(x) - x)\) gives a flow whose kinetic energy in the sense of (5.2) equals \(W_2^2\), the transport cost of (5.1).

  5. 3A fluidphysics

    Mass flows with a velocity field, the continuity equation keeps it from appearing or vanishing, and the cost is the total kinetic energy (5.2). The cheapest flow moves every particle on a straight line at constant speed (Figure 5.3).

  6. 3 → 4Read (5.2) as a Riemannian metric on densities: a small change \(\partial_t \rho = -\nabla\cdot(\rho \nabla \phi)\) has squared length \(\int \rho\, |\nabla\phi|^2\). Along it, \(\tfrac{d}{dt} F = \int \rho\, \nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} \cdot \nabla \phi\), and minimizing this plus half the squared length over \(\phi\) gives \(\nabla \phi = -\nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho}\), so steepest descent is

    \[ \partial_t \rho = \nabla \cdot \Big( \rho\, \nabla \frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} \Big). \]

  7. 4A gradient flowpartial differential equations

    Many evolution equations are steepest descent of an energy in this metric. The heat equation descends \(\int \rho \log \rho\), Fokker-Planck descends the free energy (Theorem 5.3, Figure 5.4), and the porous-medium equation \(\partial_t \rho = \Delta \rho^m\) descends \(\tfrac{1}{m-1}\int \rho^m\). A time step of size \(\tau\) is the JKO step:

    \[ \rho_{k+1} = \arg\min_\rho \Big\{ F(\rho) + \frac{W_2(\rho, \rho_k)^2}{2\tau} \Big\}. \]

5.7Where it breaks and what is open

Every picture above is exact for the true distributions, and every method sees samples. Two samples of size \(n\) from the same distribution on \([0, 1]^d\) sit at a \(W_1\) distance of order \(n^{-1/d}\) for \(d \ge 3\), the distance the figure plots, and \(W_2\) shrinks at the same rate once \(d \gt 4\) (Fournier and Guillin), so halving the error takes \(2^d\) times the data. A coupling computed on a minibatch carries this error, and in high dimension most of it is noise. Entropic regularization trades the error for bias: the Sinkhorn divergence converges at the rate \(n^{-1/2}\) in every dimension (Genevay et al.), and it measures a blurred cost.

Figure 5.6Empirical transport in high dimension

Two samples of n points from the same law sit at a transport distance that shrinks only like n^(−1/d), so in high dimension no feasible sample size makes empirical transport accurate.

Pick a dimension. The true distance is 0 for every d. At d = 1 the fitted slope is −0.498, the n^(−1/2) of the theory. At the default d = 20 it is −0.075 against the theory's −1/20: at n = 256 the two samples still sit 1.196 apart, the best matching costs 0.663 of a random pairing, and halving the distance would take about 10 000 times more points. The distance here is W1 with the Euclidean cost, and W2 shrinks at the same rate n^(−1/d) once d ≥ 5 (Weed and Bach 2019).

  1. Minibatch couplings for flow matching. Pairing noise and data by OT inside each minibatch straightens flow-matching paths (Tong et al.), and the pairing within a batch of \(n\) is a sample estimate with the error above. How the batch size should grow with the data's dimension, and whether the straighter paths still pay off at image scale, is open.
  2. Transport between data types never measured together. Translating between data types never measured together is transport with an unknown cost. Whether a few pairs can pin down the cost and let OT or a Schrödinger bridge carry the rest is open, and the project below measures it.
  3. Rates set by the data's own dimension. Empirical transport converges at a rate set by the intrinsic dimension of the data, below the ambient one (Weed and Bach). Which learned flows achieve rates of that kind is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 5.1The JKO velocity

    Start from \(F(\rho) = \int V\rho + \int \rho\log\rho\) and the continuity equation. Derive the velocity of steepest descent in \(W_2\), show that the resulting equation is Fokker-Planck, and derive the dissipation (5.3).

    Solution

    The first variation is \(\frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} = V + \log \rho + 1\). For a change \(\partial_t \rho = -\nabla\cdot(\rho v)\), integrating by parts (the constant drops because mass is conserved) gives

    \[ \frac{d}{dt}F = -\int \Big(V + \log\rho\Big)\, \nabla\cdot(\rho v) = \int \rho\, v \cdot \nabla(V + \log \rho). \]

    Minimizing \(\frac{d}{dt}F + \tfrac12 \int \rho |v|^2\) pointwise in \(v\) gives \(v = -\nabla(V + \log\rho)\). Since \(\rho \nabla\log\rho = \nabla\rho\), the continuity equation becomes \(\partial_t\rho = \nabla\cdot(\rho\nabla V) + \Delta\rho\), and substituting \(v\) back gives \(\frac{d}{dt}F = -\int \rho\, |\nabla(V + \log\rho)|^2\).

  2. Derivation 5.2Tight prices never cross

    For a plan \(\pi\) with marginals \(p, q\) and prices with \(\varphi_i + \psi_j \le C_{ij}\), show that \(\sum_i p_i \varphi_i + \sum_j q_j \psi_j \le \sum_{ij} \pi_{ij} C_{ij}\), with equality exactly when \(\pi\) puts mass only on tight pairs. Then show that on a line with \(c = |x - y|^2\) two tight pairs carrying mass never cross.

    Solution

    Using the marginals,

    \[ \sum_i p_i\varphi_i + \sum_j q_j\psi_j = \sum_{ij}\pi_{ij}(\varphi_i + \psi_j) \le \sum_{ij}\pi_{ij} C_{ij}, \]

    and the gap is \(\sum_{ij} \pi_{ij}(C_{ij} - \varphi_i - \psi_j)\), a sum of nonnegative terms that vanishes exactly when every pair with mass is tight.

    Suppose \(a \lt b\), \(c \lt d\), and the pairs \((a, d)\) and \((b, c)\) are tight. The pairs \((a, c)\) and \((b, d)\) satisfy the constraint, so subtracting gives \(C(a, d) + C(b, c) \le C(a, c) + C(b, d)\). The crossing identity of Section 5.4 says the left side exceeds the right by \(2(b - a)(d - c) \gt 0\), a contradiction.

Chapter 6

The geometry of a step

Information geometry

Steepest descent depends on how the length of a step is measured. Measure it in KL between the model before and after, and the step stops depending on the parametrization, and its size follows from a budget.

Uses Chapter 2 and Appendix A.2 and A.5.

6.1Motivation

Suppose a model forecasts tomorrow's high temperature as a bell curve, with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\) in degrees, and a gradient step moves the mean by 0.1 degree. If \(\sigma\) is 5 degrees the forecast barely changes, and the KL divergence between the forecasts before and after is 0.0002. If \(\sigma\) is 0.5 degrees, the same step is a hundred times larger in KL, 0.02, because a sharp forecast notices a shift that a vague one absorbs. Gradient descent counts both as the same step. But how large is a step, really, and how large should it be?

Gradient descent assumes that a step of a given length means the same thing in every parameter, yet the same change to a standard deviation is tiny when the deviation is large and enormous when it is small: raising \(\sigma\) by 0.1 costs 0.0004 in KL at 5 degrees and 0.03 at 0.5 degrees. Reparametrizing a model changes the path that gradient descent takes, so writing the forecast with \(\log\sigma\) in place of \(\sigma\) sends it somewhere else from the same start. Practitioners compensate with tuned learning rates, warmups, and per-parameter scalings. Measuring a step by how much it changes the model's predictions, the KL between before and after, fixes the units once, so the step stops depending on the parametrization, to first order in its size, and its size can be computed from a budget.

6.2Intuition

Take the forecast at \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\), and allow a budget of 0.005 in KL. Which steps stay within it? Move the mean alone by \(\delta_\mu\), and the KL is exactly \(\delta_\mu^2 / 2\sigma^2\), so the budget allows \(\delta_\mu = 0.1\). Move the spread alone by \(\delta_\sigma\), and the KL is close to \(\delta_\sigma^2 / \sigma^2\), so the budget allows about \(\delta_\sigma = 0.071\). The exact limits are 0.075 upward and 0.067 downward, since a forecast that grows sharper pays a little more. Move both at once, and the two costs add, with no cross term (Derivation 6.1 checks this):

\[ \mathrm{KL} \approx \tfrac12 \Big( \frac{\delta_\mu^2}{\sigma^2} + \frac{2\, \delta_\sigma^2}{\sigma^2} \Big) = \tfrac12\, \delta^\top F \delta, \qquad F = \mathrm{diag}\Big( \frac{1}{\sigma^2},\, \frac{2}{\sigma^2} \Big). \]

The forecasts within budget fill an ellipse with half-widths 0.1 along \(\mu\) and 0.071 along \(\sigma\). At \(\sigma = 0.5\) the same budget gives an ellipse half as wide in each direction, 0.05 and 0.035, and a gradient step of 0.1 in \(\mu\) there costs 0.02, four times the budget. The matrix \(F\) is called the Fisher information of the Gaussian, and Theorem 6.2 shows that every smooth model has one.

A step's true size is how much it changes what the model predicts, and the set of models one small step away is an ellipse whose shape the Fisher information sets.

Figure 6.1KL balls are Fisher ellipses that shrink with σ

In the parameters (μ, σ) of a Gaussian, the models within KL ε of a center nearly fill the Fisher ellipse ½δᵀFδ = ε, and the ellipses shrink in proportion to σ, so one step in the parameters is a large step between distributions where σ is small.

Slide ε. Each ball is the ball at (0, 1) scaled by σ, so a step of 0.1 in μ costs a KL of 0.0016 at σ = 1.75 and 0.0247 at σ = 0.45. At the default ε = 0.05 the exact ball and the ellipse differ by at most 22.2% along any ray, most straight up in σ, where the ball reaches 0.2733 against the ellipse's 0.2236. At ε = 0.005 the gap is 6.2%, and at ε = 0.5 it is 113.7%. Switch to estimates: 300 maximum-likelihood fits from n = 50 draws give n·Var(μ̂) = 1.129 and n·Var(σ̂) = 0.486 against F⁻¹ = diag(1, 0.5), and 60.7% of them land inside δᵀFδ ≤ 2/n against 63.2% for the limiting normal law, within the 8.2% Monte Carlo error of 300 datasets.

6.3Statement

The toy measured steps with one matrix for one model and never asked what the loss wants. Two questions are left: once a step's length is measured by a matrix, which step of a given length lowers the loss the most, and which matrix does KL give for a model other than the Gaussian? Proposition 6.1 answers the first for any matrix \(M\), and Theorem 6.2 answers the second.

Proposition 6.1 (steepest descent under a norm)

For a gradient \(g\) and the norm \(\|\delta\|_M^2 = \delta^\top M \delta\) of a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(M\), the step of length \(\varepsilon\) that decreases the loss fastest to first order, where a step \(\delta\) changes the loss by \(\langle g, \delta \rangle\), is

\[ \delta^* = \arg\min_{\|\delta\|_M \le \varepsilon} \langle g, \delta \rangle = -\varepsilon\, \frac{M^{-1} g}{\sqrt{g^\top M^{-1} g}}. \tag{6.1} \]

Positive definite means every nonzero step has positive length. With \(M = \mathrm{diag}(1, 0)\), steps along the second axis cost nothing, and if \(g\) has a component there the loss falls without limit inside the ball, so no fastest step exists. With \(M = I\), (6.1) is plain gradient descent scaled to length \(\varepsilon\). With the toy's \(M = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma^2, 2/\sigma^2)\), it multiplies the mean's gradient by \(\sigma^2\) and the spread's by \(\sigma^2/2\) before scaling, so the step shrinks where the forecast is sharp.

Write \(p_\theta(x)\) for the model's probability of an outcome \(x\). The gradient \(\nabla \log p_\theta(x)\) in \(\theta\) is called the score, and in the next statement the expectation is over outcomes drawn from the model itself. The model must be smooth enough in \(\theta\) to differentiate under the integral. For the forecast \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(z = (x - \mu)/\sigma\), the scores are \(z/\sigma\) and \((z^2 - 1)/\sigma\), and their outer product averages to the toy's \(F = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma^2,\, 2/\sigma^2)\) (Derivation 6.1).

Theorem 6.2 (Fisher information is the curvature of KL)

\[ \mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \,\|\, p_{\theta + \delta}) = \tfrac12\, \delta^\top F(\theta)\, \delta + O(|\delta|^3), \qquad F(\theta) = \mathbb E\big[\nabla \log p_\theta\, \nabla \log p_\theta^\top\big]. \tag{6.2} \]

A step has KL \(\varepsilon\), to second order, when \(\tfrac12 \delta^\top F \delta = \varepsilon\), that is, when its length in the norm of \(F\) is \(\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\). So (6.1) with \(M = F\) and that length gives the step whose KL is \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta^* = -\sqrt{2\varepsilon / g^\top F^{-1} g}\; F^{-1} g\), the natural gradient with a computed size.

6.4Derivation

(6.1). A linear function with \(g \ne 0\) has no minimum inside the ball, so the best step lies on its boundary, \(\delta^\top M \delta = \varepsilon^2\). Minimize \(g^\top \delta + \lambda (\delta^\top M \delta - \varepsilon^2)\) with a multiplier \(\lambda\). Its gradient in \(\delta\) is \(g + 2\lambda M \delta\), and setting it to zero gives

\[ \delta = -\frac{M^{-1} g}{2\lambda}. \]

Put this into the constraint:

\[ \delta^\top M \delta = \frac{g^\top M^{-1} M M^{-1} g}{4\lambda^2} = \frac{g^\top M^{-1} g}{4\lambda^2} = \varepsilon^2. \]

So \(2\lambda = \sqrt{g^\top M^{-1} g} / \varepsilon\), taking the positive root, because the negative root gives the step that raises the loss fastest. Putting \(2\lambda\) back into \(\delta\) gives (6.1). It is the minimum, by Cauchy-Schwarz in the inner product of \(M\):

\[ g^\top \delta = (M^{-1} g)^\top M \delta \ge -\|M^{-1} g\|_M\, \|\delta\|_M = -\varepsilon \sqrt{g^\top M^{-1} g}, \]

with equality only when \(\delta\) points along \(-M^{-1} g\).

(6.2). Expand \(\log p_{\theta + \delta}\) to second order in \(\delta\), at each outcome:

\[ \log p_{\theta+\delta} = \log p_\theta + \delta^\top \nabla \log p_\theta + \tfrac12\, \delta^\top \nabla^2 \log p_\theta\, \delta + O(|\delta|^3). \]

Put it inside \(\mathrm{KL} = \mathbb E_\theta[\log p_\theta - \log p_{\theta+\delta}]\). The \(\log p_\theta\) terms cancel, which leaves a first-order and a second-order term:

\[ \mathrm{KL} = -\delta^\top\, \mathbb E[\nabla \log p_\theta] + \tfrac12\, \delta^\top \big( -\mathbb E\, \nabla^2 \log p_\theta \big)\, \delta + O(|\delta|^3). \]

The first-order term is \(-\delta^\top \mathbb E[\nabla \log p_\theta] = 0\), because the score has mean zero. The score is \(\nabla p_\theta / p_\theta\), and averaging it against \(p_\theta\) cancels the denominator:

\[ \mathbb E_\theta[\nabla \log p_\theta] = \int p_\theta\, \frac{\nabla p_\theta}{p_\theta} = \nabla \int p_\theta = \nabla 1 = 0. \]

For the second-order term, differentiate \(\nabla \log p = \nabla p / p\) once more:

\[ \nabla^2 \log p = \frac{\nabla^2 p}{p} - \nabla \log p\, \nabla \log p^\top. \]

By the same cancellation, the first piece averages to \(\nabla^2\) of the total mass, which is \(\nabla^2 1 = 0\), so \(-\mathbb E\, \nabla^2 \log p_\theta = F\), and the second-order term is \(\tfrac12 \delta^\top F \delta\).

Invariance. Let \(\theta = \varphi(\eta)\) with an invertible Jacobian \(J\). By the chain rule every gradient in \(\eta\) is \(J^\top\) times the gradient in \(\theta\), so \(g_\eta = J^\top g_\theta\). The score obeys the same rule, and its outer product gives \(F_\eta = J^\top F_\theta J\). A step \(\delta_\eta\) moves \(\theta\) by \(J \delta_\eta\) to first order, so the natural step in \(\eta\) moves \(\theta\) along

\[ J\, F_\eta^{-1} g_\eta = J\, J^{-1} F_\theta^{-1} J^{-\top} J^\top g_\theta = F_\theta^{-1} g_\theta. \]

To first order both parametrizations take the same step in distribution space. Plain gradient descent in \(\eta\) moves \(\theta\) along \(J J^\top g_\theta\), which depends on the parametrization. For the forecast with \(\eta = (\mu, \log\sigma)\), \(J = \mathrm{diag}(1, \sigma)\), so a gradient step in \(\log\sigma\) moves \(\sigma\) by \(\sigma^2\) times the step that gradient descent in \(\sigma\) would take: a quarter of it at \(\sigma = 0.5\), and 25 times it at \(\sigma = 5\). ∎

  • Softmax policies. In the logits, \(F = \mathrm{diag}(\pi) - \pi\pi^\top\) and the gradient of \(\mathbb E_\pi[r]\) is \(F A\) with \(A\) the advantage, \(A_a = r(a) - \mathbb E_\pi[r]\), how much more action \(a\) pays than the policy's average. \(F\) is singular, because adding a constant to every logit leaves \(\pi\) unchanged, so the natural step uses the pseudo-inverse: \(F^{+} F A = A - \bar A\, \mathbf 1\) with \(\bar A\) the plain average of the entries of \(A\), and the step is \(\pi \leftarrow \pi\, e^{\eta A} / Z\). This is multiplicative weights (Chapter 8) and a tilt (Chapter 2).
  • Weight matrices. Under the spectral norm, \(\max_{\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}} \le 1} \langle G, \Delta \rangle\) is the nuclear norm of \(G\), attained at \(U V^\top\) from the reduced SVD \(G = U \Sigma V^\top\) (uniquely when \(G\) has full rank). Muon applies this orthogonalization to its momentum. The Frobenius norm gives the normalized gradient \(G / \|G\|_F\), and the largest-entry norm gives the sign update.

6.5Figures

Figure 6.2One fit, two parametrizations

The natural gradient step −F⁻¹∇L is defined by the distributions it moves between, so to first order it takes the same path whether σ or log σ is the parameter, while plain gradient descent changes with the choice.

Slide the step size. At the default η = 0.5, plain gradient descent never settles in (μ, σ) and fits in 13 steps in (μ, log σ), while the natural steps fit in 13 steps in both charts, on paths that stay within 0.086 of each other. At η = 1 the natural steps fit in 5 and 6 steps, and plain descent takes 138 steps in one chart and never settles in the other. Switch to fixed KL per step: every path converges at every budget on the slider, and at KL 0.010 per step all four fit in 17 to 19 steps.

Figure 6.3Natural policy gradient is multiplicative weights

For a softmax policy the natural gradient of E_π[r] is the advantage itself, up to a constant shift of every logit, so the step is π ← π·exp(ηA)/Z, and it keeps moving where the vanilla gradient π⊙A vanishes.

Slide η. At η = 1 the natural steps reach π(arm 1) ≥ 0.95 in 17 steps and vanilla policy gradient needs 166. Near the corner π⊙A is tiny: the first vanilla step moves the policy by a KL of 8.6e−7 and the first natural step by 5.3e−3. The vanilla gradient vanishes near the boundary, while the natural step moves every logit by ηA whatever π is.

6.6Four ways to see it

The Fisher metric shows up in four places: as the length that defines steepest descent, as the limit on how precisely data can pin a parameter down, as the local shape of a Bregman divergence, and as the Gauss-Newton matrix of least squares.

  1. 1A metricoptimization

    Steepest descent is defined only once the length of a step is. In the length \(\|\delta\|_M\) it points along \(-M^{-1} g\) (6.1), and with \(M = F\) the length is the KL between the models before and after (6.2).

  2. 1 → 2By (6.2) the models within KL \(\varepsilon\) of \(\theta\) fill the ellipse \(\tfrac12 \delta^\top F \delta \le \varepsilon\). An unbiased estimate from \(n\) samples has covariance at least \(F^{-1}/n\), and maximum likelihood attains this as \(n\) grows, so its scatter fills the ellipse \(\delta^\top F \delta \lesssim d/n\) (Figure 6.1). Distance in the Fisher metric counts how many samples it takes to tell two models apart.

  3. 2The Cramér-Rao boundstatistics

    No unbiased estimator beats the inverse Fisher information:

    \[ \mathrm{Cov}\big(\hat\theta(X_1, \dots, X_n)\big) \succeq \frac1n\, F(\theta)^{-1}. \]

  4. 1 → 3Replace the quadratic \(\tfrac12 \|\delta\|_M^2\) by the Bregman divergence of a convex function \(\psi\),

    \[ D_\psi(x', x) = \psi(x') - \psi(x) - \langle \nabla\psi(x), x' - x\rangle. \]

    The step \(x_{k+1} = \arg\min_x \{\langle g, x\rangle + \tfrac1\eta D_\psi(x, x_k)\}\) satisfies \(\nabla\psi(x_{k+1}) = \nabla\psi(x_k) - \eta g\). Since \(D_\psi(x + \delta, x) = \tfrac12 \delta^\top \nabla^2\psi(x)\, \delta + O(|\delta|^3)\), small mirror steps are steepest descent in the metric \(\nabla^2 \psi\).

  5. 3Mirror descentconvex optimization

    For an exponential family with log-partition \(A\), \(\nabla^2 A = F\) and \(D_A(\theta', \theta) = \mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \,\|\, p_{\theta'})\). Mirror descent in the natural parameters with \(\psi = A\) moves the mean parameters \(\mu = \nabla A(\theta)\) by \(-\eta \nabla_\theta L\), the same move as a natural-gradient step in \(\mu\) (Raskutti and Mukherjee). On the simplex with \(\psi = \sum_i x_i \log x_i\), mirror descent is multiplicative weights (Chapter 8).

  6. 1 → 4Let a model predict a Gaussian mean, \(y \sim \mathcal N(f_\theta(x), I)\), and let \(J\) be the Jacobian of \(f_\theta(x)\). The score is \(J^\top (y - f_\theta(x))\), so

    \[ F = \mathbb E_x\, \mathbb E_y \big[ J^\top (y - f_\theta)(y - f_\theta)^\top J \big] = \mathbb E_x \big[ J^\top J \big], \]

    the Gauss-Newton matrix of the squared loss. For other exponential-family outputs, when the network outputs the natural parameters (a canonical link), the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix equals the Fisher (Martens).

  7. 4Gauss-Newtonnumerical analysis

    To fit residuals \(r(\theta) = f_\theta(x) - y\), linearize \(r\) and solve the least-squares problem in the step: \(\delta = -(J^\top J)^{-1} J^\top r\). With unit noise this is the natural-gradient step with \(\eta = 1\), and Levenberg-Marquardt's damping \(J^\top J + \lambda I\) is a trust region.

6.7Where it breaks and what is open

Every view needs \(F\) or \(\nabla^2 \psi\), a \(p \times p\) matrix. At \(10^8\) parameters it takes \(4 \cdot 10^{16}\) bytes in float32, and inverting it takes about \(10^{24}\) operations, so every practical method approximates it: Kronecker factors per layer (K-FAC, Shampoo), a diagonal (Adam divides by the square root of a running average of squared gradients, a rough diagonal of the empirical Fisher), or a norm whose steepest step has a closed form (Muon). The cheapest substitute, the empirical Fisher built from per-example gradients at the observed labels, is a different matrix. It vanishes at a perfect fit and distorts steps elsewhere (Kunstner et al.).

Figure 6.4The exact Fisher is too big, and its cheap stand-in points the wrong way

The exact Fisher matrix of a p-parameter model takes p² numbers to store and about p³ operations to invert, and its cheap stand-in, the empirical Fisher (the mean outer product of per-example gradients), can point a step away from the fit.

The data follow the model of Kunstner et al.'s Figure 1, y = 2 + 2x + ε with lognormal x and ε ~ N(0, 1), here with 100 points. For this model the true Fisher is the Hessian, so the natural step is Newton's. At the default η = 0.25, from start 1 the natural steps run straight to the fit in 28 steps and gradient descent takes 98. The empirical-Fisher step leaves at 99.6° from the natural one and takes 223 steps: far from the fit the residuals are large, so the empirical Fisher is large and its steps are short. Slide η to 1: the natural step lands in one step, gradient descent diverges (it is stable only below η = 0.623), and the empirical Fisher takes 54. Slide p: at 10⁸ parameters the exact Fisher takes 40 PB in float32 and 10²⁴ flops to invert, 31.7 years at 10¹⁵ flop/s, and it fits on one 80 GB GPU only up to p = 141,421.

  1. A metric worth its cost. Which approximation of the geometry buys the most loss per flop at scale is open: K-FAC, Shampoo, and SOAP keep curvature, and Muon keeps only a norm. A step can only be computed, rather than tuned, in a metric that is affordable.
  2. The KL budget for post-training. TRPO fixes a KL radius per step and PPO approximates it by clipping. Which reference to measure the distance from, and how large a total budget a run should spend, are open. One proposal uses training checkpoints as references, each weighted by the data it saw.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 6.1Fisher information is the curvature of KL

    Derive (6.2), including why the first-order term vanishes and why \(-\mathbb E\, \nabla^2 \log p_\theta = \mathbb E[\nabla \log p_\theta \nabla \log p_\theta^\top]\). Then compute \(F\) for \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) in the parameters \((\mu, \sigma)\) and in \((\mu, \log\sigma)\).

    Solution

    The score has mean zero: \(\mathbb E_\theta[\nabla \log p_\theta] = \int \nabla p_\theta = \nabla \int p_\theta = 0\). Differentiating \(\log p\) twice gives \(\nabla^2 \log p = \nabla^2 p / p - \nabla\log p\, \nabla\log p^\top\), and \(\mathbb E[\nabla^2 p / p] = \nabla^2 \int p = 0\). So the second-order term of \(\mathbb E_\theta[\log p_\theta - \log p_{\theta + \delta}]\) is \(-\tfrac12 \delta^\top \mathbb E[\nabla^2 \log p_\theta]\, \delta = \tfrac12 \delta^\top F \delta\).

    For the Gaussian, with \(z = (x - \mu)/\sigma\), the scores are \(\partial_\mu \log p = z/\sigma\) and \(\partial_\sigma \log p = (z^2 - 1)/\sigma\). Since \(\mathbb E z^2 = 1\), \(\mathbb E (z^2 - 1)^2 = 2\), and \(\mathbb E z(z^2 - 1) = 0\), \(F = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma^2,\, 2/\sigma^2)\). With \(s = \log\sigma\), \(\partial_s = \sigma\, \partial_\sigma\), so \(F = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma^2,\, 2)\).

  2. Derivation 6.2The Cramér-Rao bound in one dimension

    Let \(T(X)\) be an unbiased estimator of a scalar \(\theta\) from one sample. Show \(\mathrm{Var}\, T \ge 1 / F(\theta)\), and extend it to \(n\) independent samples.

    Solution

    Let \(s = \partial_\theta \log p_\theta(X)\), with mean zero and variance \(F\). Unbiasedness gives \(\mathbb E[T s] = \int T\, \partial_\theta p_\theta = \partial_\theta\, \mathbb E_\theta T = 1\), so \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, s) = 1\). By Cauchy-Schwarz, \(1 = \mathrm{Cov}(T, s)^2 \le \mathrm{Var}(T)\, \mathrm{Var}(s) = \mathrm{Var}(T)\, F\).

    The score of \(n\) independent samples is the sum of their scores, so its variance is \(nF\), and \(\mathrm{Var}\, T \ge 1/(nF)\).

Notes and further reading

Guides. Nielsen, An Elementary Introduction to Information Geometry (2020), the Fisher metric from definitions: arXiv:1808.08271. Then Martens, New Insights and Perspectives on the Natural Gradient Method (JMLR, 2020), the natural gradient as a second-order method: arXiv:1412.1193. For the Riemannian prerequisites, Sigmundur Gudmundsson's An Introduction to Riemannian Geometry (lecture notes), the chapters on metrics and geodesics. The Fisher metric of \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) is twice the hyperbolic half-plane metric in the coordinates \((\mu/\sqrt 2, \sigma)\), with curvature \(-\tfrac12\), so the geodesics of the hyperbolic half-plane are the shortest paths between Gaussians.
