Chapter 10

Entropy is a code length

Information theory, from communication

Describe an outcome \(x\) with \(-\log_2 p(x)\) bits, and no code does better on average. Prediction and compression are then one task: a model that predicts well is a short code, and a language model's loss in bits per token is the size of the file it would compress its text to.

Uses Chapter 2 and Appendix A.5.

10.1Motivation

Suppose a weather station on a mountain sends one report an hour down a wire that carries only 0s and 1s. Half the hours are sunny, a quarter are cloudy, an eighth rainy, and an eighth snowy. Two bits name four reports, as 00, 01, 10, and 11, so the plain code spends two bits an hour. Yet sun comes up every other hour. A one-bit word for sun should pay, as long as the rarer reports can take longer words and the receiver can still tell where each word ends. How few bits per report can any code manage on average? And what does a code cost when it was built for the wrong probabilities? A language model faces the station's question at every token, with its predicted probabilities in place of the weather's.

Before 1948, engineers designed codes and modulation schemes case by case, and the measures of capacity they had, from Nyquist and Hartley, counted symbols and signal levels as if every message were equally likely. Shannon asked the station's question of every source, how many bits it needs on average, and found one number, the entropy, that bounds every code at once and is reached by long ones. The same number measures how well a model predicts, so compression, prediction, and, through Kelly, betting became one problem.

PAPERA document that moved capital

A Mathematical Theory of Communication

Information is measured in bits, and a noisy channel carries it reliably up to a fixed capacity.

Claude E. Shannon, 1948 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

It founded information theory, and with it the digital communication, storage, and compression that followed.

The link to this chapter: Theorem 2 derives \(H = -K \sum_i p_i \log p_i\) from three requirements, and the fundamental theorem for a noiseless channel (Theorem 9) proves that a source can be sent at \(C/H - \varepsilon\) symbols per second and no faster, with codewords between \(\log_2(1/p)\) and \(1 + \log_2(1/p)\) bits long, which is (10.2). Section 28 defines the rate at a given fidelity as a minimized mutual information, the rate-distortion function of Chapter 11.

PAPERA document that moved capital

Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

A language model's loss falls as a power law in parameters, data, and compute, so capability can be planned.

Jared Kaplan et al., 2020 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

It turned model training into a planned investment and helped justify the compute buildout that followed. Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022, also on the site) revised the split toward more data.

The link to this chapter: the loss is "the cross entropy loss in nats" per token (Section 1.3), a code length by (10.3). Kaplan's power laws have no constant term, and they contradict each other near 1.7 nats per token (Section 6.3), which the paper offers as a rough estimate of the entropy of the text. Chinchilla's fit has one, \(E = 1.69\) nats per token, read the same way: the code length no model can beat.

10.2Intuition

Take the station's four reports. Give the common report the short word and the rare ones longer words: sun 0, cloud 10, rain 110, and snow 111. No codeword begins another, so a stream reads back without separators. The stream 0110100 splits one way only, as 0, 110, 10, 0, which is sun, rain, cloud, sun. The average length is

\[ \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 = 1.75 \text{ bits}, \]

a quarter of a bit, or an eighth, below the plain code's two bits. Can a cleverer code beat 1.75? Try giving snow the word 11. Rain's word 110 then begins with it, and the stream 110 could be rain, or snow followed by sun. Draw the words as leaves of a binary tree, with 0 for a left branch and 1 for a right one. A word of length \(\ell\) blocks everything below it, which is the fraction \(2^{-\ell}\) of the tree. The four words block \(\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = 1\), the whole tree, and snow at 11 would need \(\tfrac98\) of it.

Now set the lengths beside the probabilities. The report with probability \(\tfrac12\) gets one bit, \(\tfrac14\) gets two, and \(\tfrac18\) gets three, so each length is \(-\log_2 p\), the number of times the probability halves on its way down from 1. Call \(-\log_2 p(x)\) the surprisal of \(x\). The code spends exactly the surprisal on each report, so its average is the average surprisal,

\[ H = -\sum_x p(x) \log_2 p(x) = 1.75 \text{ bits}, \]

and we call this average the entropy of the source. Theorem 10.1 shows that no code of this kind, for this source or any other, averages less.

Next, send a hundred reports in a row. The day's message is the hundred words strung together, so its length is the sum of their lengths, with mean 175 bits and standard deviation 8.3 bits. In 95 days of 100 it falls between 159 and 191 bits, and in all but about 2 days of 1000 it is shorter than the plain code's 200. Each word has length \(-\log_2 p\), so a day whose message has \(L\) bits has probability exactly \(2^{-L}\). The days in the band from 159 to 191 bits therefore hold 95% of the probability, and each has probability between \(2^{-191}\) and \(2^{-159}\), that is, between \(2^{-1.91 n}\) and \(2^{-1.59 n}\) for \(n = 100\). With 10,000 reports the band narrows to 1.734 to 1.766 bits per report, and it keeps closing on 1.75 as \(n\) grows. The probabilities of all days add to one, so a set of days that holds nearly all of it, each day with probability near \(2^{-nH}\), must have about \(2^{nH}\) members, with an exponent per report that tends to \(H\).

So almost all the probability of a long run of draws sits on about \(2^{nH}\) nearly equally likely sequences, and naming one of them takes about \(nH\) bits.

Figure 10.1Long runs are typical, and the likeliest run is not

For long runs of coin flips, −(1/n) log₂ p of the run actually drawn concentrates on the entropy H, so about 2ⁿᴴ typical runs carry almost all the probability while the single most likely run sits far below them.

Every run with k ones has the same probability, so the binomial mass over k gives the exact distribution of bits per flip, with no sampling. At the defaults, n = 200 flips with p(1) = 0.1 and ε = 0.05, the entropy is H = 0.469 bits. The band H ± ε holds probability 0.591 and 2^99.7 of the 2^200 runs, so (1/n) log₂ of its size is 0.498, inside [0.419, 0.519]. The all-zeros run is the most likely single run, at 0.152 bits per flip and probability 7.1e−10. Slide n to 2000: the band holds 0.981 of the probability, (1/n) log₂ of its size is 0.514, and all zeros has probability 3.1e−92. Shrink ε to 0.01 there: the size exponent falls to 0.476, nearer H, and the band holds 0.372. At p = 0.5 every run has probability 2^−n and all of them are typical.

10.3Statement

The station's code reached 1.75 bits because its lengths were the surprisals and its tree was full. The statements below settle the same questions for every source: which lengths a prefix code can have, why none averages less than the entropy, what a code built for the wrong probabilities costs, how many sequences a long run of draws really uses, and what the same count pays a bettor.

Theorem 10.1 (Kraft and the source coding theorem)

The codeword lengths \(\ell(x)\) of a prefix code, in which no codeword begins another, satisfy

\[ \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1, \tag{10.1} \]

and any lengths that satisfy (10.1) belong to some prefix code. For a source \(p\), every prefix code has expected length at least the entropy, and the lengths \(\lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil\) come within one bit of it:

\[ H(p) = -\sum_x p(x) \log_2 p(x) \;\le\; \mathbb E_p\, \ell(X) \;\lt\; H(p) + 1. \tag{10.2} \]

Proposition 10.2 (the wrong model costs KL)

Coding a source \(p\) with lengths \(-\log_2 q(x)\) built for a model \(q\) costs the cross-entropy, and the extra bits are the KL:

\[ \mathbb E_p\big[-\log_2 q(X)\big] = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q). \tag{10.3} \]

Theorem 10.3 (asymptotic equipartition)

For \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) drawn independently from \(p\), \(-\frac1n \log_2 p(X_1, \dots, X_n) \to H(p)\) in probability: the chance that it lies farther than any fixed distance from \(H\) tends to zero. Independence is what makes it settle. If every draw copied the first, the surprisal per symbol would be \(-\frac1n \log_2 p(X_1)\), which tends to zero whatever \(X_1\) is. For \(\varepsilon \gt 0\) and \(n\) large, the typical set \(A_\varepsilon^{(n)}\) of sequences whose surprisal per symbol is within \(\varepsilon\) of \(H\) has probability above \(1 - \varepsilon\), and

\[ (1 - \varepsilon)\, 2^{n(H - \varepsilon)} \le \big|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}\big| \le 2^{n(H + \varepsilon)}. \tag{10.4} \]

Code lengths also price bets. Suppose a coin lands heads 60% of the time and a bookmaker pays even money, so a winning stake comes back doubled. Stake everything on heads every toss and one tail ruins you: you survive ten tosses with probability \(0.6^{10} \approx 0.006\). Split your wealth instead, 0.6 on heads and 0.4 on tails, and each toss multiplies it by 1.2 or 0.8, the same as staking a fifth of it on heads. Then \(\log_2\) wealth grows on average by

\[ 0.6 \log_2 1.2 + 0.4 \log_2 0.8 = 0.029 \text{ bits per toss}, \]

which is \(1 - H(0.6)\), so over a thousand tosses it rises by about 29, give or take 9. The split 0.7 and 0.3 changes it by \(-0.0035\) bits per toss, a slow loss. Which split grows fastest, and what does a wrong belief about the coin cost?

Theorem 10.4 (Kelly)

In a race with odds \(o_i\), a unit staked on outcome \(i\) returns \(o_i\) if \(i\) wins and nothing otherwise. Betting the fractions \(b_i\) of wealth on outcome \(i\), with \(\sum_i b_i = 1\) so that all of it is spread over the outcomes, multiplies wealth by \(b_i o_i\) when \(i\) wins, so \(\log_2\) wealth grows at the rate

\[ W(b) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 (b_i o_i) \]

per race. The rate is largest at \(b = p\), and

\[ W(p) - W(b) = \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, b). \tag{10.5} \]

10.4Derivation

(10.1). For a finite alphabet, put the codewords on a binary tree, and let \(L\) be the longest length. A codeword of length \(\ell\) is a node whose descendants at depth \(L\) number \(2^{L - \ell}\), and in a prefix code these sets of descendants are disjoint, so \(\sum_x 2^{L - \ell(x)} \le 2^L\). Conversely, assign codewords in order of increasing length, each the leftmost free node at its depth. Inequality (10.1) guarantees one is always free.

(10.2). Write \(S\) for the sum in (10.1), which is at most 1, and let \(r\) be the distribution built from the lengths:

\[ S = \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)} \le 1, \qquad r(x) = \frac{2^{-\ell(x)}}{S}. \]

A length is the surprisal of its own weight, \(\ell(x) = -\log_2 2^{-\ell(x)}\), so

\[ \mathbb E_p\,\ell(X) - H(p) = \sum_x p(x) \Big[\log_2 p(x) - \log_2 2^{-\ell(x)}\Big] = \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{2^{-\ell(x)}}. \]

Put \(2^{-\ell(x)} = S\, r(x)\) and split the logarithm:

\[ \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{S\, r(x)} = \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{r(x)} - \log_2 S = \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, r) - \log_2 S \;\ge\; 0, \]

since KL is nonnegative (Chapter 2) and \(S \le 1\) makes \(-\log_2 S \ge 0\). The lengths \(\lceil -\log_2 p(x)\rceil\) satisfy (10.1), because \(2^{-\ell(x)} \le p(x)\), and each is less than \(-\log_2 p(x) + 1\).

(10.3).

\[ -\sum_x p \log_2 q = -\sum_x p \log_2 p + \sum_x p \log_2 (p/q). \]

(10.4). The surprisal per symbol \(\frac1n \sum_i -\log_2 p(X_i)\) is an average of independent terms with mean \(H\), so the law of large numbers gives the limit. Each typical sequence has probability between \(2^{-n(H + \varepsilon)}\) and \(2^{-n(H - \varepsilon)}\), so \(1 \ge P(A) \ge |A|\, 2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}\) and \(1 - \varepsilon \le P(A) \le |A|\, 2^{-n(H - \varepsilon)}\).

(10.5).

\[ W(b) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 o_i + \sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i - \sum_i p_i \log_2 (p_i / b_i), \]

and only the last term, \(-\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, b)\), depends on \(b\). ∎

Whole sequences. Arithmetic coding turns any predictive model \(p(x_t \mid x_{\lt t})\) into a code for a whole sequence. It narrows an interval in \([0, 1)\) by each symbol's probability, so the final interval has width \(p(x_1, \dots, x_n)\), and naming a point inside it takes at most \(-\log_2 p(x_1, \dots, x_n) + 2\) bits, for a decoder that knows the length \(n\) or reads an end symbol. The two extra bits pay for alignment. Let \(w\) be the final width and \(k = \lceil \log_2 (1/w) \rceil + 1\), so that \(2^{-k} \le w/2\). The first block \([j\, 2^{-k}, (j + 1)\, 2^{-k})\) that starts at or after the interval's left end, for an integer \(j\), ends less than \(2 \cdot 2^{-k} \le w\) beyond it, so the whole block lies inside the interval, and the \(k\) binary digits of \(j\) name it. Since \(k \lt \log_2(1/w) + 2\), that is the bound. The code length of a text is at most the model's summed loss in bits, plus two.

10.5Figures

Figure 10.2Arithmetic coding spends −log₂ p bits, plus under 2

Arithmetic coding narrows an interval by each symbol's model probability, so a string costs −log₂ p(string) bits plus under 2, and a worse model costs its cross-entropy.

The string aabaaaadcabaadcabaab was drawn with seed 23 from the letter probabilities 0.6, 0.2, 0.1, and 0.1, and holds 12 a, 4 b, 2 c, and 2 d. The intervals are exact fractions, and the decoder knows the length. With Adaptive counts, which give each letter its count so far plus one, the final interval has width 2^−36.45, and the code length ⌈36.45⌉ + 1 is 38 bits, 1.55 over. The 38-bit codeword under the rows is the shortest dyadic interval inside the final one, and it decodes back to the string. Switch to Own frequencies, whose counts the decoder would also need: the string costs 31.42 bits, 20 times its empirical entropy of 1.571. Uniform costs 40.00, and its extra 8.58 bits equal 20 KL(empirical ‖ uniform). Adaptive counts pay 5.03 bits over own frequencies to learn the counts as they go. Step through the symbols or press Play: over every prefix and model the codeword stays at most 1.82 bits above −log₂ p.

Figure 10.3A bettor with the wrong belief loses KL(p‖q) bits per bet

Betting on a coin at even odds grows wealth by log₂(1 + f) bits per win and log₂(1 − f) per loss, so the best fraction f* = 2p − 1 earns 1 − H(p) bits per bet, and a bettor who believes q earns exactly KL(p‖q) less.

At the defaults the coin lands heads with p = 0.6, and the bettor believes q = 0.7 and stakes f = 0.4 of wealth on heads at even odds. Kelly's fraction f* = 0.2, found by a search over f, grows wealth at G(f*) = 0.0290 bits per bet, which equals 1 − H(0.6). The bettor's rate is G(0.4) = −0.0035, so a coin tilted in the bettor's favor still loses money, and the drop of 0.0326 bits equals KL(0.6 ‖ 0.7). Every f above 0.389 loses at this p. Over 2000 seeded paths of 500 bets the median final log₂ wealth is −1.77 against 500 G(f) = −1.77, and 54.5% of the bettor's paths end below the start against 1.6% of Kelly's. Slide q to 0.6: the gap closes to 0. Slide q to 0.95: f = 0.9, the rate falls to −0.773 bits per bet, and the median path ends at −386.59 bits.

10.6Four ways to see it

Entropy counts possibilities, sets the length of a code, measures how well a model predicts, and prices a bet. Each picture follows from the one before it.

  1. 1Countingcombinatorics and physics

    By Stirling's formula, the number of binary sequences of length \(n\) with \(k\) ones is \(\binom{n}{k} = 2^{n H(k/n) + O(\log n)}\). Entropy is the logarithm of the number of equally likely possibilities, which is Boltzmann's \(S = k_B \ln W\) for the microstates of a gas (Figure 10.1).

  2. 1 → 2Number the roughly \(2^{nH}\) typical sequences, so naming one takes about \(nH\) bits, and give each atypical sequence its own index of \(n \log_2 |\mathcal X| + 1\) bits behind a flag. The atypical ones carry probability below \(\varepsilon\), so the expected length per symbol tends to \(H\): the source coding theorem by counting.

  3. 2Codingengineering

    Kraft's inequality (10.1) is a budget: a codeword of length \(\ell\) spends \(2^{-\ell}\) of a unit of space. Huffman's algorithm spends it optimally symbol by symbol, and arithmetic coding spends it on whole sequences, within two bits of \(-\log_2 p\) (Figure 10.2).

  4. 2 → 3Feed arithmetic coding a model's predictions \(p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\lt t})\). The code for a text has length at most \(\sum_t -\log_2 p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\lt t}) + 2\), and its average over text from the true source is the cross-entropy, \(H\) plus the KL of (10.3). Lowering a model's loss and shortening its code are the same act.

  5. 3Predictionmachine learning and statistics

    A language model's cross-entropy loss, in bits per token, is the size of its compressed text. Minimum description length picks the model that makes the total, the model's own length plus the data's code length under it, shortest. Kolmogorov complexity, the length of the shortest program that prints \(x\), is the limit: no algorithm computes it, and for \(n\) draws from a computable source its expected value is \(nH\) up to the length of a program for the source plus \(O(\log n)\).

  6. 3 → 4Let the odds be fair for some distribution \(r\), so \(o_i = 1/r_i\). Then

    \[ W(b) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 \frac{b_i}{r_i} = \mathbb E_p\big[-\log_2 r(X)\big] - \mathbb E_p\big[-\log_2 b(X)\big], \]

    the bookmaker's log loss on the outcomes minus the bettor's, so wealth grows by the number of bits per race by which the bettor predicts better than the bookmaker.

  7. 4Bettingfinance

    At even odds on a coin with \(p \gt \tfrac12\), the Kelly bettor stakes \(f^* = 2p - 1\) of wealth and grows it by \(1 - H(p)\) bits per bet. Betting about twice that fraction drives the growth rate to zero when the edge is small, and a bettor who believes \(q\) gives up \(\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)\) bits per bet (Figure 10.3).

10.7Where it breaks and what is open

The most probable sequence is atypical. For a coin with \(p(1) = 0.1\), the all-zeros sequence is the single most likely sequence of every length, yet its surprisal per flip is \(-\log_2 0.9 = 0.152\) bits against \(H = 0.469\), so it lies outside the typical set, and the chance of drawing it, \(0.9^n\), vanishes. A language model behaves the same way: the highest-probability continuation, which beam search approximates, carries little surprisal per token and often repeats itself, while samples land at the model's entropy rate (Figure 10.4). Differential entropy fails in another way. For continuous \(X\), \(h(X) = -\int p \log p\) changes under a change of variables, \(h(aX) = h(X) + \log |a|\), and can be negative, so only differences such as KL and mutual information carry meaning, and a code for continuous data must first quantize it.

Figure 10.4The most probable sequence looks nothing like a sample

The most probable sequence of a language model is atypical: its surprisal per token sits far below the entropy rate, it repeats itself, and samples never come near it.

The chain has eight tokens a to h. Token a repeats with probability 0.5, b → c → d → b runs at 0.4 per step, and the entropy rate is 2.704 bits per token. At the default n = 20 the 2000 samples average 2.712 bits per token, against an exact mean of 2.717 that counts the first token's 2.966 bits. The most probable sequence, found exactly by Viterbi and by beam search of width 4, is twenty a's at 1.088 bits per token, with probability 2.8e−7. It uses 1 token where samples use 7.22 on average, and no sample is as probable: the lowest sample sits at 1.757. Set the width to 1 (greedy): decoding falls into the cycle c d b at 1.387 bits per token. Slide n down to 4: the mode aaaa has probability 0.019, and 1.60% of samples equal it. From n = 8 on none of the 2000 samples reaches the mode, and at n = 40 its probability is 2.7e−13.

  1. The mode or the typical set. One can ask whether the sequence with the lowest entropy per token is the most probable one. Equipartition answers that the most probable sequence is atypical and that each typical sequence is improbable. Which of the two a decoder should aim at is open for tasks with checkable answers, where the mode is sometimes right, and branch-and-bound decoding for diffusion language models needs an answer to choose its objective.
  2. Compression as a measure of capability. Language models compress text far better than general-purpose compressors when their own size is not counted (Delétang et al.), and loss in bits tracks downstream ability in many settings. When fewer bits per token stops predicting capability, as with memorized or contaminated data, is open.
  3. Kolmogorov complexity in practice. It cannot be computed. A trained model's code length, plus the length of the model, bounds it from above. The prequential code length of a training run, the sum of the losses as the model learns, minus the final model's loss, measures the information the trained parameters hold about the data (Blier and Ollivier). Whether it ranks models and datasets usefully at scale is open.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 10.1 Entropy is a code length

    • A source emits a, b, c, d with probabilities p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125]. A model that has the order backwards believes q = [0.125, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5].
    • Build the Huffman code for p: its lengths, and its mean length in bits. Then code the source with the Huffman code built for q. How many bits per symbol now, and where do the extra bits come from?
    Answer
    huffman_lengths([0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125])                        # [1, 2, 3, 3]
mean_bits([0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125], [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125])   # 1.75
mean_bits([0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125], [0.125, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5])   # 2.625

  2. Exercise 10.2 A language model's loss is its file size

    • A bigram model over {a, b, c} gives the first character probability 1/3 each. After that it predicts from the character before: a, b, c get probabilities 0.1, 0.7, 0.2 after a, then 0.2, 0.1, 0.7 after b, and 0.7, 0.2, 0.1 after c.
    • Arithmetic-code the 20 characters "abcabcabcabcabacabca". What is −log₂ p of the string, how many bits does the coder send, and what is the model's loss in bits per character?
    Answer
    ideal_bits("abcabcabcabcabacabca")      # 14.9766
coded_bits("abcabcabcabcabacabca")      # 16
bits_per_char("abcabcabcabcabacabca")   # 0.7488

  3. Exercise 10.3 Kelly on a biased coin

    • A coin lands heads with probability 0.6 and pays even odds. Every round you bet the same fraction f of your wealth on heads, forever.
    • Which f grows wealth fastest, and at how many bits per bet? A bettor who believes heads has probability 0.7 picks f by the same rule. How many bits per bet does the wrong belief cost?
    Answer
    kelly_fraction(0.6)          # 0.2
growth_bits(0.6, 0.2)        # 0.02905
belief_cost_bits(0.6, 0.7)   # 0.03258

  4. Exercise 10.4 The most likely sequence is rare

    • The same coin, 1 with probability 0.1 and H = 0.469 bits per flip, writes 100 tokens. Greedy decoding and beam search of any width return its single most likely sequence, all zeros.
    • How likely is that sequence, and what is its surprisal per flip against H? How likely is a sample to hold exactly 10 ones?
    Answer
    mode_probability(100)        # 2.6561e-05
mode_bits_per_flip()         # 0.152
count_probability(10, 100)   # 0.1319

  5. Exercise 10.5 The typical set

    • A coin shows 1 with probability 0.1, so H = 0.469 bits. Flip it n times. A sequence is typical when its surprisal per flip, −(1/n)·log₂ p(sequence), is within ε = 0.05 of H.
    • For n = 100, what is the probability of the typical set, and how many sequences does it hold, in bits? What does the probability become at n = 1000?
    Answer
    typical_probability(100)    # 0.3822
log2_typical_size(100)      # 47.1926
typical_probability(1000)   # 0.898

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 10.1The best code lengths

    Minimize \(\sum_x p(x)\, \ell(x)\) over real lengths with \(\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} = 1\) by a Lagrange multiplier (Appendix A.5), and show that the minimum is \(H(p)\), reached at \(\ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x)\).

    Solution

    Differentiate \(\sum_x p\,\ell + \lambda (\sum_x 2^{-\ell} - 1)\) in \(\ell(x)\): \(p(x) - \lambda \ln 2\; 2^{-\ell(x)} = 0\), so \(2^{-\ell(x)} = p(x)/(\lambda \ln 2)\). Summing over \(x\) and using the constraint gives \(\lambda \ln 2 = 1\), so \(\ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x)\), and the objective is \(H(p)\).

    The objective is linear and the constraint set \(\{\sum 2^{-\ell} \le 1\}\) is convex, so this stationary point is the minimum. Integer lengths cost at most one more bit, which is (10.2).

  2. Derivation 10.2Kelly on a coin

    At even odds on a coin with \(P(\text{heads}) = p\), staking a fraction \(f\) of wealth on heads multiplies wealth by \(1 + f\) or \(1 - f\). Derive the growth rate \(G(f)\), the best \(f\), and \(G(f^*) = 1 - H(p)\) bits. Then show that \(G\) returns to about zero near \(f = 2f^*\) when the edge is small.

    Solution

    \(G(f) = p \log_2(1 + f) + (1 - p)\log_2(1 - f)\). Setting \(G'(f) = 0\) gives \(p/(1 + f) = (1-p)/(1 - f)\), so \(f^* = 2p - 1\). Then \(1 + f^* = 2p\) and \(1 - f^* = 2(1-p)\), so

    \[ G(f^*) = p\log_2 2p + (1-p)\log_2 2(1-p) = 1 - H(p). \]

    In nats, \(G(f) \approx (2p - 1) f - f^2/2\) for small \(f\), which is zero at \(f = 0\) and at \(f = 2(2p - 1) = 2 f^*\).

Project. On a small open language model, take 200 prompts and compare the continuations of greedy decoding, beam search, plain sampling, and locally typical sampling by their surprisal per token against the model's conditional entropy at each step. Report the share of tokens each decoder keeps within 0.5 bits of the entropy.

Chapter 11

Information never grows downstream

Information theory, from estimation

The information \(Y\) carries about \(X\) is the KL between their joint law and the product of their marginals. Processing \(Y\) can only lose it, and in a Gaussian channel it grows at exactly half the error of the best denoiser, so information is integrated denoising error.

Uses Chapters 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, and 10, and Appendix A.1.

11.1Motivation

Suppose a camera photographs a handwritten digit, a phone shrinks the photo to a thumbnail, and an app compresses the thumbnail before a classifier reads it. Could a sharpening filter applied to the thumbnail put back a stroke that the shrinking blurred away? Could a larger classifier? And how would we measure what each stage kept about the digit, in one unit for every stage?

Every learning system processes data in stages like these: a sensor, a pipeline, an encoder, a decoder. Each stage can be engineered, and none can recover information about the source that an earlier stage discarded. Mutual information makes that precise. It gives the speed limit of a noisy channel, the fewest bits a lossy code needs, and, in a Gaussian channel, half the area under the best denoiser's error curve plotted against the signal-to-noise ratio, which ties it to the diffusion models of Chapter 1.

PAPERA document that moved capital

Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

Train word vectors to predict their neighbors, and meaning becomes geometry.

Tomas Mikolov et al., 2013 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Word embeddings became a standard way to represent words and set up the representation learning behind later language models.

The link to this chapter: the skip-gram model it introduced, trained with the negative sampling of its companion paper, implicitly factorizes the matrix of pointwise mutual information between words and contexts, shifted by \(\log k\) for \(k\) negative samples: \(w \cdot c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log k\) when the vectors are wide enough (Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014). The average of the pointwise mutual information over pairs is the mutual information (11.1).

11.2Intuition

Take the smallest chain. A fair coin flip \(X\) goes down a wire that flips the bit one time in ten, and the far end receives \(Y\). Before \(Y\) arrives, \(X\) is a fair bit, so its uncertainty is \(H(X) = 1\) bit. After \(Y\) arrives, \(X\) equals \(Y\) nine times in ten, and the uncertainty left is the binary entropy

\[ h(0.1) = -0.1 \log_2 0.1 - 0.9 \log_2 0.9 = 0.469 \text{ bits}. \]

So \(Y\) told the receiver \(1 - 0.469 = 0.531\) bits about \(X\). Call this drop in uncertainty the information \(Y\) carries about \(X\).

Now a relay copies \(Y\) onto a second wire of the same kind, and the far end receives \(Z\). The bit arrives wrong when exactly one wire flips it, which happens with probability \(2 \cdot 0.1 \cdot 0.9 = 0.18\), so \(Z\) carries \(1 - h(0.18)\) bits, and since \(h(0.18) = 0.680\), that is 0.320 bits. The relay lost 0.211 bits. Could a cleverer relay lose less? Suppose it sends \(Y\) down two such wires at once, so the far end gets two noisy copies and can compare them. The pair carries 0.411 bits, more than one copy and still below the 0.531 that \(Y\) held. Do you see why no relay can reach past 0.531? The relay sees only \(Y\), so whatever it sends depends on \(X\) only through \(Y\), and the far end can do no better than a receiver holding \(Y\) itself. A second wire from the source is another matter. \(Y\) together with a fresh noisy copy of \(X\) carries 0.742 bits, because that copy reads \(X\) directly.

So information about a source is a quantity that each processing step can keep or lose but never create.

Figure 11.1Each noisy channel leaves less information about the bit

A bit sent through two noisy channels in a row keeps less information about its source after each one, and Fano's inequality turns the information left into a floor on how often any guess of the source is wrong.

At the defaults ε₁ = 0.10 and ε₂ = 0.15, the first channel keeps I(X; Y) = 0.531 bits of the 1 bit in X, the second channel alone would keep 0.390, and the pair keeps I(X; Z) = 0.240, under its ceiling of 0.390. The two channels act as one that flips with probability 0.220. The best guess of X from Z errs 0.220 of the time, and Fano's floor is also 0.220, because a fair bit through symmetric channels meets the bound with equality. Slide ε₂ to 0.5: I(X; Z) falls to 0 and the guess errs half the time. Switch to the biased bit: the best guess from Z errs 0.200 of the time, the rate of the rarer value, against a floor of 0.133. Over every setting of both sliders and both sources, I(X; Z) stays at or under its ceiling.

11.3Statement

The relay raises questions that the statements below settle for every source: how to define the information one variable carries about another, why no step that sees only \(Y\) can raise it, and how a small error rate limits the uncertainty left. Two more results follow from the same quantity: a channel with Gaussian noise turns it into denoising error, and a lossy code asks how few bits a description within a given error needs.

Definition 11.1 (mutual information)

\[ I(X; Y) = \mathrm{KL}\big(p_{XY} \,\big\|\, p_X \otimes p_Y\big) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y), \qquad I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y). \tag{11.1} \]

Here \(p_X \otimes p_Y\) is the law that \(X\) and \(Y\) would have if they were independent, \(p_X(x)\, p_Y(y)\). The conditional entropy \(H(X \mid Y) = -\mathbb E \log p(X \mid Y)\) is the uncertainty left in \(X\) once \(Y\) is seen, and the conditional information \(I(X; Z \mid Y)\) is (11.1) computed under \(p(\cdot \mid Y = y)\) and averaged over \(y\). For the wire of Section 11.2, \(H(X) = 1\), \(H(X \mid Y) = 0.469\), and \(I(X; Y) = 0.531\) bits.

Theorem 11.2 (data processing and Fano)

If \(X \to Y \to Z\) is a Markov chain, meaning that \(Z\) depends on \(X\) only through \(Y\), so that \(p(z \mid x, y) = p(z \mid y)\), then

\[ I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y). \tag{11.2} \]

The relay of Section 11.2 is such a chain. Without the Markov property the bound fails: if \(Z\) is \(Y\) together with a fresh noisy copy of \(X\), then \(I(X; Z) = 0.742\) bits against \(I(X; Y) = 0.531\).

If \(X\) and its estimate \(\hat X(Y)\) both take values in a finite set \(\mathcal X\), the estimate errs with a probability \(P_e\) that satisfies, with \(h\) the binary entropy,

\[ H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e \log\big(|\mathcal X| - 1\big). \tag{11.3} \]

Now give the noise a dial. Suppose \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) is measured as \(Y = \sqrt{\mathrm{snr}}\, X + Z\), with independent noise \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and a signal-to-noise ratio \(\mathrm{snr} \ge 0\). At \(\mathrm{snr} = 3\), \(Y\) has variance 4, and given \(X\) its only randomness is \(Z\), so in nats

\[ I(X; Y) = h(Y) - h(Z) = \tfrac12 \ln(2\pi e \cdot 4) - \tfrac12 \ln(2\pi e) = \tfrac12 \ln 4 = 0.693, \]

exactly one bit. The best estimate of \(X\) from \(Y\) is \(\tfrac{\sqrt 3}{4}\, Y\), and its mean squared error is \(\tfrac14\). At every \(\mathrm{snr}\) the error is \(1/(1 + \mathrm{snr})\), and half the area under that curve from 0 to 3 is

\[ \tfrac12 \int_0^3 \frac{d\gamma}{1 + \gamma} = \tfrac12 \ln 4 = 0.693, \]

the same number. Is that an accident of the Gaussian, or is information always integrated denoising error?

Theorem 11.3 (I-MMSE and de Bruijn)

Let \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\) be independent of \(X\), with \(\mathbb E|X|^2 \lt \infty\). For \(Y_{\mathrm{snr}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{snr}}\, X + Z\), in nats,

\[ \frac{d}{d\,\mathrm{snr}}\, I(X; Y_{\mathrm{snr}}) = \tfrac12\, \mathrm{mmse}(\mathrm{snr}), \qquad \mathrm{mmse}(\mathrm{snr}) = \mathbb E\, \big|X - \mathbb E[X \mid Y_{\mathrm{snr}}]\big|^2, \tag{11.4} \]

and the differential entropy of \(X_t = X + \sqrt t\, Z\) rises at half its Fisher information \(J(p) = \mathbb E\, |\nabla \log p|^2\):

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\, h(X_t) = \tfrac12\, J(X_t). \tag{11.5} \]

Run the wire the other way. Suppose you must describe a long run of fair coin flips and may get one flip in ten wrong. One bit per flip is exact, so how few bits per flip will do? The answer is \(1 - h(0.1) = 0.531\) bits, the information the noisy wire of Section 11.2 carried. The best description makes the reconstruction look as if the flips had passed through that wire.

Proposition 11.4 (rate-distortion)

Let a distortion \(d(x, \hat x) \ge 0\) be the cost of reproducing \(x\) as \(\hat x\), such as squared error, or 1 for a wrong bit and 0 for a right one. The least rate per symbol at which long sequences of independent copies of \(X\) can be described within expected distortion \(D\) per symbol is \(R(D) = \min I(X; \hat X)\) over channels \(p(\hat x \mid x)\) with \(\mathbb E\, d(X, \hat X) \le D\). Put a price \(\beta \ge 0\) on distortion and minimize \(I(X; \hat X) + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d(X, \hat X)\) instead. The minimizing channel is a tilt of its own output marginal \(q\):

\[ p(\hat x \mid x) = \frac{q(\hat x)\, e^{-\beta\, d(x, \hat x)}}{\sum_{\hat x'} q(\hat x')\, e^{-\beta\, d(x, \hat x')}}, \qquad q(\hat x) = \sum_x p(x)\, p(\hat x \mid x). \tag{11.6} \]

For a Gaussian source \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) with squared error, \(R(D) = \tfrac12 \log(\sigma^2 / D)\) for \(D \le \sigma^2\). For a fair bit with the wrong-bit distortion, \(q\) is uniform by symmetry, the tilt at \(\beta = \ln 9\) is the wire that flips a bit with probability \(e^{-\beta}/(1 + e^{-\beta}) = 0.1\), and \(R(0.1) = 1 - h(0.1)\), which is 0.531 bits.

11.4Derivation

(11.1).

\[ \mathbb E \log \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x) p(y)} = \mathbb E \log \frac{p(x \mid y)}{p(x)} = H(X) - H(X \mid Y). \]

For the chain rule, split \(\frac{p(x \mid y, z)}{p(x)} = \frac{p(x \mid y)}{p(x)} \cdot \frac{p(x \mid y, z)}{p(x \mid y)}\) and take expectations of the logarithm.

(11.2). Expand \(I(X; Y, Z)\) by the chain rule both ways:

\[ I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y). \]

The Markov property makes \(I(X; Z \mid Y) = 0\), and \(I(X; Y \mid Z) \ge 0\).

(11.3). Let \(E\) indicate an error. \(E\) is a function of \(X\) and \(Y\), so

\[ H(X \mid Y) = H(X, E \mid Y) = H(E \mid Y) + H(X \mid E, Y). \]

The first term is at most \(h(P_e)\). Given no error, \(X = \hat X(Y)\) is known, and given an error, \(X\) has at most \(|\mathcal X| - 1\) values left, so the second term is at most \(P_e \log(|\mathcal X| - 1)\).

(11.5). The density \(p_t\) of \(X_t\) solves the heat equation \(\partial_t p = \tfrac12 \Delta p\) (Chapter 1, with \(g = 1\)). Differentiate under the integral, using \(\partial_t (p \log p) = \partial_t p\, (\log p + 1)\):

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\Big(-\int p_t \log p_t\Big) = -\int \partial_t p_t\, (\log p_t + 1) = -\int \partial_t p_t\, \log p_t. \]

The 1 drops out because total probability stays one, so \(\int \partial_t p_t = 0\). Substitute the heat equation:

\[ -\int \partial_t p_t\, \log p_t = -\tfrac12 \int \Delta p_t\, \log p_t. \]

Integrate by parts once, moving one derivative of \(\Delta p_t = \nabla \cdot \nabla p_t\) onto \(\log p_t\). The boundary term \(\log p_t\, \nabla p_t\) vanishes at infinity, because a Gaussian-smoothed density's gradient decays faster than its logarithm grows. Then use \(\nabla \log p_t = \nabla p_t / p_t\):

\[ -\tfrac12 \int \Delta p_t\, \log p_t = \tfrac12 \int \nabla p_t \cdot \nabla \log p_t = \tfrac12 \int \frac{|\nabla p_t|^2}{p_t}. \]

Write the last integrand as \(p_t\, |\nabla \log p_t|^2\), an expectation under \(X_t\):

\[ \tfrac12 \int \frac{|\nabla p_t|^2}{p_t} = \tfrac12 \int p_t\, |\nabla \log p_t|^2 = \tfrac12\, J(X_t). \]

(11.4). Write \(\mathrm{snr} = 1/t\), so that \(Y_{\mathrm{snr}} = X_t / \sqrt t\). Scaling by \(\sqrt t\) does not change information. Given \(X\), the only randomness left in \(X_t\) is \(\sqrt t\, Z\), a Gaussian in \(n\) dimensions with entropy \(\tfrac n2 \log(2\pi e t)\), so

\[ I(X; Y_{\mathrm{snr}}) = I(X; X_t) = h(X_t) - h(X_t \mid X) = h(X_t) - \tfrac{n}{2}\log(2\pi e t). \]

By Tweedie's formula (Chapter 1) the score of \(X_t\) is \(s = (m - X_t)/t\), with \(m = \mathbb E[X \mid X_t]\). Call the estimation error \(\varepsilon = X - m\), so that \(\mathrm{mmse} = \mathbb E|\varepsilon|^2\). Since \(X_t - m = \varepsilon + \sqrt t\, Z\), expanding the square gives

\[ J(X_t) = \mathbb E\,|s|^2 = \frac{\mathbb E\,|\varepsilon|^2 + 2\sqrt t\; \mathbb E[\varepsilon \cdot Z] + t\, \mathbb E\,|Z|^2}{t^2}, \qquad \mathbb E\,|Z|^2 = n. \]

For the middle term, the posterior mean's error is orthogonal to every function of \(X_t\) with finite second moment, \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon \cdot g(X_t)] = 0\), which is where \(\mathbb E|X|^2 \lt \infty\) is used. Take \(g(X_t) = X_t\) and \(g(X_t) = m\). Since \(\sqrt t\, Z = X_t - X\) and \(X = \varepsilon + m\),

\[ \sqrt t\; \mathbb E[\varepsilon \cdot Z] = \mathbb E[\varepsilon \cdot X_t] - \mathbb E[\varepsilon \cdot \varepsilon] - \mathbb E[\varepsilon \cdot m] = 0 - \mathrm{mmse} - 0. \]

So

\[ J(X_t) = \frac{\mathrm{mmse} - 2\,\mathrm{mmse} + n\,t}{t^2} = \frac{n\,t - \mathrm{mmse}}{t^2}. \]

Differentiate the first display in \(t\), using (11.5) for \(h(X_t)\):

\[ \frac{dI}{dt} = \tfrac12 J(X_t) - \frac{n}{2t} = \frac{n\,t - \mathrm{mmse}}{2t^2} - \frac{n\,t}{2t^2} = -\frac{\mathrm{mmse}}{2t^2}. \]

Finally \(t = 1/\mathrm{snr}\) gives \(\frac{dt}{d\,\mathrm{snr}} = -t^2\), and the chain rule turns \(\frac{dI}{dt}\) into \(\frac{dI}{d\,\mathrm{snr}} = \tfrac12\,\mathrm{mmse}\), which is (11.4).

(11.6). Minimize \(I(X; \hat X) + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\) over channels, with a multiplier \(p(x)\, \nu(x)\) for the constraint that the row of the channel at \(x\) sums to one. The information is

\[ I(X; \hat X) = \sum_{x, \hat x} p(x)\, p(\hat x \mid x) \log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q(\hat x)}, \]

and \(q\) depends on the channel too. Differentiate in one entry \(p(\hat x \mid x)\). The entry's own appearances give \(p(x) \big[\log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q(\hat x)} + 1\big]\). Through \(q(\hat x)\), which moves by \(p(x)\) per unit change of the entry, the sum changes by

\[ -\sum_{x'} p(x')\, p(\hat x \mid x')\, \frac{p(x)}{q(\hat x)} = -p(x), \]

which cancels the \(+1\). The distortion adds \(\beta\, p(x)\, d(x, \hat x)\) and the constraint adds \(p(x)\, \nu(x)\). Set the total to zero and divide by \(p(x)\):

\[ \log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q(\hat x)} + \beta\, d(x, \hat x) + \nu(x) = 0, \quad\text{so}\quad p(\hat x \mid x) = q(\hat x)\, e^{-\beta\, d(x, \hat x) - \nu(x)}. \]

Summing over \(\hat x\) and using the constraint fixes the normalizer,

\[ e^{\nu(x)} = \sum_{\hat x'} q(\hat x')\, e^{-\beta\, d(x, \hat x')}, \]

which is (11.6). For the Gaussian,

\[ I(X; \hat X) = h(X) - h(X \mid \hat X) \ge h(X) - h(X - \hat X) \ge \tfrac12 \log(2\pi e \sigma^2) - \tfrac12 \log(2 \pi e D). \]

The first inequality holds because, given \(\hat X\), subtracting \(\hat X\) only shifts \(X\), so \(h(X \mid \hat X) = h(X - \hat X \mid \hat X)\), and conditioning cannot raise entropy. The second holds because \(\mathbb E (X - \hat X)^2 \le D\) and a Gaussian has the largest entropy at a given variance. Taking \(X = \hat X + N\) with independent \(\hat X \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 - D)\) and \(N \sim \mathcal N(0, D)\) reaches the bound. ∎

Blahut-Arimoto. Alternate the two halves of (11.6): fix \(q\) and tilt the channel, then fix the channel and recompute \(q\). Each half minimizes the joint objective \(\sum_x p(x)\, \mathrm{KL}\big(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q\big) + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\) in one block of variables, so the objective is a potential that never rises (Chapter 9), and the iteration is a fixed-point method (Chapter 4) whose fixed points are the tilts of Chapter 2. The information bottleneck replaces the distortion by the information lost about a target \(Y\) and has a tilted solution of a similar form, though its distortion depends on the encoder, so three equations are iterated and the solution need not be unique, and a \(\beta\)-VAE's loss is a distortion plus \(\beta\) times a rate (the encoder's KL from its prior, an upper bound on \(I(X; Z)\)), which is the objective above with multiplier \(1/\beta\). Under squared error, uniform scalar quantization of a smooth source at high resolution, followed by an ideal entropy code, pays \(\tfrac12 \log_2(\pi e / 6) \approx 0.254\) bits per sample above \(R(D)\).

11.5Figures

Figure 11.2Information is integrated denoising error

In a Gaussian channel the information that Y = √snr·X + Z carries about X grows at exactly half the error of the best denoiser, so I(snr) is half the integral of mmse(γ) from 0 to snr.

Every input has mean 0 and variance 1, and I and mmse are computed separately. At the default ±1 input and snr = 1, the finite difference of I gives dI/dsnr = 0.22480, and the best denoiser's error is mmse = 0.44960, half of which is also 0.22480. The information is I = 0.33683 nats, and half the area under the mmse curve up to snr = 1 is 0.33683. A Gaussian input of the same power carries more, 0.34657 nats, and is harder to denoise, with mmse 0.50000. Slide snr to 100: I reaches 0.69315 = ln 2, all that one sign can carry, the error falls to 2.3884e−23, and the finite difference still matches half of it. Switch to the Chapter 1 mixture, the three-bump density of the first figures standardized: from snr 0.01 to 100 the two sides of the integral identity differ by at most 7.3e−10 nats.

Figure 11.3Blahut-Arimoto finds the best lossy code

Blahut-Arimoto finds the least rate at each distortion by alternating two updates, the tilted channel p(x̂ | x) ∝ q(x̂)·exp(−β d(x, x̂)) and its output marginal q, and on a Gaussian source its curve meets ½ log₂(σ²/D).

The source is N(0, 1) on 201 grid points from −5 to 5, with variance σ² = 0.99999 on the grid, and the reproductions use the same grid with squared error. Each run starts from a uniform q and stops when an iteration lowers the potential F = −Σ p(x) log₂ Z(x) by less than 1e−9 bits. At the default β = 1.995, Blahut-Arimoto stops after 36 iterations at D = 0.2506 and R = 0.99828 bits, and ½ log₂(σ²/D) gives 0.99828. The measured slope dR/dD is −2.879, equal to −β/ln 2, so β prices distortion in bits. At x = 1 the optimal channel has mean 0.7494 and standard deviation 0.4334, which are (1 − D/σ²)x and √(D(1 − D)) for the Gaussian test channel. Slide β down to 0.631, where R falls to 0.168 and nears 0: the run needs 147 iterations. Over all 23 points of the curve, R stays within 6.4e−7 bits of the closed form.

Figure 11.4Unmasking tokens together costs their total correlation

Unmasking several tokens at once, each from its own conditional, costs exactly their total correlation given the tokens already seen, so the sampler's KL from the true model is the sum of these costs over the steps, and the grouping decides how large they are.

The chain has three tokens over eight positions, all 6,561 sequences are enumerated, and positions 1 and 2 share 0.347 nats. At the default two tokens per step in adjacent pairs, the steps pay 0.347, 0.214, 0.212, and 0.211 nats of total correlation, and their sum, 0.984, equals KL(true ‖ sampler) = 0.984. Neighbours in its samples agree 0.578 of the time against 0.742 in the chain. Switch to spread, pairs 1 and 5, 2 and 6, and so on: only the first step pays, 0.0185 nats, because given the tokens already seen each later pair is independent in a Markov chain. Greedy by MI takes the least informative pair at each step, opens with positions 1 and 8, and must close with neighbours 4 and 5, which cost 0.134 of its 0.156. Over all 105 ways to pair the positions, spread has the least summed pairwise information. At four tokens per step the pairwise sum double counts: adjacent groups pay 1.857 nats of total correlation while their pairwise informations add to 2.382. One token per step pays nothing.

11.6Four ways to see it

Mutual information is a distance from independence, the capacity of a channel, the area under a denoising curve, and the score of a contrastive classifier.

  1. 1Distance from independenceprobability

    By (11.1), \(I(X; Y)\) is the KL between the joint law and the product of the marginals: the extra bits per pair that a code assuming independence pays (Chapter 10), and the evidence per sample against independence (Figure 11.1).

  2. 1 → 2Fix the channel \(p(y \mid x)\) and choose the input law. The largest information, \(C = \max_{p(x)} I(X; Y)\), is the capacity, and Shannon's channel coding theorem says it is the largest rate of reliable communication. For a Gaussian channel \(Y = X + W\) with signal power \(P\) and noise power \(N\),

    \[ I = h(Y) - h(W) \le \tfrac12 \log 2\pi e(P + N) - \tfrac12 \log 2\pi e N, \]

    with equality for a Gaussian input, so \(C = \tfrac12 \log(1 + P/N)\).

  3. 2Channel capacitycommunication engineering

    Capacity is the speed limit of a noisy channel. Codes approach it by spreading each message over many uses of the channel, which is the equipartition of Chapter 10 applied to pairs of sequences.

  4. 1 → 3Integrate (11.4) from \(\mathrm{snr} = 0\), where \(Y\) is pure noise and carries no information:

    \[ I(X; Y_{\mathrm{snr}}) = \tfrac12 \int_0^{\mathrm{snr}} \mathrm{mmse}(\gamma)\, d\gamma. \]

    In a diffusion model \(Y_{\mathrm{snr}}\) is the data noised to level \(1/\mathrm{snr}\), and the best denoiser is Tweedie's posterior mean (Chapter 1), so the information the noisy data keeps is half the area under the denoising-error curve.

  5. 3Estimationstatistics and diffusion models

    Information and estimation are one quantity read two ways (Figure 11.2). Applied to each data point rather than on average, the same identity writes \(-\log p(x)\) exactly as an integral over noise levels of how far the best denoiser's error at \(x\) falls below the error for a Gaussian of the same scale, and a trained denoiser turns it into an upper bound on the model's own \(-\log p_\theta(x)\), and on \(\mathbb E_p[-\log p(X)]\) on average (Kong et al.).

  6. 1 → 4Apply Donsker-Varadhan (Chapter 2) to the KL in (11.1): every critic \(T(x, y)\) gives \(I \ge \mathbb E_{p_{XY}}[T] - \log \mathbb E_{p_X \otimes p_Y}[e^{T}]\). A multi-sample bound of the same family averages the critic over the \(N\) candidates in a batch, the true pair included, and is still a lower bound (Poole et al.). It is InfoNCE,

    \[ I(X; Y) \ge \mathbb E \Big[\log \frac{e^{T(x_1, y_1)}}{\frac1N \sum_{j=1}^N e^{T(x_1, y_j)}}\Big], \]

    whose value can never exceed \(\log N\), since the fraction is at most \(N\).

  7. 4Contrastive learningmachine learning

    CLIP and contrastive predictive coding train a critic to pick the true pair out of a batch, and the InfoNCE loss they minimize, a cross-entropy over the batch, equals \(\log N\) minus the bound above. The information the loss can certify is capped at \(\log N\) (Figure 11.5).

11.7Where it breaks and what is open

Mutual information is defined by distributions and measured from samples, and the measurement fails twice. Any distribution-free high-confidence lower bound from \(n\) samples stays below a quantity of order \(\log n\) (McAllester and Stratos, and the open problems of Chapter 2). InfoNCE with a batch of \(N\) cannot exceed \(\log N\) even with the perfect critic, and bounds without that cap, such as the NWJ bound, pay with a variance that, even with the optimal critic, is at least exponential in the information (Song and Ermon). A measured spread can hide that variance: the rare large terms go undrawn, so at high information the spread across batches shrinks while the mean drifts above the truth (Figure 11.5). And the data processing inequality ignores computation. Encrypting an image with a fixed secret key keeps every bit of its information, yet no efficient learner without the key can classify the ciphertext, and decrypting it is a downstream step that raises the information a model family can use, though the information itself cannot grow. Usable information makes this precise relative to a family of predictors (Xu et al.).

Figure 11.5InfoNCE cannot report more than log N

With a batch of N pairs, InfoNCE never reports more than log N nats, even with the perfect critic, while NWJ, which has no cap, pays with a spread across batches that grows with the information.

X and Y have five coordinates each, and each coordinate pair has correlation ρ, so the true information is −(5/2) log(1 − ρ²) nats. Both estimators use the optimal critic log p(y | x)/p(y). At the default ρ = 0.99 and N = 64, the truth is 9.793 nats. InfoNCE reads 4.151 over 200 batches, just under log 64 = 4.159, and no batch passes the cap. NWJ averages 9.669 with a standard deviation of 5.550, and one batch reads −57.1. Slide ρ down: InfoNCE first falls 0.5 nats short at a truth of 3.610, and at ρ = 0.684 NWJ reads 1.579 ± 0.197 against 1.576. Slide ρ up to 0.999: NWJ reads 16.510 ± 0.575 against 15.538, because the shuffled pairs' ratio, whose mean should be 1, averages 0.035 when its rare large values go undrawn. Raising N to 1024 lifts the cap only to 6.931, and InfoNCE reads 6.809 at the default ρ over 10 batches.

  1. Estimating large information. Predicting pairwise information between tokens works because the values are small. Estimating information of hundreds of nats, between a prompt and a long response or between two layers, is open, because the cap of \(\log N\) and the variance of uncapped bounds both stand in the way.
  2. How many tokens to unmask at once. If each token's distribution given the context is exact, a parallel unmasking step costs exactly the total correlation of the tokens it reveals, conditional on that context, and the sum of their pairwise informations approximates it, missing synergy and double-counting redundancy (Figure 11.4). Choosing the least informative group one step at a time is myopic: on a Markov chain it leaves neighbours for the last step and pays several times what a fixed spread schedule pays. Whether pairwise information is enough for long-range structure, and how to budget total correlation per step against the number of steps, is open.
  3. Likelihoods from denoisers. The I-MMSE likelihood of a diffusion model is exact for the best denoiser, and a trained denoiser gives an upper bound on its own \(-\log p_\theta\) and, on average, on the data's (Kong et al.). For masked discrete diffusion the cross-entropy of each revealed token plays the part of the denoising error, and with exact conditionals the negative ELBO equals \(-\log p(x)\), because every unmasking order is a chain rule. How tight these bounds are for trained models, and which noise schedule makes them tightest per unit of compute, are open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 11.1From de Bruijn to I-MMSE

    Starting from the heat equation for \(X_t = X + \sqrt t\, Z\) in one dimension, derive de Bruijn's identity (11.5). Then use Tweedie's formula to show \(J(X_t) = (t - \mathrm{mmse}_t)/t^2\), and conclude (11.4). Check it on \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), where \(I = \tfrac12\log(1 + \mathrm{snr})\).

    Solution

    As in Section 11.4,

    \[ \frac{d}{dt} h = -\int \partial_t p\, (\log p + 1) = -\tfrac12 \int p'' \log p = \tfrac12 \int (p')^2/p = \tfrac12 J, \]

    with the boundary terms vanishing for a Gaussian-smoothed density.

    Tweedie gives the score \(s(y) = (m(y) - y)/t\) with \(m(y) = \mathbb E[X \mid X_t = y]\). Write \(e = X - m(X_t)\), so \(X_t - m = e + \sqrt t\, Z\). Since \(\sqrt t\, Z = X_t - X\), \(\mathbb E[e \sqrt t Z] = \mathbb E[e X_t] - \mathbb E[e X] = 0 - \mathbb E[e^2]\), using \(\mathbb E[e\, g(X_t)] = 0\) and \(\mathbb E[e X] = \mathbb E[e (e + m)] = \mathbb E e^2\). So

    \[ J = \mathbb E(e + \sqrt t Z)^2 / t^2 = (\mathrm{mmse} - 2\,\mathrm{mmse} + t)/t^2 = (t - \mathrm{mmse})/t^2. \]

    With \(I = h(X_t) - \tfrac12 \log(2\pi e t)\), \(\frac{dI}{dt} = -\mathrm{mmse}/(2t^2)\), and \(\mathrm{snr} = 1/t\) gives \(\frac{dI}{d\,\mathrm{snr}} = \tfrac12\,\mathrm{mmse}\). For \(X \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\mathrm{mmse} = 1/(1 + \mathrm{snr})\), and \(\frac{d}{d\,\mathrm{snr}} \tfrac12 \log(1 + \mathrm{snr}) = \tfrac12 \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \mathrm{snr}}\).

  2. Derivation 11.2The rate-distortion tilt, and why Blahut-Arimoto descends

    Show that \(I(X; \hat X) = \min_q \sum_x p(x)\, \mathrm{KL}\big(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q\big)\), with the minimum at the output marginal. Then derive the channel update (11.6) for fixed \(q\), and explain why alternating the two updates never raises \(I + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\).

    Solution
    \[ \sum_x p(x)\, \mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q) = I(X; \hat X) + \mathrm{KL}(q^\circ \,\|\, q), \]

    where \(q^\circ\) is the output marginal, because the log ratio splits as \(\log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q^\circ(\hat x)} + \log \frac{q^\circ(\hat x)}{q(\hat x)}\). The second term is nonnegative and zero at \(q = q^\circ\).

    For fixed \(q\), minimizing \(\sum_{\hat x} p(\hat x \mid x) \big[\log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q(\hat x)} + \beta d(x, \hat x)\big]\) for each \(x\) is Theorem 2.1 with \(f = -\beta d(x, \cdot)\) and base \(q\), so the minimizer is the tilt \(q\, e^{-\beta d}/Z\).

    The joint objective

    \[ F(\text{channel}, q) = \sum_x p(x)\,\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q) + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d \]

    is minimized exactly in each block by each update, so \(F\) never rises. After each update of \(q\), \(F\) equals \(I + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\) of the current channel, so that quantity never rises either.

On a masked diffusion model for Sudoku or short text, estimate the total correlation of the tokens revealed at each parallel step, exactly on a small vocabulary and with a learned pairwise-information estimator, and report the correlation between the estimated total correlation and the drop in sample quality per step.

Chapter 12

The adjoint method

Optimal control and automatic differentiation

To differentiate one number computed by a long chain of steps with respect to every input of every step, run the chain forward once and a chain of costates backward once. The backward chain is backpropagation for networks, the adjoint equation for differential equations, and the costate of optimal control.

Uses Chapters 3 and 4 and Appendix A.5.

12.1Motivation

Suppose you simulate a rocket's flight in a thousand time steps and choose the angle of its engine at each step. One number comes out at the end: how far the rocket lands from the pad. Which way should each of the thousand angles turn? You could nudge one angle, rerun the flight, and see how far the landing point moves, but that takes a thousand and one flights for one answer. Yet a nudge at step 500 and a nudge at step 499 both reach the landing point through steps 501 to 1000, so most of each rerun repeats work already done. Could one pass, run backward from the landing point, price every angle at once?

Training a model with a billion parameters is the same problem at a larger size, since it needs the gradient of one loss with respect to all of them at every step. Perturbing the parameters one at a time costs a billion forward passes, and carrying sensitivities forward through the computation costs one pass per parameter too. Control engineers met the same problem around 1960, designing flight trajectories in which the parameters are a whole control signal. The adjoint method computes every sensitivity at once by running one linear recursion backward, at a cost of a small multiple of one forward pass. Reverse-mode differentiation (Linnainmaa, 1970) and backpropagation, popularized for neural networks in 1986, are the same computation.

PAPERA document that moved capital

Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

Let each block learn a correction to its input instead of a new representation, and networks train hundreds of layers deep.

Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun, 2015 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Residual networks took first place in the ImageNet and COCO competitions of 2015, and the residual connection has been part of nearly every deep architecture since, the Transformer included.

The link to this chapter: a residual block computes \(x_{l+1} = x_l + F(x_l)\), an explicit Euler step of \(\dot x = f(x)\) with unit step, a reading that Haber and Ruthotto made precise (Section 3, equations 2.1 and 3.5). Backpropagation through it is the discrete adjoint (12.1) with Jacobian \(I + \partial_x F\), so the costate passes back through the identity path intact, and as the steps shrink it becomes the continuous adjoint (12.2) that neural ODEs train with.

12.2Intuition

Take the smallest chain with a bend in it. Start at \(x_0 = 1\), triple it, then square it, and let the loss be the result:

\[ x_1 = 3 x_0 = 3, \qquad x_2 = x_1^2 = 9, \qquad L = x_2 = 9. \]

How much does \(L\) move if \(x_0\) moves? Carry a small nudge \(\delta\) forward. Tripling turns it into \(3\delta\) at \(x_1\). Squaring near \(x_1 = 3\) multiplies small changes by its slope \(2 x_1 = 6\), so \(x_2\) moves by \(6 \cdot 3\delta = 18\delta\), and \(dL/dx_0 = 18\). Check: \(L = 9 x_0^2\), whose slope at \(x_0 = 1\) is 18.

Now walk backward instead. A nudge to \(x_2\) moves \(L\) one for one, so write 1 beside \(x_2\). A nudge to \(x_1\) reaches \(L\) through the squaring, which multiplies it by 6, so write \(6 \cdot 1 = 6\) beside \(x_1\). A nudge to \(x_0\) is tripled on its way to \(x_1\), where each unit is worth 6, so write \(3 \cdot 6 = 18\) beside \(x_0\). The same 18 arrives. What do the backward numbers 1, 6, and 18 mean? Each is the change in the final loss per unit nudge of that step's state, and each came from the one after it by a single multiplication with the local slope.

The backward walk pays off when there are many knobs. Put a knob in the first step, \(x_1 = \theta x_0\) with \(\theta = 3\). A unit change in \(\theta\) moves \(x_1\) by \(x_0 = 1\), and the walk already priced a unit of \(x_1\) at 6, so \(dL/d\theta\) is \(1 \cdot 6 = 6\). Check: \(L = \theta^2 x_0^2\), whose slope in \(\theta\) at 3 is 6. Carrying nudges forward takes one pass for \(x_0\) and another for \(\theta\). The one backward walk priced both, and with a billion knobs it would still be one walk.

These backward numbers are the costates: the costate at each step says how much the final loss would change if that step's state moved, and it can be handed backward one step at a time.

Figure 12.1Costates handed back through a 24-step chain

Each costate λₖ is the gradient of the final loss with respect to the state xₖ, each one comes from the next by a single vector-Jacobian product, and the same backward sweep gives the gradient for all 144 weights and biases.

Each step is xₖ₊₁ = xₖ + 0.2 tanh(Wₖxₖ + bₖ), with seeded weights that drift from step to step, and the loss is ½|x₂₄ − target|² = 1.802. The arrows are the costates. At the end λ₂₄ = x₂₄ − target has length 1.90, and passed back through 24 Jacobians it grows to length 13.66 at λ₀ = (11.635, 7.160), which finite differences in x₀ match to five decimals. The same sweep gives all 144 entries of the gradient, and central finite differences with step 10⁻⁴ agree with them to 3.8e−9 of the largest entry, at a cost of 288 forward passes against one forward and one backward. Slide the parameter count down to 6: finite differences cost 12 passes for those six entries, and the one backward sweep still covers all 144. Press Train 80 steps: gradient descent with step 0.2 on the adjoint's gradient bends the path onto the target and takes the loss to 3.6e−4.

12.3Statement

In the toy, each backward number came from the next by one multiplication with a local slope, and the knob's slope was the costate of the state it moved, times how far it moved it. Theorem 12.1 says the same holds for any chain of vector-valued steps, Theorem 12.2 shrinks the steps into a differential equation, and Theorem 12.3 lets the knob be a whole control signal chosen to minimize a cost.

Theorem 12.1 (the discrete adjoint)

Let \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k; \theta)\) for \(k \lt N\) and \(L = \ell(x_N)\). Write \(\partial_x F_k\) and \(\partial_\theta F_k\) for the Jacobians of step \(k\), the matrices of partial derivatives of its outputs in its state and in its parameters, like the toy's slopes 3 and 6 in the state and 1 in \(\theta\). Set \(\lambda_N = \nabla \ell(x_N)\) and \(\lambda_k = \big(\partial_x F_k(x_k)\big)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\). Then

\[ \nabla_{x_0} L = \lambda_0, \qquad \nabla_\theta L = \sum_{k \lt N} \big(\partial_\theta F_k(x_k)\big)^\top \lambda_{k+1}. \tag{12.1} \]

Each \(\lambda_k\) costs one vector-Jacobian product, the row \(\lambda_{k+1}^\top\) times the Jacobian, which reverse-mode code computes from the step's own operations without forming the matrix, so the whole gradient costs a small multiple of the forward pass, whatever the number of parameters.

Theorem 12.2 (the continuous adjoint)

Let \(\dot x = f(x, t; \theta)\) on \([0, T]\) and \(L = \ell(x(T))\). Solve \(\dot\lambda = -(\partial_x f)^\top \lambda\) backward from \(\lambda(T) = \nabla \ell(x(T))\). Then

\[ \nabla_{x(0)} L = \lambda(0), \qquad \nabla_\theta L = \int_0^T (\partial_\theta f)^\top \lambda\; dt. \tag{12.2} \]

Now let the knob be a whole signal. Suppose a cart starts at \(x = 1\), you set its velocity \(u(t)\) for one second, and you pay \(\tfrac12 u^2\) per second plus \(\tfrac12 x(1)^2\) at the end. A constant push \(u\) lands the cart at \(1 + u\) and costs \(\tfrac12 u^2 + \tfrac12 (1 + u)^2\), which is least at \(u = -\tfrac12\). The cart lands at \(\tfrac12\), the total is \(\tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = \tfrac14\), and no varying push does better, since by Jensen's inequality a push that ends at the same place costs at least as much as the constant one. Started from \(x\), the best cost is \(x^2/4\), whose slope at \(x = 1\) is \(\tfrac12\). Now carry a costate back along the best path. It starts at the slope of the end cost, \(\lambda(1) = x(1)\), which is \(\tfrac12\), and stays there, since neither the running cost \(\tfrac12 u^2\) nor the motion \(\dot x = u\) depends on where the cart is. The push that minimizes \(\tfrac12 u^2 + \lambda u\) is \(u = -\lambda\), which is \(-\tfrac12\), the push already found, and the costate equals the slope of the best cost. Do both facts hold for every control problem?

Theorem 12.3 (Pontryagin's costate)

Minimize \(\int_0^T c(x, u)\, dt + \ell(x(T))\) subject to \(\dot x = f(x, u)\), and let \(H(x, u, \lambda) = c(x, u) + \lambda \cdot f(x, u)\). An optimal control minimizes \(H\) at each time, and along the optimal trajectory

\[ \dot x = \partial_\lambda H, \qquad \dot \lambda = -\partial_x H, \qquad \lambda(T) = \nabla \ell(x(T)). \tag{12.3} \]

Let the value function \(V(t, x)\) be the least cost still to pay from state \(x\) at time \(t\), as \(V(0, x) = x^2/4\) for the cart. Where \(V\) is twice continuously differentiable, the costate is its gradient, \(\lambda(t) = \nabla_x V(t, x(t))\). Smoothness fails where two plans tie. With \(\dot x = u\), running cost \(\tfrac12 u^2\), and end cost \(-|x(T)|\), a cart at 0 does equally well pushed left or right, and \(V\) has a kink at 0. The costate is \(-1\) along the push to the right and \(+1\) along the push to the left, the slopes of \(V\) on the two sides.

12.4Derivation

(12.1). Write \(\lambda_k = \nabla_{x_k} L\), the gradient of the loss with respect to the state at step \(k\) with all later steps held as functions. The chain rule through \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k)\) gives \(\lambda_k = (\partial_x F_k)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\), and at the end \(\lambda_N = \nabla \ell\). The parameters enter every step, and their effect at step \(k\) passes through \(x_{k+1}\), so their gradient is the sum of \((\partial_\theta F_k)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\) over \(k\). Read as Lagrange multipliers (Appendix A.5), \(\lambda_{k+1}\) prices the constraint \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k)\): stationarity of the Lagrangian

\[ \mathcal L = \ell(x_N) - \sum_{k \lt N} \lambda_{k+1} \cdot \big(x_{k+1} - F_k(x_k)\big) \]

in each \(x_k\) is the same recursion. A middle state \(x_k\), one with \(k\) strictly between 0 and \(N\), appears twice, as the output of step \(k - 1\) and as the input of step \(k\), and the last state appears in \(\ell\) and as the output of step \(N - 1\). Setting the two kinds of derivative to zero gives

\[ -\lambda_k + (\partial_x F_k)^\top \lambda_{k+1} = 0, \qquad \nabla \ell(x_N) - \lambda_N = 0. \]

(12.2). Take Euler steps \(F_k(x) = x + h f(x, t_k)\) with \(t_k = k h\) and \(N h = T\). The Jacobian of a step is \(\partial_x F_k = I + h\, \partial_x f\), so the recursion of (12.1) reads

\[ \lambda_k = \lambda_{k+1} + h\, (\partial_x f)^\top \lambda_{k+1}. \]

Move \(\lambda_{k+1}\) to the left and divide by \(h\):

\[ \frac{\lambda_{k+1} - \lambda_k}{h} = -(\partial_x f)^\top \lambda_{k+1}. \]

The left side is the change in \(\lambda\) over one step divided by the step, so as \(h \to 0\) it becomes \(\dot\lambda = -(\partial_x f)^\top \lambda\), started from \(\lambda(T) = \nabla \ell\), the value of \(\lambda_N\). The parameters enter each step as \(\partial_\theta F_k = h\, \partial_\theta f\), so the sum in (12.1) is a Riemann sum:

\[ \sum_{k \lt N} h\, (\partial_\theta f)^\top \lambda_{k+1} \;\to\; \int_0^T (\partial_\theta f)^\top \lambda\; dt. \]

(12.3). The value function solves the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation \(-\partial_t V = \min_u \{c + \nabla V \cdot f\}\). Write \(u^*(t, x)\) for the minimizing control, so that \(-\partial_t V = c(x, u^*) + \nabla V \cdot f(x, u^*)\) at every \(x\). Differentiate both sides in \(x\). The control moves with \(x\), and that contributes

\[ (\partial_x u^*)^\top\, \partial_u \big(c + \nabla V \cdot f\big), \]

whose second factor is zero at an interior minimizer, which is the envelope theorem. The product rule on the rest gives

\[ -\partial_t \nabla V = \partial_x c + (\partial_x f)^\top \nabla V + \nabla^2 V\, f. \]

Along the trajectory,

\[ \frac{d}{dt} \nabla V(t, x(t)) = \partial_t \nabla V + \nabla^2 V\, f = -\partial_x c - (\partial_x f)^\top \nabla V = -\partial_x H, \]

with \(\nabla V(T, \cdot) = \nabla \ell\). So \(\nabla V\) along the path obeys the costate equation. This proof needs a smooth \(V\); the general principle is proved with needle variations of the control. ∎

Back to Chapter 3. In the control problem (3.3), \(V = -\log h\), so \(\nabla V = -\nabla \log h\) and the optimal control \(u^* = -\nabla V\) is the drift of the h-transform. Along a noisy path, \(\nabla V\) follows the costate equation in its drift plus a martingale term. Adjoint matching fine-tunes a diffusion model by regressing its control onto an adjoint computed backward along sampled trajectories, which is a pared-down (12.2), the lean adjoint, used as a training target. A fixed point \(x^* = F(x^*, \theta)\), as in deep equilibrium models (Chapter 4), has the adjoint \(\lambda = (I - \partial_x F)^{-\top} \nabla \ell\): one linear solve in place of a backward pass through the iterations, which is the implicit function theorem.

12.5Figures

Figure 12.2The pendulum's costate, run backward in time

Integrating the costate backward along a stored trajectory gives the gradient of a final loss with respect to the initial state, as λ(0), and with respect to a parameter, as the area under λᵀ∂f/∂c.

The pendulum is θ' = ω, ω' = −sin θ − cω, and the loss is the energy left at time T, L = ½ω(T)² + 1 − cos θ(T). The costate starts at λ(T) = ∇E(x(T)) and runs back along the stored path. At the defaults c = 0.3 and T = 8, L = 0.176968, the adjoint gives dL/dc = −1.246502 and λ(0) = (0.138295, 0.044966), and central finite differences agree to 6.6e−10 relative. Slide c to 0: energy is conserved, λ(0) equals ∇E(x(0)) = (sin 2, 0) = (0.909297, 0), and dL/dc = −10.0275 equals −∫ω² dt along the path. Slide T to 20 at c = 0.3: the pendulum has nearly stopped, L = 0.004114, and dL/dc shrinks to −0.080885. Press Run backward to watch the costate travel from x(T) back to x(0) and the area build up.

Figure 12.3The costate is the slope of the value function

Along an optimal path the costate, integrated backward from the end, equals ∂V/∂x from dynamic programming, so the adjoint and the Riccati equation compute the same slope from two ends.

The problem is ẋ = ax + u with cost ½∫₀³ (qx² + u²) dt + ½s·x(3)², from x(0) = 1. Dynamic programming integrates the Riccati equation −Ṗ = 2aP + q − P² back from P(3) = s, which gives V for every state. The adjoint integrates λ' = −(qx + aλ) back from λ(3) = s·x(3) along this one path. At the defaults a = 0.5, q = 1, and s = 0, the two agree to 2.6e−13, the cost J = 0.805455 equals V(0, x₀), and u*(0) = −λ(0) = −1.61091. In the slices, each tangent touches its slice at the path's point, and at t = 3 the slice is flat because s = 0. Slide s to 3: λ(3) = 0.0648, and the gap is 5.2e−13. Over the whole slider grid the largest gap is 3.6e−11.

12.6Four ways to see it

The adjoint is the chain rule run backward, a set of prices on constraints, a differential equation run in reverse time, and the momentum of optimal control.

  1. 1Backpropagationmachine learning

    A network is a chain of layers, and (12.1) is backpropagation: one backward sweep of vector-Jacobian products gives the gradient for every weight. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation applies the same sweep to any program.

  2. 1 → 2Treat each layer as a constraint \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k)\) with a multiplier \(\lambda_{k+1}\). Stationarity of the Lagrangian in \(x_k\) is the backward recursion, so the backpropagated gradient at a layer is the multiplier of that layer's equation, the rate at which the loss changes if the equation is relaxed.

  3. 2Shadow pricesoptimization and economics

    A Lagrange multiplier is the price of a constraint: how much the optimum improves per unit of slack. The costate prices the state at each step, which is why the same numbers appear as sensitivities in engineering design and as shadow prices in economics.

  4. 2 → 3Shrink the steps to an ODE. The recursion becomes \(\dot\lambda = -(\partial_x f)^\top \lambda\) run from \(T\) back to 0, and the gradient with respect to the parameters becomes an integral along the trajectory (12.2). Memory no longer grows with the number of steps if the state can be recomputed backward.

  5. 3The continuous adjointnumerical analysis

    Shape optimization of wings and the calibration of weather models solve one adjoint equation per loss instead of one forward solve per parameter, and neural ODEs train the same way (Figure 12.2).

  6. 3 → 4Let the parameters be a whole control signal \(u(t)\) and the loss the control objective. The gradient with respect to \(u(t)\) is \(\partial_u H\), so at an optimum \(\partial_u H = 0\), Pontryagin's principle strengthens this to \(u\) minimizing \(H\), and the costate equals the gradient of the value function (12.3).

  7. 4The costateoptimal control and mechanics

    Pontryagin's principle turns an optimal control problem into a two-point boundary problem for the state and the costate, with the costate playing the part of momentum in Hamiltonian mechanics. Dynamic programming computes \(\nabla V\) everywhere, and the adjoint computes it along one trajectory (Figure 12.3).

12.7Where it breaks and what is open

The costates are products of Jacobians, \(\lambda_0 = (\partial_x F_0)^\top (\partial_x F_1)^\top \cdots (\partial_x F_{N-1})^\top \lambda_N\), so their size grows or shrinks like \(e^{\Lambda N}\), with \(\Lambda\) the largest Lyapunov exponent of the dynamics. Through chaotic dynamics the gradient of a long-horizon loss explodes and stops describing how the expected loss changes, which is the trouble with differentiating through long rollouts and unrolled optimizers (Metz et al.; Figure 12.4). For contracting dynamics the same products vanish, so the loss stops depending on early states: the vanishing gradients of recurrent networks. Memory breaks next: the backward sweep needs the forward states, and recomputing them by running a dissipative ODE backward amplifies errors, so practical methods store checkpoints and recompute between them. And a step that samples a discrete token has no Jacobian, so the chain breaks there, and score-function estimators (Chapter 3) take over.

Figure 12.4Through chaos the gradient explodes

Through chaotic dynamics the adjoint of a long-horizon loss grows like exp(ΛN), with Λ the Lyapunov exponent, so the exact derivative soon says nothing about how the loss changes over any step one could take.

The loss is x_N for the logistic map xₖ₊₁ = r xₖ(1 − xₖ) from x₀ = 0.3, and one backward sweep gives dx_N/dr exactly. At the default r = 3.9 the Lyapunov exponent along 60 steps is Λ = 0.448 (0.496 over a million steps), and ln|dx_N/dr| grows at 0.459 per step. At N = 50 the adjoint gives −3.675e10 and a difference quotient with step 10⁻⁸ gives −2.120e6. Within that step x₅₀ swings from 0.776 below its value to 0.104 above it, and no difference quotient can exceed 1/(2·10⁻⁸) = 5e7, a size the gradient passes at N = 36. Slide r to 3.2: Λ = −0.659, the orbit is periodic, and both give 0.2815. At r = 2.8 the gradient settles at 1/r² = 0.1276, the derivative of the fixed point 1 − 1/r. The first r on the slider where the two differ by more than 1% at N = 50 is 3.67, and above it they agree only in periodic windows such as r = 3.84.

  1. Adjoints for value-function samplers. A sampler trained with a learned value function as its energy has terminal cost \(-Q\), so the adjoint starts from \(\lambda(T) = -\nabla_a Q\), a learned and noisy gradient. How errors in \(\nabla Q\) propagate through the backward adjoint to the learned control, and whether the costate's own dynamics damp or amplify them, is open.
  2. Gradients through long rollouts. World models, differentiable simulators, and backpropagation through time all face exploding or vanishing costates at long horizons. Which remedy (shorter windows, multiple shooting, smoothing the dynamics with noise) gives gradients that still point downhill on the expected loss is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 12.1Backpropagation for two layers

    For \(L = \tfrac12 |W_2\, \sigma(W_1 x) - y|^2\) with \(\sigma\) applied entrywise, derive \(\nabla_{W_2} L\) and \(\nabla_{W_1} L\) from (12.1), naming each costate.

    Solution

    The steps are \(a = W_1 x\), \(z = \sigma(a)\), \(\hat y = W_2 z\). The costates run backward: \(\lambda_{\hat y} = \hat y - y\), then \(\lambda_z = W_2^\top \lambda_{\hat y}\), then \(\lambda_a = \sigma'(a) \odot \lambda_z\).

    Each weight enters one step, so \(\nabla_{W_2} L = \lambda_{\hat y}\, z^\top\) and \(\nabla_{W_1} L = \lambda_a\, x^\top\).

  2. Derivation 12.2The costate of a linear-quadratic problem

    For \(\dot x = u\) with cost \(\tfrac12 \int_0^T u^2\, dt + \tfrac s2\, x(T)^2\), solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation with \(V = \tfrac12 P(t)\, x^2\), find the optimal control, and check that \(\lambda = P x\) satisfies (12.3).

    Solution

    \(H = \tfrac12 u^2 + \lambda u\) is minimized at \(u = -\lambda\). The HJB equation \(-\partial_t V = \min_u \{\tfrac12 u^2 + V_x u\} = -\tfrac12 V_x^2\) gives \(\dot P = P^2\) with \(P(T) = s\), so \(P(t) = s/(1 + s(T - t))\) and \(u^* = -P(t)\, x(t)\).

    Along the optimal path, \(\frac{d}{dt}(P x) = P^2 x + P(-P x) = 0 = -\partial_x H\), since \(H\) does not depend on \(x\), and \(P(T)x(T) = s\, x(T) = \nabla \ell\).

In a chaotic simulator such as the Lorenz system, fit the initial condition to a target trajectory by gradient descent, comparing the full adjoint gradient, adjoints truncated to windows of one, two, and five Lyapunov times, and a smoothed finite-difference estimate.
