Project. Fit EDMD to a damped pendulum and a double pendulum with polynomial dictionaries of growing degree and with a learned encoder trained on multi-step linear prediction. Report the horizon at which prediction error passes 10% of the state's range, and compare it, for the double pendulum, with the horizon its largest Lyapunov exponent predicts.

Chapter 16

Martingales

Probability, from gambling

A martingale is a process whose next value, given everything seen so far, is expected to equal its current value: a fair game. No rule for when to stop playing a fair game makes it favorable, and that one fact prices gambler's ruin, bounds sequential tests at any stopping time, and explains why likelihood ratios, posterior means, and fair prices all behave alike.

Uses Chapters 3, 9, 10, and 13 and Appendices A.1 and A.6.

16.1Motivation

Suppose you walk into a casino with 3 dollars and play a fair game: each round you win or lose 1 dollar with equal probability. You plan to leave when you reach 10 dollars or go broke. What is the chance that you leave with 10? And could a cleverer rule for when to leave, or how much to stake, give you an edge? Gamblers have looked for such a rule for centuries. In eighteenth-century France a martingale was a betting system: double the stake after every loss, so that the first win recovers every loss plus one unit.

The same question comes up far from a casino. Suppose you compare two language models on a stream of prompts, and a judge says which answer is better each time. You would like to stop as soon as one model is clearly ahead. The usual test declares a winner when the first model's wins after \(n\) prompts sit more than 1.96 standard deviations from \(n/2\). Run once, after 500 prompts, it declares a winner between two equally good models in 5.4% of streams. Suppose instead you run it after every prompt from the tenth on and stop the first time it fires. How often do you now declare a winner between equal models? In 42% of streams by the five-hundredth prompt, more than eight times what the test is meant to allow. Stopping when the data look good is the gambler's rule for when to leave, played with evidence in place of dollars, so whatever answers the gambler also says how to watch data safely. A likelihood ratio, a posterior mean, and a fair price turn out to be fortunes in fair games too (Section 16.6). Ville (1939) brought the word into probability theory, and Doob (1953) built the theory around it.

ESSAYA document that moved capital

The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville

When the market's winners keep coming from one small village of investors, luck stops being the best explanation.

Warren E. Buffett, 1984 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

It answered the claim that prices already reflect everything known with a test: a group of investors whose records it reported had been chosen, by their shared training, before the results were in.

The link to this chapter: the essay imagines 225 million people each staking a dollar on a coin and letting the winnings ride. Each fortune is a nonnegative martingale with mean one dollar, so a flipper named in advance reaches \(2^{20}\) dollars with probability exactly \(2^{-20}\), Ville's inequality (16.3) holding with equality, and about \(225 \times 10^6 \cdot 2^{-20} \approx 215\) millionaires appear by chance. Buffett's defense, that he named his winners years before their results, is the condition under which (16.5) is a valid test: the bettor is fixed before the data arrive.

16.2Intuition

Start with the casino. Write \(M_t\) for your fortune after \(t\) rounds, so \(M_0 = 3\). Whatever happened before, the next round adds \(+1\) or \(-1\) with equal probability, so the expected fortune after the next round, given the whole history, is the fortune now:

\[ \mathbb E[M_{t+1} \mid M_0, \dots, M_t] = \tfrac12 (M_t + 1) + \tfrac12 (M_t - 1) = M_t. \]

Taking expectations, \(\mathbb E M_t = 3\) after any fixed number of rounds. Now suppose this stays true at the moment \(\tau\) you leave, even though \(\tau\) depends on how the game went. You leave with 10 or with 0, so

\[ 3 = \mathbb E M_\tau = 10\, P(\text{reach } 10) + 0 \cdot P(\text{go broke}), \qquad P(\text{reach } 10) = 0.3. \]

No sum over paths was needed, and the answer, 0.3, is the starting fortune divided by the target. Check it against the extremes: starting at 0 you never reach 10, and starting at 10 you are already there. A slower route agrees. The chance \(h(x)\) of reaching 10 from \(x\) is the average of the chances from the two neighbors, \(h(x) = \tfrac12 h(x - 1) + \tfrac12 h(x + 1)\), so \(h\) is a straight line from \(h(0) = 0\) to \(h(10) = 1\), and \(h(3) = 0.3\). The argument used two facts: the next round is fair given the past, and your decision to leave at time \(t\) looks only at what has happened by time \(t\). Could a cleverer rule for leaving, one that waits for a lucky streak, beat the mean of 3? Try the smallest such rule: leave the moment you are ahead, and in any case after two rounds. With probability \(\tfrac12\) you win the first round and leave with 4. Otherwise you are at 2, and the second round leaves you with 3 or with 1, each with probability \(\tfrac14\):

\[ \mathbb E M_\tau = \tfrac12 \cdot 4 + \tfrac14 \cdot 3 + \tfrac14 \cdot 1 = 3. \]

The rule doubles your chance of leaving ahead, from \(\tfrac14\) when you play both rounds regardless to \(\tfrac12\), and pays for it with a smaller win, 1 dollar instead of 2, while the chance of losing 2 dollars stays at \(\tfrac14\), so the mean stays at 3. A rule that sees the future does break it. Play the first round only when it is going to be a win, and you leave with 4 or with 3, each with probability \(\tfrac12\), a mean of 3.5. That is why the decision to leave may use only the past. The mean can also escape when you may wait forever or borrow without limit, which is how the doubling system of Section 16.7 seems to win.

A fair game stays fair at any quitting time chosen from the past alone, as long as you cannot wait forever or borrow without limit.

Figure 16.1A fair walk stopped by any rule ends, on average, where it began

A fair ±1 walk started at x₀ and stopped at 0 or N ends, on average, exactly where it began, whatever the barriers, so it reaches N with probability x₀/N.

Every game ends at ruin 0 or at N, and the other two rules also quit sooner. Each rule decides from the path so far, so each is a stopping time, and each stopped walk is bounded. At the defaults x₀ = 3 and N = 10, the 400 paths stop at a mean of 2.975 (standard error 0.229) against x₀ = 3, and 29.7% of them reach N against x₀/N = 0.3. They stop after 21.77 steps on average against x₀(N − x₀) = 21. The thick line averages all 400 paths at each time and stays within 0.23 of x₀ the whole way. Switch to 2 ahead, or t = 50: the exact chance of quitting ahead rises to 0.600, ruin takes the other 0.400 at a loss of 3 each, and the exact mean is still 3. Switch to t = 20: ruin takes an exact 0.503, and the survivors spread up to N. Over all 570 settings of the sliders and rules, the exact mean of the stopped value equals x₀ to 7e−14.

16.3Statement

The casino computation needs three things made precise: what "fair given the past" means, which rules for stopping are allowed, and when the expected fortune at the stopping time still equals the start. The definition names the first two, and optional stopping settles the third.

Definition 16.1 (martingales and stopping times)

Let \(\mathcal F_t\) be the information available at time \(t\), such as the history of a game up to round \(t\). A sequence \(M_t\) with \(\mathbb E |M_t| \lt \infty\), each \(M_t\) known at time \(t\), is a martingale if

\[ \mathbb E[M_{t+1} \mid \mathcal F_t] = M_t, \tag{16.1} \]

a supermartingale if \(\le\) holds (a game that favors the house) and a submartingale if \(\ge\) holds. A random time \(\tau\) is a stopping time if whether \(\tau = t\) is decided by \(\mathcal F_t\) alone.

Theorem 16.2 (optional stopping)

If \(M\) is a martingale and \(\tau\) a stopping time, then

\[ \mathbb E M_\tau = \mathbb E M_0 \tag{16.2} \]

whenever (a) \(\tau \le N\) for a fixed \(N\), or (b) \(\tau \lt \infty\) almost surely and \(|M_{t \wedge \tau}| \le K\) for all \(t\), or (c) \(\mathbb E \tau \lt \infty\) and \(|M_{t+1} - M_t| \le K\). For a supermartingale, \(\mathbb E M_\tau \le \mathbb E M_0\) under the same conditions.

Each condition closes one way out. Start with 3 dollars and leave only when broke. The fair walk reaches 0 with probability one, so \(M_\tau = 0\) and \(\mathbb E M_\tau = 0\), less than the 3 you started with. No fixed \(N\) bounds this \(\tau\), so (a) fails. The fortune before ruin can climb without limit, so (b) fails. And the expected wait for ruin is infinite, so (c) fails. The doubling system of Section 16.7 breaks them too, with stakes that grow without limit.

The casino is case (b): you leave with probability one, and the fortune stays between 0 and 10 until you do. The same reasoning gives the chance of reaching \(N\) from \(x_0\) as \(x_0/N\), and the martingale \(M_t^2 - t\) gives the expected length of the visit, \(x_0(N - x_0)\) rounds, 21 for the casino (Derivation 16.1).

The next result asks how likely a fortune that may never go negative is to ever grow large. The casino answers one case exactly: start with 1 dollar and leave at 0 or 20, and you reach 20 with probability \(1/20\). Ville's inequality says that no fair or unfavorable game without borrowing, stopped by any rule, does better. Each hypothesis matters. A walk that may go negative reaches 20 eventually with probability one. And the fair walk never settles down, since every round moves it by 1, and its \(\mathbb E M_t^2 = M_0^2 + t\) grows without bound, which is why the convergence statement asks for \(\sup_t \mathbb E M_t^2 \lt \infty\).

Theorem 16.3 (Ville's inequality, and convergence)

If \(M \ge 0\) is a supermartingale with \(M_0 = 1\), then for every \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\)

\[ P\Big(\sup_{t} M_t \ge \tfrac1\alpha\Big) \le \alpha. \tag{16.3} \]

A martingale with \(\sup_t \mathbb E M_t^2 \lt \infty\) converges almost surely and in mean square to a limit \(M_\infty\), and every nonnegative supermartingale converges almost surely.

Ville's inequality bounds the chance of ever reaching a level. A different question is how far a martingale with bounded steps can stray in a fixed number of rounds. Play the fair game of Section 16.1 for 100 rounds with no barriers. A fortune 30 or more dollars above the start has probability 0.0018, and the next bound gives \(e^{-4.5} = 0.011\) from the step sizes alone.

Theorem 16.4 (Azuma-Hoeffding)

If \(M\) is a martingale with \(|M_t - M_{t-1}| \le c_t\), then for \(s \gt 0\)

\[ P(M_n - M_0 \ge s) \le \exp\Big(-\frac{s^2}{2 \sum_{t \le n} c_t^2}\Big). \tag{16.4} \]

The last statement turns a fortune into evidence. Suppose a bettor watches draws \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) and, before each one, stakes their wealth on the claim that the draws come from a density \(q\) instead of the density \(p\) of a null hypothesis, at odds that are fair if \(p\) is true.

Proposition 16.5 (likelihood ratios, and testing by betting)

Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be independent with density \(p\), and let \(q_t\) be any density chosen from \(X_1, \dots, X_{t-1}\). Then \(L_t = \prod_{i \le t} q_i(X_i)/p(X_i)\) is a nonnegative martingale with \(L_0 = 1\), so rejecting \(p\) the first time

\[ L_t \ge 1/\alpha \tag{16.5} \]

has probability at most \(\alpha\) when \(p\) is true, at whatever time the data lead you to stop. If the draws come from \(q\) and \(q_t = q\), then \(\frac1t \log L_t \to \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)\), the growth rate of a Kelly bettor in Chapter 10.

Back to the two models of Section 16.1. Count a prompt as heads when the first model wins, and bet on \(q = 0.6\) against the null \(p = 0.5\), so the wealth is multiplied by \(0.6/0.5 = 1.2\) after a win and by \(0.4/0.5 = 0.8\) after a loss. When the models are equally good, the wealth reaches \(1/\alpha = 20\) within 500 prompts in 4.5% of streams, under the promised 5%, although it is checked after every prompt. The test checked after every prompt from the tenth on fired in 42%. When the first model wins 60% of the time, the wealth reaches 20 within 500 prompts in 97.8% of streams. Its logarithm grows on average by \(\mathrm{KL}(0.6 \,\|\, 0.5) = 0.0201\) nats per prompt, so the expected log wealth reaches \(\log 20\) after 149 prompts.

16.4Derivation

(16.2). Start with a bounded stopping time, \(\tau \le N\). The stopped fortune is the starting fortune plus the increments of the rounds actually played:

\[ M_\tau = M_0 + \sum_{t \lt N} \mathbf 1\{\tau \gt t\}\, (M_{t+1} - M_t). \]

Whether \(\tau \gt t\) is known at time \(t\), so it can be pulled out of the conditional expectation:

\[ \mathbb E\big[\mathbf 1\{\tau \gt t\} (M_{t+1} - M_t)\big] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbf 1\{\tau \gt t\}\, \mathbb E[M_{t+1} - M_t \mid \mathcal F_t]\big] = 0. \]

Every term has mean zero, which is (16.2) in case (a). For (b) and (c), apply (a) to the bounded time \(\tau \wedge N\) and let \(N \to \infty\). In case (b) the stopped values are bounded by \(K\), and in case (c) they are bounded by \(|M_0| + K\tau\), which has finite mean, so dominated convergence carries \(\mathbb E M_{\tau \wedge N} = \mathbb E M_0\) to the limit. For a supermartingale each term has mean at most zero.

(16.3). Let \(\sigma\) be the first time \(M_t \ge 1/\alpha\). For a fixed \(N\), \(\sigma \wedge N\) is a bounded stopping time, so (16.2) for supermartingales gives \(\mathbb E M_{\sigma \wedge N} \le 1\). On the event \(\sigma \le N\) the stopped value is at least \(1/\alpha\), and elsewhere it is at least 0, so \(\tfrac1\alpha P(\sigma \le N) \le 1\). Letting \(N \to \infty\) gives \(P(M_t \ge 1/\alpha \text{ for some } t) \le \alpha\). Applying this at every level \(c \lt 1/\alpha\) and letting \(c\) rise to \(1/\alpha\) covers a supremum that is never attained and gives (16.3). The argument is Markov's inequality applied at the stopping time \(\sigma \wedge N\). For the mean-square convergence, write \(D_t = M_t - M_{t-1}\). For \(s \lt t\), \(D_s\) is known at time \(t - 1\), so it comes out of the inner expectation:

\[ \mathbb E[D_s D_t] = \mathbb E\big[D_s\, \mathbb E[D_t \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}]\big] = 0, \]

and the same holds with \(M_0\) in place of \(D_s\). Expanding the square of \(M_n = M_0 + \sum_{t \le n} D_t\), every cross term has mean zero:

\[ \mathbb E M_n^2 = \mathbb E M_0^2 + \sum_{t \le n} \mathbb E D_t^2. \]

A bounded left side makes the sum on the right finite. For \(m \lt n\) the same expansion gives

\[ \mathbb E (M_n - M_m)^2 = \sum_{m \lt t \le n} \mathbb E D_t^2, \]

a tail of a convergent sum, which goes to zero as \(m\) grows. So \(M_n\) is a Cauchy sequence in mean square, and it converges in mean square to a limit \(M_\infty\). The almost-sure statements rest on Doob's upcrossing inequality, which bounds how often a supermartingale can cross a band, and are used here without proof.

(16.4). Write \(D_t = M_t - M_{t-1}\). Given \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), \(D_t\) has mean zero and lies in \([-c_t, c_t]\), so Hoeffding's lemma (Appendix A.6) gives \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda D_t} \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}] \le e^{\lambda^2 c_t^2/2}\). Peel off the last increment. \(M_{n-1}\) is known at time \(n - 1\), so it comes out of the inner expectation, and the lemma bounds what is left:

\[ \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda (M_n - M_0)} = \mathbb E\Big[e^{\lambda (M_{n-1} - M_0)}\, \mathbb E[e^{\lambda D_n} \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}]\Big] \le e^{\lambda^2 c_n^2/2}\; \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda (M_{n-1} - M_0)}. \]

Repeating this for \(D_{n-1}, \dots, D_1\) gives \(\mathbb E\, e^{\lambda (M_n - M_0)} \le e^{\lambda^2 C/2}\), with \(C = \sum_{t \le n} c_t^2\). For any \(\lambda \gt 0\), Markov's inequality applied to \(e^{\lambda (M_n - M_0)}\) then gives

\[ P(M_n - M_0 \ge s) = P\big(e^{\lambda (M_n - M_0)} \ge e^{\lambda s}\big) \le e^{-\lambda s}\, \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda (M_n - M_0)} \le e^{-\lambda s + \lambda^2 C/2}. \]

The exponent is a parabola in \(\lambda\), smallest at \(\lambda = s/C\), where it equals \(-s^2/C + s^2/(2C) = -s^2/(2C)\), which is (16.4). With each step confined to an interval of length \(c_t\) known at time \(t - 1\), the same proof gives \(\exp(-2s^2/\sum_t c_t^2)\), and Hoeffding's inequality (13.2) of Chapter 13 is that bound for independent steps.

(16.5). Given the past, \(q_{t+1}\) is fixed, and under \(p\)

\[ \mathbb E\Big[\frac{q_{t+1}(X_{t+1})}{p(X_{t+1})} \,\Big|\, \mathcal F_t\Big] = \int \frac{q_{t+1}(x)}{p(x)}\, p(x)\, dx = \int q_{t+1}(x)\, dx = 1, \]

so \(\mathbb E[L_{t+1} \mid \mathcal F_t] = L_t\). Ville's inequality (16.3) bounds the chance of ever reaching \(1/\alpha\). Under \(q\), \(\log L_t\) is a sum of \(t\) independent copies of \(\log(q(X)/p(X))\), whose mean is \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)\), and the law of large numbers gives the growth rate. ∎

Martingales already in this book. Girsanov's density \(Z_t\) in Chapter 3 is a nonnegative martingale with mean one, and so is \(h(t, X_t)/h(0, x_0)\) for the base process of the h-transform, which is why reweighting by it keeps the total probability at one. An Itô integral \(\int \sigma\, dW\) is a martingale, so Itô's lemma (Appendix A.1) splits any \(f(X_t)\) into a drift and a martingale. The gambler's-ruin exercise of Chapter 9 used the potential \((q/p)^x\), a martingale for the biased walk, and the Kelly bettor's wealth in Chapter 10 is a likelihood ratio. In a Markov decision process the value of the current state plus the rewards collected so far is a martingale under the policy (in the undiscounted case), and the temporal-difference errors are its increments, which Chapter 17 builds on.

16.5Figures

Figure 16.2Testing a coin by betting against it

Wealth from betting a fixed fraction against the null "the coin is fair" is a martingale under the null, so it reaches 1/α with probability at most α, and under a biased coin its logarithm grows at up to KL(p‖½) bits per flip, the Kelly rate.

Each flip multiplies wealth by 1 + λ on heads and 1 − λ on tails, and the bettor rejects the fair coin the first time wealth reaches 1/α = 20. At the defaults p = 0.5 and λ = 0.2 the wealth is a martingale. Dynamic programming over the number of heads gives the exact chance of reaching 20 within 500 flips, 0.0450, under Ville's bound of 0.05, and 0.0490 of the 2000 seeded bettors get there (standard error 0.0046). Over every λ on the slider the exact chance peaks at 0.0453. Log wealth falls by 0.0294 bits per flip, because the mean of ln(1 + λ(2X − 1)) is negative on a fair coin. Slide p to 0.6: at Kelly's λ = 2p − 1 = 0.2 log wealth grows by 0.0290 bits per flip, which is KL(0.6‖0.5), the rate from Chapter 10. An exact 0.9778 of bettors then reach 20, and the exact median first crossing comes at flip 117. Slide λ to 0.4, twice Kelly's fraction: the growth turns negative at −0.0035 bits per flip.

Figure 16.3The Pólya urn settles on a random limit

In a Pólya urn the fraction of red balls is a martingale, so its average never moves, yet each run settles on its own random limit, and the limits are uniform when the urn starts with one ball of each color.

Each draw takes a ball at random, puts it back, and adds one more of its color. At the defaults a = b = 1 and t = 59, the 200 runs average 0.4995 against a/(a + b) = 0.5, and over all 300 draws their mean never strays more than 0.0073 from 1/2. Their spread is 0.2885 against the exact 0.2839, near the uniform limit's 0.2887. With one ball of each color the exact law is already uniform, 0.0500 in each bin, yet 0.275 of the runs still move by more than 0.05 before draw 300, against an exact 0.266. Slide t to 0: every run sits at 1/2, and 0.890 of them will move, against an exact 0.897. Press Play 300 draws to watch the histogram spread from the spike at 1/2. Set a = b = 5: the limits gather near 1/2 with a limiting spread of 0.1508. Set a = 2 and b = 1: they lean red, with mean 2/3.

16.6Four ways to see it

A martingale is a fair game, a sequence of best guesses, a bettor's wealth against a hypothesis, and a fair price.

  1. 1Fair gamesgambling

    A fortune in a fair game is a martingale, and optional stopping says no rule for when to quit changes its expected value (Figure 16.1). Gambler's ruin, the expected waiting time for a pattern of coin flips, and the value of a stopping problem all follow from choosing the right martingale.

  2. 1 → 2Take any random quantity \(X\) with finite mean and let \(M_t = \mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal F_t]\), the best guess of \(X\) given what is known at time \(t\). The tower property gives \(\mathbb E[M_{t+1} \mid \mathcal F_t] = \mathbb E[\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal F_{t+1}] \mid \mathcal F_t] = M_t\), so a sequence of best guesses is a fair game.

  3. 2Best guessesBayesian statistics

    A posterior mean is a martingale under the prior's predictive distribution, and Lévy's theorem says it converges to the best guess given all the data. A Pólya urn shows the mechanism. It starts with one red ball and one blue. Draw a ball, return it with one more of the same color, and repeat. After the first draw the fraction of red is \(2/3\) or \(1/3\) with equal probability, so its mean is still \(1/2\). The fraction is a martingale whose average never moves, and since it stays in \([0, 1]\), Theorem 16.3 says it converges. Each run settles on its own random limit, uniform on \([0, 1]\) for this start (Figure 16.3).

  4. 2 → 3Let \(X\) be the density \(dQ/dP\) of Chapter 3 on the first \(T\) observations. Its best guess given the first \(t \le T\) is \(\mathbb E_P[dQ/dP \mid \mathcal F_t]\), the likelihood ratio of those \(t\) observations. On an infinite stream of independent draws \(Q\) and \(P\) are mutually singular, so no single density closes this martingale: under \(P\) it goes to 0 while its mean stays 1 (Section 16.7). A bettor whose wealth equals it is playing a fair game under \(P\).

  5. 3Testing by bettingsequential statistics

    Wald's sequential probability ratio test stops when a likelihood ratio, a bettor's wealth against the null, leaves a band. An e-value is such a wealth read at any stopping time, a nonnegative number whose mean under the null is at most 1. An anytime-valid confidence sequence keeps every parameter value whose own bettor has not yet reached \(1/\alpha\). All three reject a hypothesis when a bettor's wealth against it passes \(1/\alpha\), and Ville's inequality holds the error at \(\alpha\) however long the data are watched (Figure 16.2). The wealth grows at the Kelly rate of Chapter 10 when the bet matches the true alternative, and a bet that is too large can still cross \(1/\alpha\) while its log wealth falls on average.

  6. 1 → 4Take a stock at 100 dollars that will be worth 120 or 90 tomorrow, with no interest. An option that pays the excess over 100 pays 20 or 0. Holding \(2/3\) of a share while borrowing 60 dollars pays the same, \(\tfrac23 \cdot 120 - 60 = 20\) or \(\tfrac23 \cdot 90 - 60 = 0\), and costs \(\tfrac23 \cdot 100 - 60 = 6.67\) today, so any other price for the option hands someone a sure profit. Pretending the stock is a fair game gives the same number. The probability \(q\) with \(120 q + 90(1 - q) = 100\) is \(q = 1/3\), and the option's mean payoff under it is \(20/3 = 6.67\), whatever the real chance of a rise. In general, if prices discounted at the risk-free rate are martingales under a measure equivalent to the real one, the risk-neutral measure of Chapter 3, no trade earns a sure profit, since every self-financing gain is then a martingale with mean zero. The fundamental theorem of asset pricing (Harrison and Kreps 1979, Harrison and Pliska 1981) gives the converse: with finitely many assets and trading dates (Dalang, Morton, and Willinger 1990 for a general probability space), no arbitrage implies that such a measure exists, and continuous time needs a slightly stronger condition, no free lunch with vanishing risk.

  7. 4Fair pricesfinance

    The price of a derivative is the risk-neutral expectation of its discounted payoff, the Black-Scholes card of Chapter 1 is this martingale computed in closed form, and Samuelson's proof that properly anticipated prices fluctuate randomly (1965) is the statement that a futures price is the best guess of the spot price at delivery, so it is a martingale.

16.7Where it breaks and what is open

Optional stopping can fail, and how it fails shows what its conditions protect. Double the stake after every loss, starting at 1 dollar, and stop at the first win. When the win comes, the fortune is up exactly 1 dollar, and with a fair coin it comes eventually, so \(\mathbb E M_\tau = 1\) while \(M_0 = 0\). The stopped fortune is unbounded below and the stakes grow without limit, so none of the conditions of Theorem 16.2 holds. With a bankroll of \(2^k - 1\) dollars the strategy wins 1 dollar with probability \(1 - 2^{-k}\) and loses \(2^k - 1\) dollars with probability \(2^{-k}\), and the mean is exactly zero (Figure 16.4). The same mechanism hides in a product of independent, identically distributed mean-one factors that are not always 1, such as an importance weight built one step at a time. Its mean is 1 at every \(t\), but its logarithm is a sum of terms with negative mean by Jensen's inequality, so almost every path goes to zero while the mean is carried by rarer and rarer large paths. Take factors of 0.5 or 1.5 with equal probability, so each has mean 1 and the mean of its logarithm is \(\tfrac12 \log 0.75 = -0.144\). After 100 steps the mean of the product is still 1, yet a path with 50 of each factor ends at \(0.75^{50} = 5.7 \times 10^{-7}\), 95.6% of paths end below 0.01, and the 0.33% that end above 1 carry 99.5% of the mean. Almost-sure convergence does not carry expectations with it, which is why importance weights over long paths degenerate (Chapter 3).

Figure 16.4Where optional stopping fails: doubling and mean-one products

Doubling after every loss wins 1 almost surely only with an infinite bankroll: with a bankroll of 2ᵏ − 1 it wins 1 with probability 1 − 2⁻ᵏ and loses 2ᵏ − 1 with probability 2⁻ᵏ, so the mean is exactly 0.

Doubling bets 1, doubles after each loss, and stops at the first win, and a bankroll of 2ᵏ − 1 covers k bets. At the default k = 6, the 2000 runs win at bets 1 to 6 in 967, 510, 249, 146, 70, and 33 runs, and 25 lose all 63, against 31.25 expected. The exact chance of winning is 0.984375, and the exact shares of the mean, +0.9844 from wins and −0.9844 from ruin, cancel to 0. The runs give 0.200 (standard error 0.177). Slide k to 12: the chance of winning reaches 0.999756, one run in 2000 loses 4095, and the measured mean swings to −1.048. Here τ ≤ k, so optional stopping holds. With no limit the bets grow without bound and the stopped process has no floor, so both conditions fail, and E M_τ = 1 although the expected number of bets stays below 2 (1.9995 at k = 12). Switch to mean-one products, M_t = Z₁⋯Z_t with Z = e^(σε − σ²/2) and E Z = 1. At σ = 0.5, E ln Z = −0.125, and by t = 200 the median is 1.39e−11 and 0.9980 of paths lie below 0.01 (0.9965 of the 2000). The sample mean first dips below 0.5 at t = 72. One path then lifts it to 7.93 at t = 140, carrying 99.95% of it, and from t = 171 on it stays below 0.5, ending at 0.0141 against E M_t = 1. Slide σ to 0.2: the sample mean ends at 1.52, though at its peak of 2.51 one path carries 67% of it. At σ = 1 it drops below 0.5 for good at t = 18.

  1. Whether in-context predictions are martingales. A Bayesian predictor's predictive distributions form a martingale: before the next example arrives, the expected prediction after it equals the current prediction. Language models that learn in context can violate this (Falck et al.), and whether a model trained only to predict can be made consistent in this sense, and what the violations cost its uncertainty estimates, is open.
  2. Anytime-valid evaluation. Comparing two models on a stream of prompts with a betting test lets an evaluation stop as soon as the evidence suffices, with error at most \(\alpha\) by (16.5). Choosing bets with good power against a composite alternative, and keeping the guarantee when prompts are correlated (Chapter 13), are open in practice.
  3. Martingale noise in reinforcement learning. Temporal-difference learning and Q-learning converge because their noise is a sequence of martingale differences, the setting of stochastic approximation. Rates with nonlinear function approximation and off-policy data, where the iteration can diverge, are open.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 16.1 Martingales

    • A fair walk starts at 4 and steps up or down by 1 with equal chance until it first hits 0 or 12.
    • By optional stopping (16.2) alone: what is the chance it reaches 12, the expected number of steps, and the expected number of steps given that it reaches 12? The last one needs a cubic martingale.
    Answer
    reach_12(4)          # 0.333333
mean_steps(4)        # 32.0
steps_given_win(4)   # 42.666667

  2. Exercise 16.2 A betting test for a coin

    • To test a coin for fairness, a bettor starts with 1 dollar and before each flip stakes 20% of it on heads at even odds: wealth multiplies by 1.2 on heads and by 0.8 on tails. The coin is called unfair as soon as wealth reaches 20 (α = 0.05), watching every flip for up to 300 flips.
    • Exactly, by dynamic programming over the number of heads: how often is a fair coin called unfair, and how often is a coin with P(heads) = 0.6?
    Answer
    rejection(0.5)   # 0.041446
rejection(0.6)   # 0.899519

  3. Exercise 16.3 A Pólya urn

    • An urn holds 2 red balls and 1 blue. Draw a ball, put it back together with one more of its color, and repeat.
    • After 10 draws, what is the expected fraction of red, and the chance that red holds the majority? What does that chance tend to as the draws go on?
    Answer
    mean_red_fraction(10)   # 0.666667
red_majority(10)        # 0.772727
red_majority_limit()    # 0.75

  4. Exercise 16.4 Azuma for balls in bins

    • Throw 100 balls into 100 bins, each ball into a uniformly random bin, and let Z be the number of empty bins.
    • What is E Z? Reveal the balls one at a time: E[Z | first t balls] is a martingale whose steps lie in an interval of length 1. What do Azuma (16.4) and McDiarmid's inequality give for P(Z − E Z ≥ 6), and what is the exact chance?
    Answer
    expected_empty(100, 100)   # 36.603234
bounds(100, 6)             # (0.83527, 0.486752)
exact_tail(100, 100, 6)    # 0.029218

  5. Exercise 16.5 Expected time to ABRACADABRA

    • A monkey types capital letters, each uniform over 26, one per second. A sequencer reads DNA letters with P(A) = P(T) = 0.3 and P(C) = P(G) = 0.2.
    • Before each letter a gambler arrives with 1 dollar and bets it all, at fair odds, that the next letters spell the word, letter by letter. How long until ABRACADABRA appears, on average, and how long until ATATA?
    Answer
    wait_for("ABRACADABRA", letters)   # 3670344487444778
wait_for("ATATA", dna)             # 451.893004

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 16.1Gambler's ruin with a bias

    A walk steps \(+1\) with probability \(p = 0.4\) and \(-1\) with probability \(q = 0.6\), starts at 5, and stops at 0 or 10. Show that \((q/p)^{X_t}\) and \(X_t - (p - q)t\) are martingales, and use optional stopping to find the probability of reaching 10 and the expected number of steps. Then show that for the fair walk \(X_t^2 - t\) is a martingale and the expected time is \(x_0(N - x_0)\).

    Solution
    \[ \mathbb E[(q/p)^{X_t + \xi}] = (q/p)^{X_t}\big(p \cdot \tfrac qp + q \cdot \tfrac pq\big) = (q/p)^{X_t}, \]

    and \(\mathbb E[X_{t+1} - X_t] = p - q\). Both stopped processes are bounded or have bounded steps with \(\mathbb E \tau \lt \infty\), so with \(r = q/p = 1.5\) optional stopping gives

    \[ r^5 = P_{10}\, r^{10} + (1 - P_{10})\, r^0, \qquad P_{10} = \frac{r^5 - 1}{r^{10} - 1} = \frac{6.594}{56.67} = 0.1164. \]

    The second martingale gives \(\mathbb E X_\tau - 5 = (p - q)\, \mathbb E \tau\), so \(\mathbb E \tau = (10 \cdot 0.1164 - 5)/(-0.2) = 19.18\) steps. For the fair walk, \(\mathbb E[X_{t+1}^2 \mid X_t] = X_t^2 + 1\), so \(X_t^2 - t\) is a martingale, and with \(P_N = x_0/N\), \(\mathbb E \tau = \mathbb E X_\tau^2 - x_0^2 = N x_0 - x_0^2\).

  2. Derivation 16.2Waiting for HTH and for HHT

    Flip a fair coin until the pattern HTH appears. Before each flip a new gambler arrives with 1 dollar and bets everything, at fair odds, that the next flips spell the pattern, letter by letter, leaving when a letter fails. Show that the casino's profit is a martingale, and use optional stopping to find the expected waiting time for HTH and for HHT.

    Solution

    Each bet is fair, so the casino's profit after \(t\) flips, \(t\) dollars taken in minus the gamblers' holdings, is a martingale with mean zero, and its steps are bounded by 8 with \(\mathbb E \tau \lt \infty\). When HTH first appears, the gambler who arrived three flips earlier holds \(2^3 = 8\) dollars, the one who arrived at the last H holds \(2^1 = 2\), and every other gambler has lost. Optional stopping gives \(\mathbb E \tau = 8 + 2 = 10\) flips.

    For HHT only the gambler who arrived three flips earlier still holds money, since no proper ending of HHT is also a beginning of it, so \(\mathbb E \tau = 8\) flips. In general the expected time is the sum of \(2^k\) over every \(k\) for which the last \(k\) letters of the pattern equal its first \(k\) letters (Li).

Project. On a stream of prompts, compare two language models with a betting test, whose wealth multiplies by \(1 + \lambda\) when the first model wins a comparison and by \(1 - \lambda\) when it loses, and with a fixed-sample test at the same \(\alpha\). Report how many prompts each needs to reach a decision over 1000 shuffled orders, and the betting test's measured false-positive rate when the two models are equally good.

Chapter 17

Stochastic optimal control

Control theory and dynamic programming

To act well under noise, price every state at every time by the least cost still to come, and act downhill on those prices. The prices solve one equation, the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, which becomes a Riccati equation for linear systems with quadratic costs and a linear equation that can be solved by sampling when the cost of control matches the noise.

Uses Chapters 2, 3, 4, 10, 12, and 16 and Appendix A.1.

17.1Motivation

Suppose you steer a boat across a river to a dock on the far bank, and gusts push the boat sideways at random. You could plan the whole crossing in advance, holding the bow at one fixed angle, but the first gust carries you off the line and the plan never notices. A pilot looks at where the boat is now and decides the next correction. What is the best correction at each place and moment? Listing a plan for every possible sequence of gusts is hopeless, since their number grows exponentially with the length of the crossing.

The pilot's habit points to something smaller than a plan. Give every place on the river, at every moment, a price: the expected cost still to come if you steer as well as possible from there. With those prices in hand, each correction is a small choice between paying for a push now and letting the wind carry you to places whose prices you know. But the price of a place depends on how well you will steer from it, which is what you are trying to find. How can you price places before you know how to act? Bellman (1957) answered with a recursion that runs backward from the end of the crossing. Kalman (1960) reduced the case of linear dynamics with quadratic costs to one matrix equation, and Merton (1969) used the continuous-time form of Bellman's recursion to decide how much of a fortune to hold in stocks.

17.2Intuition

Take the smallest crossing. A boat sits at an integer position \(x\) and has two steps left. At each step you may push it by \(u \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\), which costs \(0.5\,|u|\), and then the wind moves it by \(+1\) or \(-1\) with equal probability. At the end you pay \(x^2\), the squared distance from the dock at 0. A natural guess is to push toward the dock whenever you are off it. From \(x = 1\) that rule pays 0.5 for a push to 0, the wind carries the boat to \(\pm 1\), it pays 0.5 again, and the wind leaves it at \(\pm 1\), for a total of \(0.5 + 0.5 + 1 = 2\). Can you do better by waiting?

Start from the end, where the cost still to come is \(V_2(x) = x^2\). One step earlier, a push \(u\) leaves you at \(x + u \pm 1\), so

\[ V_1(x) = \min_{u} \Big\{ 0.5\,|u| + \tfrac12 V_2(x + u + 1) + \tfrac12 V_2(x + u - 1) \Big\} = \min_u \big\{ 0.5\,|u| + (x + u)^2 + 1 \big\}. \]

At \(x = 0\) the best is not to push, \(V_1(0) = 1\). At \(x = 1\) a push back costs 0.5 and saves 1, so \(V_1(1) = 1.5\), and \(V_1(2) = 2.5\). With two steps left at \(x = 1\), repeat the same step with \(V_1\) in place of \(V_2\), using also \(V_1(-1) = 1.5\) and \(V_1(3) = 5.5\). Each push is priced by its cost plus the average of \(V_1\) over the two places the wind can carry the boat:

\[ \begin{aligned} u = 0: &\quad \tfrac12 V_1(2) + \tfrac12 V_1(0) = 1.25 + 0.5 = 1.75, \\ u = -1: &\quad 0.5 + \tfrac12 V_1(1) + \tfrac12 V_1(-1) = 0.5 + 1.5 = 2, \\ u = +1: &\quad 0.5 + \tfrac12 V_1(3) + \tfrac12 V_1(1) = 0.5 + 3.5 = 4. \end{aligned} \]

So \(V_0(1) = 1.75\), reached by not pushing at the first step: half the time the wind carries the boat to 0, where nothing more is needed, and half the time to 2, where one push brings it back. The guess pays for a push that, half the time, the wind would have made anyway, and it costs 2. The best plan fixed in advance from \(x = 1\), one push on one of the two steps, costs 2.5. Waiting to see the wind saves 0.75 over the fixed plan, and the saving came from pricing every state at every time and reading the action off the prices. Bellman called these prices the value function, and the backward recursion that computes them dynamic programming.

Work backward from the end: price every state by the best you can still do from it, and the best action now is the one that moves you toward the cheapest prices.

Figure 17.1The value function prices every state, and the paths roll downhill

The value function prices every state at every time, and the optimal control is its downhill direction, so sample paths under the feedback u* = −∂ₓV flow into the cheap regions whatever the noise does to them.

The terminal cost g(x) = 8(|x| − 1)² has targets at ±1, and the noise sets λ = σ², so Ψ = e^(−V/λ) is a Gaussian integral of e^(−g/λ) with a closed form. At the default σ = 0.5, V(0, 0.2) = 0.6052, and 2000 Euler paths of step 1/200 under u* cost 0.6041 ± 0.0106 on average, 0.1 standard errors away. 81.3% of them end above 0, against the 81.8% that the two halves of Ψ predict. The best open-loop plan, one constant push chosen at t = 0, aims at x = 0.879 and costs 2.0940, because it cannot react to the noise it meets. Slide σ to 0.1: V = 0.3153, the open-loop plan costs 0.3812, and every path ends near +1. Slide σ to 1: V = 1.1953 against a path mean of 1.2030 ± 0.0262, 59.3% of the paths end above 0, and the open-loop plan hedges by aiming between the targets, at x = 0.047. Press New paths for another seed.

17.3Statement

The toy used a recursion from the end, \(V_t(x) = \min_u \{\text{cost now} + \mathbb E\, V_{t+1}(\text{next state})\}\), which is Bellman's equation of Chapter 4. For a state that moves continuously under Gaussian noise, the statements below answer three questions: what equation the prices solve when the step shrinks to zero, how to know a solution of it is the optimum, and when it can be solved in closed form or by sampling.

Theorem 17.1 (the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation)

Let \(dX = b(X, u)\, dt + \sigma\, dW\) on \([0, T]\), where \(u\) is the control, and let a policy pay \(\mathbb E\big[\int_0^T c(X_t, u_t)\, dt + g(X_T)\big]\). The value function \(V(t, x)\), the least expected cost from state \(x\) at time \(t\), satisfies, where it is smooth,

\[ -\partial_t V = \min_u \big\{ c(x, u) + b(x, u) \cdot \nabla V \big\} + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}\big(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 V\big), \qquad V(T, \cdot) = g, \tag{17.1} \]

and the optimal control is the feedback \(u^*(t, x)\) that attains the minimum.

In the boat, \(X\) is the position, \(u\) the steering, \(b(X, u)\) the drift that the steering gives, \(\sigma\, dW\) the gusts, \(c\) the cost of steering per unit time, and \(g\) the price of where the crossing ends. The minimum in (17.1) is the toy's choice among pushes, made at every instant. The trace term is the toy's average over the two gusts. In one dimension it is \(\tfrac12 \sigma^2 V''\), and in the toy, where a gust has variance 1 and \(V_2'' = 2\), it is the \(+1\) in the formula for \(V_1\). The condition that \(V\) be smooth matters at a place where two ways of steering are equally good, such as the midpoint between two docks, where with no noise the value has a kink (Section 17.6).

Theorem 17.2 (verification)

If a function \(\phi\), twice continuously differentiable in \(x\) and once in \(t\), with \(\phi\) and its derivatives growing at most polynomially, solves (17.1), and a feedback \(u^*\) attains its minimum and gives the closed loop a solution, then \(\phi = V\) and \(u^*\) is optimal among controls under which \(X\) has finite moments of every order.

Smoothness lets Itô's lemma apply to \(\phi\), and the growth bound, with the finite moments, keeps the noise integral in the proof a fair game with mean zero. Without the bound the theorem fails. With \(b = 0\), \(c = 0\), \(g = 0\), and \(\sigma = 1\) in one dimension, (17.1) is \(-\partial_t \phi = \tfrac12 \phi''\) with \(\phi(T, \cdot) = 0\), and the value is \(V = 0\). Yet the equation has other solutions, found by Tychonoff, that grow faster than \(e^{a x^2}\) for every \(a\).

Theorem 17.3 (linear dynamics, quadratic cost)

Let \(b = Ax + Bu\), \(c = x^\top Q x + u^\top R u\), and \(g = x^\top Q_T x\), with \(Q\) and \(Q_T\) symmetric positive semidefinite and \(R\) positive definite. Then \(V(t, x) = x^\top P(t)\, x + s(t)\), where

\[ -\dot P = A^\top P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^\top P + Q, \quad P(T) = Q_T, \qquad -\dot s = \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top P), \quad s(T) = 0, \tag{17.2} \]

and \(u^* = -R^{-1} B^\top P(t)\, x\). The gain does not depend on \(\sigma\): the noise only adds the constant \(s(t)\) to the cost.

A positive definite \(R\) makes every push cost something. With \(R = 0\) the bracket in (17.1) is linear in \(u\), it has no minimum wherever \(B^\top \nabla V \ne 0\), and the best push there would be infinitely large.

Proposition 17.4 (linearly solvable control)

Let \(b = f(x) + u\) and \(c = q(x) + \tfrac12 u^\top R u\), and suppose the noise and the price of control are tied by \(\sigma\sigma^\top = \lambda R^{-1}\) for some \(\lambda \gt 0\). Then \(\Psi = e^{-V/\lambda}\) solves a linear equation, and

\[ \Psi(t, x) = \mathbb E\Big[\exp\Big(-\tfrac1\lambda\Big(\int_t^T q(Y_s)\, ds + g(Y_T)\Big)\Big)\Big], \qquad u^* = \sigma\sigma^\top \nabla \log \Psi, \tag{17.3} \]

where \(Y\) follows the uncontrolled dynamics \(dY = f(Y)\, ds + \sigma\, dW\) from \(Y_t = x\).

The tie says that a push is cheap in the directions where the noise already moves the state a lot, so a cheap push looks like a likely gust. Without it, the two squares of \(\nabla V\) in the derivation of (17.3) do not cancel, and the equation stays nonlinear. A check with numbers: in one dimension take \(f = 0\), \(q = 0\), \(R = 1\), and \(\sigma = 1\), so \(\lambda = 1\), with the final cost \(g(y) = y^2/2\). With \(\tau = T - t\) left, \(Y_T = x + \sqrt\tau\, Z\) for a standard normal \(Z\), and the average in (17.3) is a Gaussian integral:

\[ \Psi(t, x) = \mathbb E\, e^{-(x + \sqrt\tau\, Z)^2/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \tau}}\, e^{-x^2/(2(1 + \tau))}, \qquad u^* = \partial_x \log \Psi = -\frac{x}{1 + \tau}. \]

With one unit of time left, the best push from \(x = 2\) is \(-1\). Theorem 17.3, with \(A = 0\), \(B = 1\), \(Q = 0\), \(R = \tfrac12\), and \(Q_T = \tfrac12\), gives the same feedback.

17.4Derivation

(17.1). Over a short step \(h\), the best you can do is to pay for the step and then act optimally from wherever you land:

\[ V(t, x) = \min_u \Big\{ c(x, u)\, h + \mathbb E\, V(t + h, X_{t+h}) \Big\} + o(h). \]

Itô's lemma (Appendix A.1) expands the second term, with the control held at \(u\) over the step:

\[ \mathbb E\, V(t + h, X_{t+h}) = V(t, x) + h\Big(\partial_t V + b(x, u) \cdot \nabla V + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 V)\Big) + o(h). \]

The toy's average over the two gusts is the same expansion with a step of 1,

\[ \tfrac12 V(y + 1) + \tfrac12 V(y - 1) = V(y) + \tfrac12\big(V(y + 1) - 2V(y) + V(y - 1)\big), \]

and the bracket, a second difference, equals \(V''\) for a quadratic, which is where the \(+1\) in \(V_1\) came from. Substituting the expansion into the first line, \(V(t, x)\) cancels on both sides:

\[ 0 = \min_u \Big\{ c(x, u)\, h + h\Big(\partial_t V + b(x, u) \cdot \nabla V + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 V)\Big) \Big\} + o(h). \]

Every remaining term carries a factor \(h\). Divide by \(h\), let \(h \to 0\), and move \(\partial_t V\) and the trace term, which do not depend on \(u\), out of the minimum. That gives (17.1). The noise enters only through the second-derivative term, which is the average curvature of the prices over the spread of the next position.

Theorem 17.2. Fix any control and apply Itô's lemma to \(\phi(t, X_t)\):

\[ \phi(T, X_T) - \phi(0, x) = \int_0^T \Big(\partial_t \phi + b \cdot \nabla \phi + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 \phi)\Big) dt + \int_0^T \nabla \phi^\top \sigma\, dW. \]

By (17.1),

\[ \partial_t \phi + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 \phi) = -\min_u\{c + b \cdot \nabla \phi\} \ge -c(X_t, u_t) - b(X_t, u_t) \cdot \nabla \phi, \]

so the first integrand is at least \(-c(X_t, u_t)\). The last integral is a martingale with mean zero (Chapter 16), so taking expectations and using \(\phi(T, \cdot) = g\) gives \(\phi(0, x) \le \mathbb E\big[\int_0^T c\, dt + g(X_T)\big]\) for every control. Under \(u^*\) the inequality is an equality, so \(\phi(0, x)\) is the least cost and \(u^*\) achieves it.

(17.2). Try \(V = x^\top P x + s\), so \(\nabla V = 2 P x\) and \(\nabla^2 V = 2P\). The bracket in (17.1) is \(x^\top Q x + u^\top R u + 2 x^\top P (A x + B u)\), a quadratic in \(u\) whose gradient \(2Ru + 2B^\top P x\) vanishes at \(u^* = -R^{-1}B^\top P x\). At \(u^*\) the two terms that contain \(u\) combine into one:

\[ u^{*\top} R\, u^* + 2x^\top P B u^* = x^\top P B R^{-1} B^\top P x - 2\, x^\top P B R^{-1} B^\top P x = -x^\top P B R^{-1} B^\top P x. \]

The noise term is \(\tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \cdot 2P) = \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top P)\), and the left side of (17.1) is \(-\partial_t V = -x^\top \dot P x - \dot s\). Writing \(2x^\top P A x = x^\top (PA + A^\top P)x\), (17.1) becomes

\[ -x^\top \dot P x - \dot s = x^\top\big(Q + PA + A^\top P - P B R^{-1} B^\top P\big)x + \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top P). \]

Matching the quadratic terms and the constants gives the two equations of (17.2). The noise appears only in the constant.

(17.3). The bracket \(q + \tfrac12 u^\top R u + (f + u) \cdot \nabla V\) is smallest at \(u^* = -R^{-1}\nabla V\), where it equals \(q + f \cdot \nabla V - \tfrac12 \nabla V^\top R^{-1} \nabla V\). Write \(V = -\lambda \log \Psi\), so

\[ \nabla V = -\lambda \frac{\nabla \Psi}{\Psi}, \qquad \nabla^2 V = -\lambda \Big(\frac{\nabla^2 \Psi}{\Psi} - \frac{\nabla \Psi\, \nabla \Psi^\top}{\Psi^2}\Big), \qquad \partial_t V = -\lambda \frac{\partial_t \Psi}{\Psi}. \]

Substitute these into (17.1) with the minimum already taken. The control term and the noise term each produce a square of \(\nabla \Psi\):

\[ -\tfrac12 \nabla V^\top R^{-1} \nabla V = -\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\, \frac{\nabla\Psi^\top R^{-1} \nabla\Psi}{\Psi^2}, \]
\[ \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 V) = -\frac{\lambda}{2}\, \frac{\operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 \Psi)}{\Psi} + \frac{\lambda}{2}\, \frac{\nabla\Psi^\top \sigma\sigma^\top \nabla\Psi}{\Psi^2}. \]

With \(\sigma\sigma^\top = \lambda R^{-1}\) the last term is \(+\tfrac{\lambda^2}{2}\nabla\Psi^\top R^{-1}\nabla\Psi/\Psi^2\), which cancels the control term. With \(-\partial_t V = \lambda\, \partial_t \Psi/\Psi\), what remains of (17.1) is

\[ \lambda\, \frac{\partial_t \Psi}{\Psi} = q - \lambda\, \frac{f \cdot \nabla \Psi}{\Psi} - \frac{\lambda}{2}\, \frac{\operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 \Psi)}{\Psi}, \]

and multiplying by \(-\Psi/\lambda\) leaves

\[ -\partial_t \Psi = f \cdot \nabla \Psi + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 \Psi) - \tfrac{q}{\lambda}\, \Psi, \qquad \Psi(T, \cdot) = e^{-g/\lambda}, \]

a linear equation: the generator of the uncontrolled process acting on \(\Psi\), with a killing rate \(q/\lambda\). Its solution is the expectation in (17.3) by the Feynman-Kac formula, which takes one application of Itô's lemma. Along the uncontrolled path \(Y\) from \(Y_t = x\), discount by the cost accumulated so far,

\[ D_s = \exp\Big(-\tfrac1\lambda \int_t^s q(Y_r)\, dr\Big), \qquad dD_s = -\tfrac{q(Y_s)}{\lambda}\, D_s\, ds. \]

Itô's lemma for \(\Psi(s, Y_s)\) and the product rule give

\[ d\big(D_s \Psi(s, Y_s)\big) = D_s \Big(\partial_s \Psi + f \cdot \nabla \Psi + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 \Psi) - \tfrac{q}{\lambda}\, \Psi\Big) ds + D_s\, \nabla\Psi^\top \sigma\, dW. \]

The \(ds\) term is zero by the linear equation, so \(D_s \Psi(s, Y_s)\) is a martingale. Its mean at \(s = t\) is \(\Psi(t, x)\), and at \(s = T\) it is the expectation in (17.3), since \(\Psi(T, \cdot) = e^{-g/\lambda}\). Finally

\[ u^* = -R^{-1}\nabla V = \lambda R^{-1} \nabla \log \Psi = \sigma\sigma^\top \nabla \log \Psi. \]

∎

Earlier chapters in this form. The control problem (3.3) of Chapter 3 is Proposition 17.4 with \(f = 0\), \(q = 0\), \(R = I\), \(\sigma = I\), \(\lambda = 1\), and \(g = -r\), so \(\Psi\) is the function \(h\) of the h-transform and the optimal policy reweights the uncontrolled paths by \(e^{-\text{cost}/\lambda}\), the tilt of Chapter 2. Along a single optimal trajectory of a deterministic problem, \(\nabla V\) is the costate of Chapter 12. In discrete time, (17.1) is the Bellman equation, whose discounted form contracts in Chapter 4. The Kalman filter's error covariance obeys the same Riccati equation as (17.2), run forward in time with \(A\) replaced by \(A^\top\), \(B\) by the transposed measurement matrix, and \(Q\) and \(R\) by the covariances of the process and measurement noise, which is the duality between estimation and control. And for an investor who maximizes expected log wealth, (17.1) gives the fraction \((\mu - r)/\sigma^2\) of wealth in the risky asset (Derivation 17.2), the continuous-time Kelly bet of Chapter 10.

17.5Figures

Figure 17.2The Riccati gain does not see the noise

For a linear system with quadratic cost the value is a quadratic form whose matrix solves a Riccati equation, and the optimal gain is the same whatever the noise, which only adds a constant to the cost.

The state is position and velocity, u is the acceleration, and the cost is ∫ (xᵀQx + r u²) dt + xᵀQ_T x with Q = diag(1, 0.1), Q_T = 10·I, and T = 5, from x₀ = (2, 0). At the default r = 0.1 the Riccati equation, run backward with RK4, gives K(0) = (3.1623, 2.7064), the steady gains to four decimals, and K₂ climbs to 10/r = 100 at t = 5, where the end cost takes over. At σ = 0.5 the expected cost is 3.4234 + 0.4580 = 3.8814, and 2000 Heun paths give 3.8766 ± 0.0074. Scaling the gain by α and computing each scaled feedback's exact expected cost puts the minimum at α = 1.0000 both at σ = 0.5 and at σ = 0, and the noise lifts that minimum by σ²∫P₂₂ dt. Slide σ: the gain curves stay put, and the noise's share of the cost rises from 11.8% to 34.9% at σ = 1. Slide r to 10: the gains shrink to K(0) = (0.3308, 0.8492), and the noise carries 54.5% of the cost.

Figure 17.3The optimal control as a weighted average of noise

In the linearly solvable case the optimal control at a point is a weighted average of the noise of uncontrolled paths, weighted by e^(−cost/λ), so it can be estimated by sampling, with an error set by the effective sample size of the weights.

The problem is the two-target one above at σ = 0.5, so λ = 0.25. Each uncontrolled path from (t, x) ends at X_T = x + σ√(T − t) Z with weight e^(−g(X_T)/λ). The weighted mean of X_T − x, divided by the time left, estimates u*, because Gaussian integration by parts makes its expectation σ²∂ₓ log Ψ. At the default start (0, 0.2) the exact value is u* = 0.4112. This sample of K = 128 has an effective sample size of 19.6 and estimates 0.1782, an error of 57%. With K = 1024 the effective size is 131.2 and the error 9.1%, and with K = 16 the estimate has the wrong sign. Over 50 seeds the spread falls from 0.492 at K = 16 to 0.077 at K = 1024, while the spread times √ESS stays between 0.75 and 0.88. Slide t to 0.8: the paths end near the start, far from both wells, and at K = 1024 the effective size drops to 11.3. Slide x to 1.5, outside the targets: the weights even out and the spread at K = 128 is 0.016.

17.6Four ways to see it

Optimal control is a backward recursion, a partial differential equation, a matrix equation, and a problem of sampling paths.

  1. 1Dynamic programmingoperations research

    The toy's recursion from the end, \(V_t = \min_u\{c + \mathbb E V_{t+1}\}\), is Bellman's principle of optimality: whatever the first action, the rest of an optimal policy is optimal from where it lands. Value iteration of Chapter 4 solves it by contraction.

  2. 1 → 2Shrink the time step to \(h\) and expand \(\mathbb E V_{t+h}\) by Itô's lemma. The recursion loses its \(V\) on both sides, and what is left, divided by \(h\), is the partial differential equation (17.1).

  3. 2The HJB equationanalysis

    The value function solves (17.1), and a smooth solution certifies optimality by the martingale argument of Theorem 17.2 (Figure 17.1). Where \(V\) has kinks, as at the boundary between two targets when there is no noise (small noise rounds the kink into a steep, smooth ridge), the equation holds in the sense of viscosity solutions, which test it only through smooth functions that touch \(V\) from above or below. A boat with no noise that must reach one of two docks at \(\pm 1\) at unit speed has the time to go \(1 - |x|\), with a kink at 0. Many functions have slope \(\pm 1\) almost everywhere and vanish at both docks, and the viscosity condition picks out this one.

  4. 2 → 3With linear dynamics and quadratic costs, guess a quadratic value. The minimization in (17.1) is then a quadratic in \(u\), and matching coefficients turns the partial differential equation into an ordinary one for the matrix \(P(t)\).

  5. 3Riccati and the Kalman filtercontrol engineering

    The linear-quadratic regulator, its noisy version, and the Kalman filter share the Riccati equation (17.2), the filter in its dual form, and the gain ignores the noise, which is certainty equivalence (Figure 17.2).

  6. 2 → 4When the price of control matches the noise, the substitution \(V = -\lambda \log \Psi\) cancels the quadratic terms of (17.1) and leaves a linear equation, whose solution is an average over uncontrolled paths (17.3).

  7. 4Control as inferencemachine learning

    The optimal policy reweights uncontrolled paths by \(e^{-\text{cost}/\lambda}\), so the optimal control can be estimated by sampling them (Figure 17.3). Path integral control, KL control, soft Q-learning, MPPI in Chapter 18, and reward fine-tuning of diffusion models by adjoint matching are this view.

17.7Where it breaks and what is open

The value function is a function of the whole state, so storing it on a grid with \(m\) points per axis takes \(m^d\) numbers, which Bellman called the curse of dimensionality. Ten points per axis is a coarse grid, and in ten dimensions it already holds ten billion states. At a fixed budget of \(B\) states, the grid has only \(B^{1/d}\) points per axis, and the computed value drifts away from the exact Riccati value as the dimension grows (Figure 17.4). The other limits are a value with kinks, where (17.1) holds only in a weaker sense and the optimal control jumps, and a state the controller cannot see, where it must act on a belief, a probability distribution over where the state might be. Acting on the best estimate as if it were the state, which is certainty equivalence, is optimal in the linear-quadratic Gaussian case and fails in general outside it. Elsewhere a good action may be one that reveals the state, such as a small probing push whose response shows where the boat is.

Figure 17.4A fixed grid coarsens as the dimension grows

Solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation on a grid needs m^d states, so at a fixed budget the grid coarsens like N^(1/d) per axis and the computed value drifts from the exact Riccati value as the dimension grows.

The dynamics are x_(k+1) = x_k + 0.1u_k in d dimensions with cost 0.1(|x|² + |u|²) per step over 20 steps, so the exact value is P₀|x|² with P₀ = 1.0115. Value iteration on a grid of N states over [−2, 2]^d interpolates multilinearly and takes the exact minimum over the next state. The problem splits across axes and the interpolation keeps the split, so the grid's value is d copies of a one-axis grid with ⌊N^(1/d)⌋ points, and full runs in two to four dimensions agree with that to below 1e−14. At N = 10⁵ the relative error at (0.7, …, 0.7) is 7.2e−9 in one dimension, 7.4e−4 in two, 4.4% in three, 19% in four with 17 points per axis, and 88% in six. Staying under 1% takes 90 points per axis, which is 6.6 × 10⁷ states at d = 4 and 3.5 × 10¹⁹ at d = 10. Switch the budget to 10³: at d = 4 the grid has 5 points per axis and overshoots by 118%.

  1. High-dimensional value functions. Neural networks trained on its backward stochastic form (Han, Jentzen, and E) or on the residual of (17.1) (Sirignano and Spiliopoulos) solve problems in a hundred dimensions in practice. Error bounds that hold at that scale, and checks that tell a good solution from a plausible one, are open.
  2. The temperature of reward fine-tuning. Fine-tuning a diffusion model toward a reward is Proposition 17.4 with the base model as the uncontrolled dynamics, and \(\lambda\) sets how far the tuned model may drift from it. Choosing \(\lambda\) and the noise schedule so that the learned control reaches the tilted target, and measuring whether it did, is open.
  3. Control with a learned world model. A controller that sees images acts on a belief state that a learned model maintains. When certainty equivalence is safe outside the linear-quadratic case, and how the model's errors enter the value, are open.

  1. Exercise 17.1 Stochastic optimal control

    • A shop holds 0 to 3 units. Each morning it orders u units, with stock plus u at most 3, at 1 per unit; then demand D = 0, 1 or 2 arrives with chances 0.3, 0.4 and 0.3. Each unit short costs 4, each unit left overnight costs 0.5, and leftovers after the third day are worth nothing.
    • Price every stock level backward from the last day. What is the least expected cost from an empty shop, and up to what stock does the best policy order on each day?

    least_cost(0)    # 5.395
order_up_to()    # (2, 2, 1)

  2. Exercise 17.2 LQR by Riccati

    • A cart has position p and velocity v. Each step x' = Ax + Bu with A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and B = (0, 1), so the push u changes the velocity, and each step costs p² + v² + u².
    • Run the discrete Riccati recursion from P = 0 until it settles. What is the gain K in u = −Kx, and what does steering the cart from rest at p = 1 cost in total?
    Answer
    lqr_gain()            # (0.422082, 1.243929)
cost_from(1.0, 0.0)   # 2.947123

    • The cart again: x = (p, v), x' = Ax + Bu + w with A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and B = (0, 1), at a cost of p² + v² + u² a step. Now a gust w = (0, 0.2ε), with ε ~ N(0, 1), hits the velocity every step.
    • Search all linear gains u = −Kx for the least long-run cost per step, computed exactly from the stationary covariance. Which gain wins, and what does a step cost on average?
    Answer

average_cost(0.2)      # 0.184525

  4. Exercise 17.4 Path integral control

    • A particle moves by dX = u dt + σ dW with σ = 0.5 on [0, 1]. Steering costs ½·4·u² per unit time, and the end costs g(X_1) = 2X_1². The noise matches the price of control, σ² = λ/4 with λ = 1, as Proposition 17.4 asks.
    • With no control X_1 ~ N(x, σ²). Compute Ψ(x) = E exp(−g(X_1)/λ) by quadrature, then u* = σ² ∂x log Ψ and V = −λ log Ψ at x = 1.5. What are the optimal push and the least expected cost?
    Answer
    control(1.5)   # -0.75
value(1.5)     # 2.596574

  5. Exercise 17.5 Merton with power utility

    • A stock has drift μ = 0.09 and volatility σ = 0.2, and cash earns r = 0.03. An investor keeps a fixed fraction π of wealth in the stock, rebalancing continuously, and has power utility W^{1−γ}/(1 − γ) with γ = 3.
    • What fraction maximizes expected utility, and at what sure rate of growth would the investor be indifferent (the certainty-equivalent rate)? What is that rate if the investor holds the Kelly fraction, 1.5, instead?
    Answer
    merton(0.09, 0.03, 0.2, 3)         # (0.5, 0.045)
ce_rate(1.5, 0.09, 0.03, 0.2, 3)   # -0.015

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 17.1The scalar regulator

    For \(dX = (aX + u)\, dt + \sigma\, dW\) with the long-run average cost \(\rho = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac1T \mathbb E \int_0^T (qX^2 + ru^2)\, dt\), equation (17.1) becomes

    \[ \rho = \min_u\{qx^2 + ru^2 + V'(x)(ax + u)\} + \tfrac12 \sigma^2 V''(x). \]

    Guess \(V = Px^2\), find \(P\), the gain, and \(\rho\), and evaluate them for \(a = q = r = 1\). Where does \(\sigma\) enter?

    Solution

    The bracket \(qx^2 + ru^2 + 2Px(ax + u)\) is smallest at \(u = -Px/r\), where it equals \(qx^2 + 2aPx^2 - P^2x^2/r\). The equation becomes \(\rho = (q + 2aP - P^2/r)\,x^2 + \sigma^2 P\) for every \(x\), so the \(x^2\) terms give \(P^2 - 2arP - qr = 0\) and the constants give \(\rho = \sigma^2 P\):

    \[ P = r\big(a + \sqrt{a^2 + q/r}\big) = 1 + \sqrt 2 = 2.414, \qquad u = -2.414\, x. \]

    The closed loop is

    \[ dX = (a - P/r)X\, dt + \sigma\, dW = -\sqrt 2\, X\, dt + \sigma\, dW, \]

    stable although the uncontrolled system grows like \(e^{t}\). The noise sets the average cost, \(\rho = 2.414\,\sigma^2\), and leaves the gain unchanged.

  2. Derivation 17.2Merton's fraction

    Wealth follows \(dW = W\big(r + \pi(\mu - r)\big) dt + W \pi \sigma\, dB\), where \(\pi\) is the fraction in a stock with drift \(\mu\) and volatility \(\sigma\). For the goal of maximizing \(\mathbb E \log W_T\), find the best \(\pi\) and the growth rate, and evaluate them for \(\mu = 0.08\), \(r = 0.03\), and \(\sigma = 0.2\).

    Solution

    By Itô's lemma, \(d \log W = \big(r + \pi(\mu - r) - \tfrac12 \pi^2\sigma^2\big) dt + \pi\sigma\, dB\). The value is \(\log w\) plus the integral of the drift, so the best \(\pi\) maximizes the drift at every instant:

    \[ \pi^* = \frac{\mu - r}{\sigma^2} = 1.25, \qquad r + \frac{(\mu - r)^2}{2\sigma^2} = 0.06125 \text{ per year}. \]

    The bet is a quarter more than all of one's wealth, borrowed at \(r\). It is the Kelly fraction of Chapter 10 in continuous time, and a more risk-averse investor with power utility of parameter \(\gamma\) holds \((\mu - r)/(\gamma\sigma^2)\).
