Chapter 18

Model predictive control

Control engineering and planning

When the value function of Chapter 17 is too expensive to compute everywhere, plan a few steps ahead from the current state only, take the first step of the plan, and plan again from wherever the system lands. Replanning turns a sequence of open-loop plans into feedback, a terminal cost makes it stable, a learned value at the end of the plan bounds its loss, and sampling the plans is the tilt of Chapter 2.

Uses Chapters 2, 3, 4, 9, and 17.

18.1Motivation

Suppose you drive at night, and your headlights reach fifty meters. You cannot plan the whole route in detail, and you do not need to. You plan the stretch you can see, turn the wheel for the first moment of that plan, and plan again as more road appears. The plans are never carried out to their end, yet the car follows the road. Why should a string of plans, each abandoned after its first moment, add up to good driving? And how far must the lights reach? A plan that sees fifty meters of straight road keeps full speed toward a sharp curve at sixty, so what lies past the edge of the plan has to enter it somehow.

Process engineers met the same situation in oil refineries in the 1970s. A plant had dozens of valves, temperatures, and flows, each with limits it must never cross, and no formula gave the best feedback law under those limits. A plant changes over minutes, though, so there was time to solve one optimization over the next few minutes at every sampling instant. Richalet and colleagues (1978) and Cutler and Ramaker (1980) put this loop into production. Today the same loop flies drones, balances legged robots, and plans inside game-playing programs.

ESSAYA document that moved capital

The Bitter Lesson

General methods that scale with computation, search and learning, beat methods built on human knowledge.

Rich Sutton, 2019 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Its argument, that search and learning scaled with computation win in the long run, became a common frame for the era of scaling.

The link to this chapter: its game examples are planners. Chess fell to massive deep search in 1997, and Go fell to search at scale combined with a value function learned by self-play, which is lookahead ending in a learned terminal value (Proposition 18.3). The bound (18.3) is an exchange rate between the essay's two methods: at \(\gamma = 0.9\), halving the value's error is worth about 6.6 steps of lookahead (Derivation 18.2).

18.2Intuition

Take the smallest system that needs control: a state that doubles every step unless pushed, \(x_{t+1} = 2x_t + u_t\), with cost \(x_t^2 + u_t^2\) per step, starting at \(x_0 = 1\). Plan one step ahead. The step's cost is \(x_0^2 + u_0^2\), and \(x_0^2\) is already paid, so the best push is \(u_0 = 0\). Replanning every step gives \(u = 0\) forever and the state runs off: 1, 2, 4, 8. Every plan was optimal for its horizon, and the result is a disaster.

Plan two steps ahead. The plan pays \(u_0^2 + x_1^2 + u_1^2\), plus \(x_0^2\), which is fixed. The second push affects nothing the plan sees, so \(u_1 = 0\), and the first must minimize \(u_0^2 + (2x_0 + u_0)^2\), which gives \(u_0 = -x_0\). The state stays where it is: 1, 1, 1. Plan three steps ahead. The last two steps of that plan are a two-step plan from \(x_1\), and the calculation just done says their least cost is \(3x_1^2\): \(x_1^2\) for the state, \(x_1^2\) for the push \(u_1 = -x_1\), and \(x_1^2\) for the state \(x_2 = x_1\) it leaves. So the first push must minimize \(u_0^2 + 3(2x_0 + u_0)^2\), whose derivative \(2u_0 + 6(2x_0 + u_0)\) vanishes at \(u_0 = -1.5\,x_0\), and the state halves at every step: 1, 0.5, 0.25. Planning forever gives the best possible push, \(u = -1.618\,x\) (Derivation 18.1), and three steps of foresight, replanned at every step, are already close.

Look at what the extra steps did. The three-step plan's first push depended on the two steps after it only through the price \(3x_1^2\) they put on the state it lands in. A one-step plan that ends with that price, minimizing \(x_0^2 + u_0^2 + 3x_1^2\), makes the same push. So a short plan with a good price at its end does the work of a longer one. The best price is the least cost of planning forever, \(4.236\,x^2\) (Derivation 18.1), and a one-step plan that ends with it already pushes \(-1.618\,x\).

Plan a few steps ahead, end the plan with a price on where it lands, take only the first step, and plan again from wherever you land.

Figure 18.1A robot that keeps re-planning

A robot that plans a few steps ahead, takes the first step, and plans again from wherever it lands reaches its goal around obstacles, even though no single plan it made was followed to the end.

Each step samples 128 velocity sequences around the shifted previous plan, weights each by e^(−cost/λ), moves the plan to the weighted mean, and executes only its first step before planning again. At the default H = 15 the robot drives into the narrow gap between the two left obstacles, and the plans it makes there rise a little higher at each step until one clears the wall. It reaches the goal in 45 steps at a total cost of 188.8, comes no closer than 0.37 to an obstacle's edge, and executes 45 of the 675 steps it planned. The end of each plan misses where the robot really was 15 steps later by a median of 1.26. Slide H to 10 or below: the robot stops in front of the gap and is still there after 160 steps. Under 24 seeds every horizon up to 8 gets stuck, and every horizon from 12 up reaches the goal. Press Play to watch the plans being remade, or Step to advance one plan at a time.

18.3Statement

The toy raises three questions. When does replanning with a short horizon steer the state to rest, as three steps did and one step did not? How good is the policy when the plan ends in an estimate of the cost still to come instead of nothing? And how can each plan be solved fast enough to act on, once limits on the pushes leave no formula like the toy's? The statements answer them in that order.

Definition 18.1 (receding-horizon control)

For dynamics \(x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k)\), a stage cost \(c \ge 0\), a terminal cost \(V_f \ge 0\), and a horizon \(H\), let \(J_H^*(x)\) be the least value of

\[ \sum_{k \lt H} c(x_k, u_k) + V_f(x_H), \qquad x_0 = x, \tag{18.1} \]

over control sequences \(u_0, \dots, u_{H-1}\), with any limits on states and controls. The receding-horizon policy \(\kappa_H(x)\) applies the first control of a minimizing sequence, and the next state starts a new plan.

Theorem 18.2 (stability from a terminal cost)

Suppose \(c(x, u) \ge \alpha |x|^2\) for some \(\alpha \gt 0\), and the terminal cost satisfies \(\min_u\{c(x, u) + V_f(f(x, u))\} \le V_f(x)\) for every \(x\), so that some control keeps \(V_f\) from rising by more than the stage cost (a control Lyapunov function, Chapter 9). Then for every \(H \ge 1\), along the closed loop \(x^+ = f(x, \kappa_H(x))\),

\[ J_H^*(x^+) \le J_H^*(x) - c\big(x, \kappa_H(x)\big), \tag{18.2} \]

so \(\alpha \sum_t |x_t|^2 \le J_H^*(x_0)\) and the state goes to zero.

In the toy, a terminal price \(p x^2\) makes the one-step plan push \(u = -2p x/(1 + p)\), and the condition on \(V_f\) reads \(1 + 4p/(1 + p) \le p\), which holds exactly when \(p \ge 2 + \sqrt 5 = 4.236\). The empty price \(p = 0\) fails it, and the one-step plan ran off. The condition is only sufficient: the price \(p = 3\) fails it, yet its closed loop \(x^+ = 2x/(1 + p)\) halves the state at every step. The bound \(c \ge \alpha |x|^2\) makes the cost see the state. A cost that charges only for pushes, \(c = u^2\), meets the condition with \(V_f = 0\), and its plans leave the state to double forever.

Proposition 18.3 (lookahead with an approximate value)

In a problem with discount factor \(\gamma \lt 1\) and optimal cost \(V^*\), let the terminal cost satisfy \(|V_f(x) - V^*(x)| \le \varepsilon\) for every \(x\), and let \(\pi\) be the \(H\)-step lookahead policy, (18.1) with each stage discounted by \(\gamma^k\) and the terminal cost by \(\gamma^H\). Then its cost \(J^\pi\) satisfies

\[ J^\pi(x) \le V^*(x) + \frac{2\gamma^H \varepsilon}{1 - \gamma}, \tag{18.3} \]

and with \(V_f = V^*\) the receding-horizon policy is optimal for every \(H\).

The third question asks for a way to solve a plan without a formula. Take the one-step plan from \(x_0 = 1\) with the price \(3x^2\) at its end. A push \(u\) costs

\[ S(u) = 1 + u^2 + 3(2 + u)^2 = 4 + 4(u + 1.5)^2, \]

least at \(u = -1.5\). Suppose you could not solve for the minimum. Draw pushes from a bell curve around 0 with standard deviation 1, and average them with weights proportional to \(e^{-S/\lambda}\). As the number of draws grows, the weighted average tends to \(-12/(8 + \lambda)\): \(-1.33\) at \(\lambda = 1\), \(-1.48\) at \(\lambda = 0.1\), and the exact push \(-1.5\) as \(\lambda \to 0\), while a large \(\lambda\) leaves it near the bell curve's center at 0. The next statement says what distribution the weighted draws come from.

Proposition 18.4 (planning by sampling)

Let \(p_0\) be a density over control sequences \(U = (u_0, \dots, u_{H-1})\), such as independent Gaussian noise on each control, and \(S(U)\) the cost (18.1) of the sequence from the current state. Among densities \(p\) over sequences, \(\mathbb E_p[S] + \lambda\, \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, p_0)\) is smallest at

\[ p^*(U) \propto p_0(U)\, e^{-S(U)/\lambda}. \tag{18.4} \]

With \(K\) sequences \(U^{(i)}\) drawn from a proposal \(g\) and weights \(w_i \propto e^{-S(U^{(i)})/\lambda}\, p_0(U^{(i)})/g(U^{(i)})\) normalized to sum to one, the average \(\sum_i w_i U^{(i)}\) converges to the mean of \(p^*\) as \(K\) grows. Model predictive path integral control (MPPI) applies the first control of this average, shifts the average by one step to start the next plan, and repeats.

18.4Derivation

(18.2). Let \(u_0^*, \dots, u_{H-1}^*\) be a minimizing sequence from \(x\), with states \(x_0^* = x, x_1^*, \dots, x_H^*\). The closed loop applies \(u_0^*\), so \(x^+ = x_1^*\). From \(x^+\), try the old plan shifted by one step, with one new control \(v\) at the end, chosen to attain the minimum in the terminal-cost condition at \(x_H^*\):

\[ (u_1^*, \dots, u_{H-1}^*, v), \qquad \text{cost} = J_H^*(x) - c(x, u_0^*) - V_f(x_H^*) + c(x_H^*, v) + V_f\big(f(x_H^*, v)\big). \]

The last three terms are at most zero by the condition on \(V_f\), so this sequence costs at most \(J_H^*(x) - c(x, u_0^*)\), and the optimum from \(x^+\) costs no more. Adding (18.2) over \(t = 0, \dots, T-1\) telescopes to \(\sum_{t \lt T} c(x_t, u_t) \le J_H^*(x_0) - J_H^*(x_T) \le J_H^*(x_0)\), the potential argument of Chapter 9 with \(J_H^*\) as the potential.

(18.3). Write \(T\) for the Bellman operator of the discounted problem and \(T_\pi\) for the same operator with the action fixed by \(\pi\). Both shrink sup-norm distances by \(\gamma\) (Chapter 4). The lookahead policy picks its first action greedily with respect to \(U = T^{H-1} V_f\), the optimal cost of the remaining \(H - 1\) steps plus the terminal cost, so \(T_\pi U = T U\), and \(\|U - V^*\| \le \gamma^{H-1}\varepsilon\). That bound holds because \(V^*\) is the fixed point of \(T\), so \(U - V^* = T^{H-1} V_f - T^{H-1} V^*\), and each of the \(H - 1\) applications of \(T\) shrinks the distance \(\|V_f - V^*\| \le \varepsilon\) by \(\gamma\). Next, \(J^\pi = T_\pi J^\pi\) and \(V^* = T V^*\), and adding and subtracting \(T_\pi U = T U\) splits the error in two:

\[ J^\pi - V^* = (T_\pi J^\pi - T_\pi U) + (T U - T V^*). \]

Each part shrinks by \(\gamma\), and the triangle inequality \(\|J^\pi - U\| \le \|J^\pi - V^*\| + \|V^* - U\|\) gives the last step:

\[ \|J^\pi - V^*\| \le \|T_\pi J^\pi - T_\pi U\| + \|T U - T V^*\| \le \gamma \|J^\pi - U\| + \gamma \|U - V^*\| \le \gamma \|J^\pi - V^*\| + 2\gamma \|U - V^*\|. \]

Rearranging gives

\[ \|J^\pi - V^*\| \le 2\gamma \|U - V^*\|/(1 - \gamma) \le 2\gamma^H\varepsilon/(1 - \gamma). \]

With \(\varepsilon = 0\) the bound is zero for every \(H\).

(18.4). The Gibbs variational principle (2.1) with \(f = -S/\lambda\) reads

\[ \log \mathbb E_{p_0}[e^{-S/\lambda}] = \max_p\{-\mathbb E_p[S]/\lambda - \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, p_0)\}, \]

attained at the tilt \(p_0\, e^{-S/\lambda}/Z\). Multiplying by \(-\lambda\) turns the maximum into the minimum of \(\mathbb E_p[S] + \lambda\, \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, p_0)\). The mean of \(p^*\) is an expectation under \(p^*\), and the weights rewrite it as an expectation under \(g\), the change of measure of Chapter 3. Self-normalizing replaces the unknown \(Z\) by the sum of the weights, and the ratio of two averages converges by the law of large numbers. ∎

Learned models and values. Proposition 18.3 is why systems that learn a value function can plan with short horizons: TD-MPC plans a few steps through a learned model and ends each plan in a learned value, and MuZero's tree search does the same with a learned model of the game. Lookahead decoding in a language model, which commits one token and plans again, is receding-horizon planning with the negative log-probability as the cost, beam search approximately minimizes that cost over whole sequences, and Chapter 10's result that the most probable sequence is atypical is a reason a perfect planner for that cost can still produce poor text. With limits on states, Theorem 18.2 also needs a terminal set on which the terminal condition can be met within the limits, and the plan must be feasible from the start.

18.5Figures

Figure 18.2Short horizons, and the terminal cost that fixes them

For x⁺ = 2x + u a receding horizon of one or two steps never steers the state to zero, three steps do, and a terminal cost equal to the infinite-horizon value makes even one step optimal.

The gain comes from H − 1 steps of the backward Riccati recursion P⁺ = 1 + 4P − 4P²/(1 + P). The bars are the multiplier 2 − K without a terminal cost: 2, 1, 1/2, 2/5, 5/13, 13/34, and so on, ratios of Fibonacci numbers that fall to 2 − φ = 0.382. At the default H = 2 the gain is 1, so the state stays at x = 1 forever: the 50-step cost is 100 against the optimal 4.2361, and J*₂(x⁺) − J*₂(x) = 0, short of the decrease by c(x, κ(x)) = 2 that the stability argument asks for. Slide H to 1: no control is applied and x₁₂ = 4096. At H = 3 the gain is 3/2, the state halves each step, and the cost is 4.3333; J*₃ falls by 3 against c = 3.25, so the inequality fails even though the loop converges. Switch the terminal cost to P∞x²: every horizon, H = 1 included, gives the gain φ = 1.6180 and the cost 4.2361, and J* falls by exactly c(x, κ(x)) = 3.6180.

Figure 18.3Planning by sampling

MPPI weights sampled control sequences by e^(−cost/λ) and averages them, and on a linear problem with quadratic cost the average converges to the exact optimal first control as the samples grow, with the temperature λ trading a bias toward the starting plan against variance.

The problem is x⁺ = x + 0.2u from x₀ = 1 with cost Σₖ (xₖ² + uₖ²) over 20 steps, whose exact optimal first control is u₀* = −0.9042. Each sample is the plan plus noise of size √(λ/2r), the passive noise of Chapter 17, and its weight is e^(−S/λ) with S its cost less the control cost of its own noise, which makes the weights importance weights for the tilt e^(−cost/λ), a Gaussian whose mean is the exact optimum. At the defaults K = 128 and λ = 1, the median relative error of one update from the zero plan over 50 seeds is 0.352, and five updates, each warm-started from the last mean, bring it to 0.130. At K = 1024 the two medians are 0.095 and 0.019, and one update with 2¹⁷ samples lands within 1% of u₀*. Slide λ to 0.1: the weights collapse onto the best sample (an effective sample size of 1.0), and one update stays on average 0.66 of the way back toward the starting plan, while five updates at K = 1024 still reach 0.020. Slide λ to 10: the bias falls to 0.03, and the spread takes over, a median of 0.248 at K = 128.

18.6Four ways to see it

Model predictive control is receding-horizon feedback, lookahead on an approximate value, sampling from a tilted distribution over plans, and search with a learned model.

  1. 1Receding-horizon controlprocess control

    Each plan is an open-loop optimization that can carry hard limits on states and controls, and replanning from the measured state makes the sequence of plans a feedback law. The terminal cost decides whether that law is stable (Figure 18.2).

  2. 1 → 2If the terminal cost were the true cost still to come, the plan's first control would be the optimal one for every \(H\), so the receding-horizon policy is a greedy policy with respect to the plan's value, and (18.3) prices an error in the terminal cost.

  3. 2Lookahead and rolloutdynamic programming

    An \(H\)-step lookahead on an approximate value is a policy-improvement step, which Bertsekas reads as one step of Newton's method on Bellman's equation started from \(T^{H-1}V_f\), and rollout with a base policy as the terminal cost improves on that policy. In the toy of Section 18.2, the three-step policy's push \(-1.5\,x\), used forever, costs \(4.333\,x^2\). A one-step plan with that cost as its terminal price pushes \(-1.625\,x\), which costs \(4.2364\,x^2\), within 0.0003 of the best possible \(4.2361\,x^2\): the base policy was 0.097 above the best, and one Newton step cut the gap more than three hundredfold.

  4. 2 → 3Add a penalty \(\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}\) for moving the plan's distribution away from a base distribution of control noise. The best distribution over whole plans is then the tilt (18.4), which can be sampled instead of optimized.

  5. 3Planning as inferencesampling

    MPPI and annealed samplers such as DIAL-MPC draw plans, weight them by \(e^{-\text{cost}/\lambda}\), and average, and the cross-entropy method keeps the cheapest fraction of the plans and refits its proposal to them (Figure 18.3). On the linearly solvable problems of Chapter 17 the weighted average estimates the optimal control.

  6. 2 → 4Learn the dynamics \(f\) and the terminal value \(V_f\) from data, and search over actions with them. The plan's horizon then covers only what the learned model predicts well, and the value carries the rest.

  7. 4Search with a learned modelreinforcement learning

    PETS, TD-MPC, and MuZero plan through learned models at decision time, Dreamer trains its policy on rollouts imagined in one, and AlphaZero's tree search is lookahead with a learned value and a learned prior over moves.

18.7Where it breaks and what is open

The theorems assume that the plan's model is the plant. With a learned model, each predicted step adds error, and in unstable or chaotic dynamics the errors compound at the rate of the largest Lyapunov exponent, as in Chapter 12. A longer horizon shrinks the error of the terminal cost, which enters (18.3) through \(\gamma^H \varepsilon\), and adds model error, which grows with \(H\), so when the model overstates how unstable the system is, the closed-loop cost falls with the horizon and then rises again, and the best horizon is finite (Figure 18.4). A model that understates it improves with every added step. The toy of Section 18.2 shows it. Suppose the model says the state grows by a factor 2.2 per step while the plant grows by 2, so a prediction \(k\) steps out is off by a factor \(1.1^k\), and the plans have no terminal cost. Derivation 18.1's recursion, with 2.2 in place of 2 and 4.84 in place of 4, gives the gains. Applied to the plant from \(x_0 = 1\), the one-step plan runs off as before, and the receding-horizon policy costs 11.6 at \(H = 2\), 4.28 at \(H = 3\), 4.45 at \(H = 4\), and 4.49 at every long horizon, against the best possible 4.24. Short plans pay for what they cannot see, long ones pay the full price of the wrong model, and three steps is the best horizon. Each plan must also be solved within one sampling period, which caps the horizon and the number of samples, and a limit on the state can leave a plan with no feasible solution from states the terminal set does not reach.

Figure 18.4Where it breaks: a horizon too long for the model

With a slightly wrong model the closed-loop cost of MPC falls with the horizon while truncation error dominates and rises again once the model's error compounds, so the best horizon is finite.

The true system is x⁺ = 1.05x + u + w with seeded disturbances w ~ N(0, 0.3²) and cost Σₜ (xₜ² + 40uₜ²) over 60 steps from x₀ = 2, averaged over 40 disturbance sequences that every horizon shares. MPC plans with the model a' = 1.05(1 + δ) and no terminal cost. With the true model the cost falls with H to the optimum, 89.66. At the default δ = 10% the model's 30-step prediction is off by a factor of 1.1³⁰ = 17.45. The cost bottoms out at H = 6, within 0.34% of optimal, and climbs to 108.46 at H = 30, 21% above optimal and above the cost at H = 5. The gains show why: a short horizon under-reacts, a long one converges to the wrong model's own gain 0.341 against the optimal 0.199, and near H = 6 the two errors cancel. Slide δ to 0 and the rise disappears. At δ = 20% the cost at H = 30 is 149.49, more than at H = 4.

  1. How far to trust a learned model. Choosing the horizon from the model's own estimate of its error, for example from the disagreement of an ensemble, is done by hand today. A rule that sets the horizon from measured model error and value error, in the spirit of (18.3), is open.
  2. Guarantees for sampling-based planners. MPPI and annealed samplers such as DIAL-MPC control legged robots in real time without the stability guarantee of Theorem 18.2. Conditions under which a planner with finitely many samples stays stable, given the effective sample size of its weights (Chapter 3), are open.
  3. Planning at test time for generative models. Lookahead decoding and tree search for language models plan with a learned value as the terminal cost. When planning beats sampling, given that the most probable continuation is atypical (Chapter 10), and how the horizon should scale with the quality of the value, are open.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 18.1 Model predictive control

    • A state triples every step unless pushed, x' = 3x + u, and each step costs x² + u². The controller plans H steps ahead with no terminal cost, applies the first push, and plans again from where the state lands.
    • What does the closed loop multiply x by each step for H = 1 to 5, and what is the shortest horizon that brings the state to rest?
    Answer
    multipliers(5)      # (3.0, 1.5, 0.461538, 0.312, 0.298092)
shortest_stable()   # 3

  2. Exercise 18.2 A terminal cost that stabilizes

    • The same plant, x' = 3x + u with cost x² + u² a step, but every plan now ends in V_f(x) = 10x², the cost of pushing straight to 0 (u = −3x pays x² + 9x², and then nothing).
    • Check the condition of Theorem 18.2 for V_f. What does the loop multiply x by for H = 1, 2 and 3, and what does the H = 1 loop cost in total from x = 1, against the optimum?
    Answer
    multipliers(10.0, 3)   # (0.272727, 0.294643, 0.296558)
loop_cost(10.0, 1)     # 9.116071

  3. Exercise 18.3 Lookahead on a wrong value

    • A robot on cells 0 to 4 of a corridor steps left, steps right or stays, with costs discounted by γ = 0.9. Every step costs 1, a move costs 0.5 more, and staying on the charger at cell 4 is free.
    • Each H-step plan ends in a learned value off by ε = 0.5, V_f(x) = V*(x) + 0.5·(−1)^x. What is the worst loss of the lookahead policy, max over x of J^π(x) − V*(x), for H = 1, 4 and 5, against the bound (18.3)?
    Answer
    worst_loss(1)   # 8.5
worst_loss(4)   # 4.8415
worst_loss(5)   # 0.0

  4. Exercise 18.4 MPPI on an LQ problem

    • A plant x' = 1.2x + u starts at x = 1. A plan is U = (u_0, …, u_7), and its cost is S(U) = Σ_{k<8}(x_k² + u_k²) + x_8². MPPI samples plans with each u_k ~ N(0, 1), the p_0 of Proposition 18.4.
    • The tilted distribution (18.4) is Gaussian, so compute it exactly. What first push does its mean give at λ = 1 and at λ = 10, against the plan's own optimum, and what fraction of many samples is effective at each λ?
    Answer
    mppi(1.0)           # (-0.727488, 0.002863)
mppi(10.0)          # (-0.535716, 0.173903)
best_first_push()   # -0.793527

  5. Exercise 18.5 Horizon with a wrong model

    • The plant is x' = 3x + u with cost x² + u², but the planner's model says x' = 3.3x + u, 10% too unstable. Plans of H steps have no terminal cost, and each first push is applied to the true plant.
    • What does the loop truly cost from x = 1 at H = 3, 4 and 40, and which horizon is best? What if the model says 2.7 instead?
    Answer
    loop_costs(3.3, (3, 4, 40))   # (9.352947, 10.068696, 10.154123)
loop_costs(2.7, (3, 4, 40))   # (15.056316, 11.088334, 10.832723)
best_horizon(3.3)             # 3

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 18.1Fibonacci gains and the golden ratio

    For \(x_{t+1} = 2x_t + u_t\) with cost \(x^2 + u^2\) per step and no terminal cost, let \(P_k x^2\) be the least cost of \(k\) steps. Show that \(P_{k+1} = 1 + 4P_k/(1 + P_k)\) with \(P_0 = 0\), that the receding-horizon gain for horizon \(H\) is \(2P_{H-1}/(1 + P_{H-1})\), and compute the gains for \(H = 1\) to 5 and their limit. What gain does the terminal cost \(V_f = P_\infty x^2\) give for \(H = 1\)?

    Solution

    One more step costs \(\min_u\{x^2 + u^2 + P_k(2x + u)^2\}\), minimized at \(u = -2P_k x/(1 + P_k)\), where the cost is \(x^2 + 4P_k x^2/(1 + P_k)\). So \(P_0, P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 = 0, 1, 3, 4, 4.2\), and the first push of an \(H\)-step plan uses the value of the \(H - 1\) steps after it, which gives the gains

    \[ 0, \quad 1, \quad \tfrac32, \quad \tfrac85, \quad \tfrac{21}{13}, \qquad \text{closed loop } 2 - \text{gain} = 2, \ 1, \ \tfrac12, \ \tfrac25, \ \tfrac{5}{13}. \]

    The gains are ratios of Fibonacci numbers. The fixed point \(P_\infty = 1 + 4P_\infty/(1 + P_\infty)\) solves \(P^2 - 4P - 1 = 0\), so \(P_\infty = 2 + \sqrt 5 = 4.236\), and its gain is \(2P_\infty/(1 + P_\infty) = (1 + \sqrt 5)/2 = 1.618\), the golden ratio. With \(V_f = P_\infty x^2\) the one-step plan already minimizes \(x^2 + u^2 + P_\infty(2x + u)^2\), whose gain is the same 1.618, as Bellman's equation \(V^* = TV^*\) gives directly: a plan that ends in the true cost still to come picks the optimal first control for every \(H\). This is the \(\varepsilon = 0\) case of Proposition 18.3, which needs no discount.

  2. Derivation 18.2Lookahead on a wrong value

    Prove (18.3) from the contraction of Chapter 4, and evaluate the bound for \(\gamma = 0.9\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), and \(H = 1, 5, 20\). How long must the horizon be to bring the bound below 0.5?

    Solution

    The proof is the chain in Section 18.4: greedy with respect to \(U\) loses at most \(2\gamma\|U - V^*\|/(1 - \gamma)\), and \(H - 1\) applications of \(T\) shrink the terminal error by \(\gamma^{H-1}\).

    \[ \frac{2\gamma^H \varepsilon}{1 - \gamma} = 20 \cdot 0.9^H = 18.0, \ \ 11.8, \ \ 2.43 \quad \text{for } H = 1, 5, 20. \]

    The bound falls below 0.5 when \(0.9^H \lt 0.025\), that is \(H \ge 36\). Each step of lookahead buys a factor \(\gamma\), so a value twice as accurate saves \(\log 2/\log(1/0.9) \approx 6.6\) steps of planning.

Project. On a pendulum swing-up with a dynamics model learned from 2000 random transitions, run MPPI with horizons from 5 to 60 steps, with and without a learned value as the terminal cost. Report the closed-loop cost against the horizon, the horizon where it is lowest in each case, and how far a learned terminal value moves it.

Appendix A: Prerequisites

The chapters use seven tools without stopping to build them. Each is stated here with a short reason it holds, the chapters that use it, and where to learn it properly.

  1. A.1Itô's lemma and the generator

    For \(dX_t = b(X_t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t)\, dW_t\) in \(\mathbb R^d\) and a smooth \(\varphi\),

    \[ d\varphi(X_t) = \underbrace{\Big( b \cdot \nabla \varphi + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}\big(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 \varphi\big) \Big)}_{\mathcal L \varphi}\, dt + \nabla\varphi^\top \sigma\, dW_t. \]

    The second-order term appears because \((dW)^2 = dt\): a Taylor expansion to second order keeps \(\tfrac12 \nabla^2\varphi\) against the squared increment, whose mean is of order \(dt\). Taking expectations, \(\tfrac{d}{dt}\mathbb E\,\varphi(X_t) = \mathbb E\,\mathcal L\varphi(X_t)\), and moving \(\mathcal L\) onto the density gives the Fokker-Planck equation \(\partial_t p = \mathcal L^* p\). The function \(h(t, x) = \mathbb E[g(X_T) \mid X_t = x]\) solves the backward Kolmogorov equation \(\partial_t h + \mathcal L h = 0\) with \(h(T, \cdot) = g\), because \(h(t, X_t)\) is a martingale and its \(dt\) term must vanish.

    Used in Chapters 1 (the heat equation), 3 (Girsanov, the h-transform, Cole-Hopf), 5 (Fokker-Planck), 9, 15 (the generator of a diffusion), 16 (Itô integrals are martingales), and 17 (the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation). Learn it in Øksendal, Stochastic Differential Equations (Springer, 6th edition, 2003), Chapter 4 and Sections 7.3 and 8.1.

  2. A.2The Legendre transform

    The convex conjugate of \(f\) is \(f^*(y) = \sup_x \{\langle x, y\rangle - f(x)\}\). It is convex whatever \(f\) is, and for a closed convex \(f\) the transform inverts itself, \(f^{**} = f\) (Fenchel-Moreau). Geometrically, \(-f^*(y)\) is the intercept of the tangent to \(f\) with slope \(y\), so \(f^*\) lists the tangent lines and \(f\) is their upper envelope. Where both are differentiable, \(\nabla f\) and \(\nabla f^*\) are inverse maps.

    Used in Chapters 2 (the tilt: \(\log \mathbb E_p e^f\) and KL are conjugate), 5 (dual potentials and Brenier's convex function), 6 (Bregman divergences), and 8 (FTRL). Learn it in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (Cambridge University Press, 2004), Section 3.3.

  3. A.3Absolute continuity and the Radon-Nikodym derivative

    \(P\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(Q\), written \(P \ll Q\), if \(Q(A) = 0\) implies \(P(A) = 0\). The Radon-Nikodym theorem says that then, for \(\sigma\)-finite measures, there is a density \(dP/dQ \ge 0\) with \(P(A) = \int_A \frac{dP}{dQ}\, dQ\) for every event \(A\), unique up to \(Q\)-null sets. Without absolute continuity no reweighting exists, and \(\mathrm{KL}(P \,\|\, Q) = \mathbb E_P \log \frac{dP}{dQ}\) is infinite. Brownian motions with different noise levels are mutually singular, because the quadratic variation of a path reveals \(\sigma\), which is why Girsanov's theorem changes only the drift.

    Used in Chapters 2, 3 (throughout), and 5. Learn it in Williams, Probability with Martingales (Cambridge University Press, 1991), Section 14.13.

  4. A.4The continuity equation

    If particles move with velocity \(v_t(x)\), their density satisfies \(\partial_t \rho + \nabla\cdot(\rho v) = 0\): the mass in a region changes only by the flux through its boundary. To derive it, follow a test function along the particles, \(\tfrac{d}{dt}\int \varphi\, \rho_t = \int \nabla\varphi \cdot v_t\, \rho_t\), and integrate by parts. Any equation of the form \(\partial_t \rho = \nabla\cdot(\cdots)\) can be read this way, which is how a diffusion becomes a deterministic flow.

    Used in Chapters 1 (the probability-flow ODE), 5 (Benamou-Brenier and the gradient-flow picture), and 9 (free-energy dissipation). Learn it in Santambrogio, Optimal Transport for Applied Mathematicians (Birkhäuser, 2015), Sections 4.1.2 and 5.3, with gradient flows in Chapter 8.

  5. A.5Lagrange multipliers and the KKT conditions

    To minimize \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x) \le 0\) and \(h_j(x) = 0\), a regular optimum satisfies \(\nabla f + \sum_i \lambda_i \nabla g_i + \sum_j \nu_j \nabla h_j = 0\) with \(\lambda_i \ge 0\) and \(\lambda_i g_i(x) = 0\). The multipliers price the constraints: each is the rate at which the optimal value changes as its constraint loosens. For a convex problem with a strictly feasible point (Slater's condition), these conditions are also sufficient, and the multipliers solve the dual problem.

    Used in Chapters 2 (maximum entropy, where the multiplier is an inverse temperature), 5 (Sinkhorn's form and the dual potentials), 6 (the steepest step (6.1)), 8 (the minimax theorem as linear-programming duality), and 12 (costates as multipliers). Learn it in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (Cambridge University Press, 2004), Section 5.5.3.

  6. A.6Hoeffding's lemma

    If \(X \in [a, b]\) almost surely, then \(\log \mathbb E\, e^{s(X - \mathbb E X)} \le s^2 (b - a)^2 / 8\) for every real \(s\). Proof: the log of the moment generating function, \(\psi(s)\), has \(\psi(0) = \psi'(0) = 0\), and \(\psi''(s)\) is the variance of \(X\) under the tilt \(e^{sX}\) (Chapter 2), which is at most \((b - a)^2/4\) for a variable confined to \([a, b]\). Taylor's theorem finishes it. Combined with Markov's inequality applied to \(e^{s \sum_i X_i}\), it gives Hoeffding's inequality, \(P\big(\bar X - \mu \ge t\big) \le e^{-2 n t^2/(b - a)^2}\).

    Used in Chapters 8 (Hedge's bound), 13 (Hoeffding's inequality), and 16 (Azuma's inequality). Learn it in Boucheron, Lugosi, and Massart, Concentration Inequalities (Oxford University Press, 2013), Section 2.6.

  7. A.7The discrete Fourier transform

    \(\hat x_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\, e^{-2\pi i k n / N}\), with inverse \(x_n = \frac1N \sum_k \hat x_k\, e^{2\pi i k n/N}\). It turns circular convolution into multiplication, \(\widehat{c * x}_k = \hat c_k\, \hat x_k\), keeps energy up to a factor, \(\sum_k |\hat x_k|^2 = N \sum_n |x_n|^2\) (Parseval), and the fast Fourier transform computes it in \(O(N \log N)\) operations. Frequencies \(k\) and \(k + N\) are the same on \(N\) points, which is aliasing.

    Used in Chapters 7 (throughout), 1 (the heat equation damps high frequencies first), and the deck's card on multiplying large numbers. Learn it in Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge Press, 5th edition, 2016), Section 9.3.

Appendix B: Ideas that almost made the book

  • Stein's identity. For a standard Gaussian \(X\), \(\mathbb E[f'(X)] = \mathbb E[X f(X)]\), and this characterizes the Gaussian. It gives Stein's unbiased risk estimate, Stein's method for normal approximation, and Stein variational gradient descent, and Tweedie's formula in Chapter 1 rests on the same Gaussian fact, \(\varphi'(z) = -z\,\varphi(z)\). Its reach stays mostly inside probability, so it ranked below the eighteen.
  • The implicit function theorem. If \(F(x, \theta) = 0\) defines \(x(\theta)\), then \(\partial_\theta x = -(\partial_x F)^{-1}\partial_\theta F\), which differentiates through fixed points, equilibria, and the solutions of inner optimizations. Chapter 12's exercise on an equilibrium layer derives it as the adjoint of a fixed point, so it lives there instead of in a chapter of its own.
  • Bayesian filtering. Predict the next state, then correct the prediction by Bayes' rule when a measurement arrives: the Kalman filter, particle filters, the forward algorithm of hidden Markov models, data assimilation in weather forecasting, and the belief state of a world model. Its linear case is the dual of Chapter 17's Riccati equation and its sampling case, sequential Monte Carlo, is the importance sampling of Chapter 3 applied one step at a time, so it ranked below as a chapter of its own.
  • Hamiltonian dynamics. Give each coordinate a momentum and follow dynamics that conserve an energy: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, symplectic integrators, momentum in optimization, and volume-preserving normalizing flows. Chapter 7 derives its conservation laws and Chapter 9 its damped version, which is why it ranked below.
  • The graph Laplacian. The heat equation on a graph: spectral clustering, diffusion maps, Laplacian eigenmaps, message passing in graph neural networks, and the random walk of PageRank. Chapters 1, 4, and 7 cover its continuous, iterative, and Fourier sides.

Every figure computes its idea in the page on a toy, and the numbers in captions come from the figures' own math at the settings each caption names. The failure figure in each chapter's "Where it breaks" section computes the failure on a toy in the same way. The exercises come from a practice deck whose checker runs every answer. Claude wrote the book at Jai Sharma's direction, and separate Claude agents audited its mathematics and citations.
